items.title: What an AI Agent Can Actually Do: Running a Real Instagram Workflow
items.summary: Most AI-agent conversations end too early. We ask whether an agent can write a caption, generate an image, or answer a comment. Those are useful capabilities, but they are not a working system. The harder question is this: Can an agent own a repeatable slice of real operations without turning every step into a manual handoff? We are testing that question with Muse . Muse is helping run a live Instagram workflow for MoneySecrets , a rare-coin and money-history account. The account has passed 100 followers, 97 posts, and more than 20K views in the past 30 days. Those numbers are not the point; the point is that the work is happening in the open, on a real account, with a real operating loop. What Muse can own Muse does not just generate a one-off post. It can participate across the full content workflow: Turn a content direction into a queue of ideas Given the topic, audience, and brand rules, it develops post angles instead of waiting for a line-by-line prompt. Create the content package It writes captions, proposes hooks, creates or directs cover art, and keeps the visual language consistent with the account. Prepare publishing work It formats posts, keeps track of the publishing queue, and can execute routine publishing steps when the workflow allows it. Handle routine engagement It can monitor comments, draft replies, and reply within a defined policy. Ambiguous, sensitive, or high-stakes interactions stay with a human. Leave an operational trail The useful output is not only the post. The agent can record what was published, what it was trying to achieve, what performed, and what needs attention next. The agent is not the strategy A working agent should not be a black box with permission to do anything. For this type of workflow, people still own: brand direction and content strategy permissions and approval boundaries exceptions, edge cases, and reputation-sensitive replies reviewing outcomes and changing the operating rules Muse owns the repeatable execution inside those guardrails. That distinction matters. “Autonomous” should not mean “unaccountable.” It should mean the agent can move routine work forward without requiring a human to repeat the same instructions every day. What we are learning Real-world operation exposes the gaps that demos hide: A vague brief creates vague output. Brand rules need to be explicit and reusable. Publishing actions need clear permission boundaries. Comments cannot all be treated the same. A content workflow improves when the agent can learn from performance data, not just produce more material. This is why we are testing on a real account instead of claiming success from a polished demo. The goal is to find the boundary between work Muse can reliably own today and the moments where human judgment should stay in the loop. You can follow the experiment and Muse's public activity on Instagram at @youincomics . What would you let an agent own first: the content queue, creative production, publishing, engagement, or reporting?

items.title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
items.summary: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room. People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies. Read full article Comments

items.title: John Deere built an AI assistant to stop farmers from drowning in decades of field data
items.summary: John Deere announced its new AI assistant at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images John Deere's AI assistant, unveiled in September, helps farmers analyze data quickly. JD is embedded in John Deere's Operations Center, a digital farm management system. Farmers are warming to AI, but accuracy and data privacy remain concerns. Farmers have more data than ever about their fields, equipment, and crops. But turning it into a decision could take weeks. John Deere says its new AI assistant, JD, can do it in minutes. The agricultural manufacturing company announced the tool in September at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. JD is integrated within John Deere's Operations Center, which is a digital farm management system that connects farmers' field and machine data into one platform. Farmers can ask JD questions on their mobile devices, such as the best time to harvest based on past trends, or which sprayer covers the most acres per hour. Melissa Neuendorf, the principal product manager for customer AI solutions at John Deere, told Business Insider that JD came about because farmers consistently said they were struggling to manage their abundant data. "We're now at a point where farmers have so much data that they have a difficult time finding the insights manually themselves," Neuendorf said. While smaller agricultural tech companies such as OneSoil, VisorPro, Arable, and AgZen are developing generative AI tools to give insights on specific equipment or crop metrics, Deere is among the first major agricultural-equipment makers to put a large language model AI assistant directly inside a platform that combines farmers' field, machine, and operational data. JD's launch shows how generative AI is becoming a central part of crop management. "Prior to John Deere's announcement, this didn't exist in the industry," said Matt Darr, a professor in the agricultural and biosystems engineering department at Iowa State University, who was in the room when Deere announced JD. Why farmers are considering AI tools more than ever Farmers have been collecting data for decades. But now, modern farm equipment is outfitted with additional technology and sensors, creating large volumes of data that are difficult to keep up with. It can be stressful for farmers who must also navigate tight margins, unpredictable weather , and limited planting windows. Plus, "most farmers aren't data scientists on the side," Darr said. Neuendorf said dissecting vast datasets is complex and time-consuming, sometimes requiring weeks. That's where AI can help farmers: "AI provides them the capability to do a lot of that analysis in minutes," she said. Before coming up with JD, Deere launched an AI tool last August that allowed farmers to ask questions in natural language about Deere's help documentation and operator manuals. This replaced the manual task of farmers flipping through pages of operator manuals. The tool received positive feedback, prompting Deere to broaden its application and launch JD to answer specific questions on the spot. Farmers can input data into the Operations Center from non-John Deere equipment if they use machinery from other manufacturers. Then, if they query JD, it can analyze all of that data to deliver answers. The Operations Center and JD are free to use, Neuendorf said. The AI assistant is available through an early access program, in which interested customers sign up for a waitlist and are considered for participation. John Deere will make JD broadly available in mid-November Neuendorf told Business Insider that the feedback from farmers so far has been positive. Neuendorf said she recently spoke to a farmer who was driving past a field and noticed it had lower weed pressure, or fewer weeds present, than other fields. Through JD, the farmer was able to open John Deere's mobile app right away, ask the assistant about previous years, and understand how he managed the field differently. Winning farmer trust in AI technology A McKinsey global survey of 5,500 farmers, published in September, found that 72% expect generative AI to impact operations within five years, but only 17% use the tech right now. One reason only a minority of farmers use AI is because they're worried about data privacy and how their information could impact commodity prices, Darr said. "These are competitive businesses," Darr added. "How information is used can influence global markets and what happens to global commodity pricing." John Deere said in its release announcing JD that it doesn't sell farm data or use it for agriculture commodity trading or speculation. Katya Kheistver, the chief product and operating officer of OneSoil, an agricultural technology company, said farmers won't trust AI if it delivers generic advice rather than insights tied to specific, real field data. Farmers often start their use of AI by checking the tech's outputs against what they already know. The farmer "watches whether the answer lines up with reality," and if it does so consistently, trust grows, Kheistver said. The stakes are high if farmers make decisions based on AI-generated answers because they have "one chance a year to grow a crop," Darr said. They need to be able to trust that an AI tool is accurate. JD meshes high-quality datasets with advanced LLMs, Darr added, which sets the AI tool apart and promises a high degree of accuracy. Neuendorf said JD is configured to notify farmers when field data is missing, rather than making inaccurate assumptions or generating false advice. This configuration also encourages farmers to input additional data, so JD can derive more insights and help farmers "make better decisions for the next season," Neuendorf said. The Operations Center and JD are free to use, Neuendorf said. The AI assistant is available through an early access program, in which interested customers sign up for a waitlist and are considered for participation. John Deere will make JD broadly available in mid-November

Neuendorf told Business Insider that the feedback from farmers so far has been positive.

Neuendorf said she recently spoke to a farmer who was driving past a field and noticed it had lower weed pressure, or fewer weeds present, than other fields. Through JD, the farmer was able to open John Deere's mobile app right away, ask the assistant about previous years, and understand how he managed the field differently.

Winning farmer trust in AI technology

A McKinsey global survey of 5,500 farmers, published in September, found that 72% expect generative AI to impact operations within five years, but only 17% use the tech right now.

One reason only a minority of farmers use AI is because they're worried about data privacy and how their information could impact commodity prices, Darr said.

"These are competitive businesses," Darr added. "How information is used can influence global markets and what happens to global commodity pricing."

John Deere said in its release announcing JD that it doesn't sell farm data or use it for agriculture commodity trading or speculation.

Katya Kheistver, the chief product and operating officer of OneSoil, an agricultural technology company, said farmers won't trust AI if it delivers generic advice rather than insights tied to specific, real field data. Farmers often start their use of AI by checking the tech's outputs against what they already know. The farmer "watches whether the answer lines up with reality," and if it does so consistently, trust grows, Kheistver said.

The stakes are high if farmers make decisions based on AI-generated answers because they have "one chance a year to grow a crop," Darr said. They need to be able to trust that an AI tool is accurate.

JD meshes high-quality datasets with advanced LLMs, Darr added, which sets the AI tool apart and promises a high degree of accuracy.

Neuendorf said JD is configured to notify farmers when field data is missing, rather than making inaccurate assumptions or generating false advice.

This configuration also encourages farmers to input additional data, so JD can derive more insights and help farmers "make better decisions for the next season," Neuendorf said.

items.title: Canva’s new design model doesn’t generate images. It writes code to edit them.
items.summary: Australian graphic design software company Canva took the wraps off Canva Brush last week, its new vision-language model for designers. Brush is an editing model rather than an image generator: a vision-language model that understands the intent behind a designer’s project and interprets design change requests. Available to Canva Pro users, Canva says Brush reads a design’s content and structure, writes and executes small pieces of code to make changes, then checks its own result. Canva Brush arrived a week after Canva’s first in-house image-generation model, Canva Craft , which launched on October 22. Design is complex; design editing is even more complex According to a Canva launch blog, generating high-quality designs is one of the biggest challenges for AI models, but “editing them is even more complex” today. This is because the model needs to understand what a designer wants to change, how the design is structured, and importantly, what needs to stay exactly as it is. Otherwise, a simple edit request can result in a “whole bunch of changes” nobody asked for. In a prompt such as, “Make me a 3-page pitch deck for my bakery with Art Nouveau visuals and backgrounds,” an agent has to make a long chain of decisions. It needs to plan a narrative across pages, generate and place text, select imagery, and keep typography, color, and spacing consistent from the first page to the last. Each decision connects to the next, and small missteps can add up to a design that’s off-brand or feels out of kilter. “That’s exactly the challenge we’ve built Brush to solve. Rather than treating design as a series of isolated decisions, Brush can continually evaluate and improve its work, helping [users] take an idea from a rough sketch to a polished design that’s ready to share. Behind the scenes, it uses an agentic loop that writes and runs code to adjust design elements, and can then inspect what’s happening on the page to guide its next step,” stated Canva. “Bounded problems – for well-defined, specific tasks – are where small specialized models have been quietly beating large general ones for years.” This is not a frontier lab challenge; it’s smarter than that The question then is: can an art- and design-focused AI model lab from down under Australia challenge the frontier model behemoths on complex image design editing tasks over the long term? Enterprise AI architect & founder of Besk Tech , Vladimir Beskorovainyi , tells The New Stack that this question is “posed in the wrong frame” both metaphorically and literally. “Canva is not challenging frontier models; it is in fact declining to compete with them,” Beskorovainyi says. “A model that reads how a design is assembled (and edits it) is solving a bounded problem (one with well-defined specific tasks with clear parameters and limited scope), and bounded problems are where small specialized models have been quietly beating large general ones for years.” Urging us to look beyond the capabilities of the Canva Brush model and focus more directly on the cost per edit, Beskorovainyi thinks that “ the moat here is the artifact, not the weights”, primarily, Canva can train on how real designs are actually put together. “A frontier lab can match the base processing capability of a tool like Canva Brush; the training signal is the harder thing to match, because it comes from holding the designs,” asserts Beskorovainyi. “Verticalization wins wherever the data is a by-product of the product rather than something you have to go and buy. That is the part most model developers still underestimate.” Design expertise, plus anonymized insights Brush started by drawing from an unspecified open-weights model, which Canva then post-trained on real design and editing tasks, using a combination of design expertise and anonymized insights from people who opted in to help improve Canva AI. As a result, it understands not only what a finished result looks like, but also the steps needed to get there. “We combined post-training with large-scale reinforcement learning, giving the model opportunities to work through complete design and editing tasks, learn from what worked, and continually shape its future behavior,” the company notes in its announcement. “A beautiful edit can still be an expensive proofreading assignment.” Sensitive to designers’ real-world needs as they’re urged to put down their Rotring pens and Pantone color guides and adopt agentically driven toolsets, many in the marcoms industry have opinions on these new services. Founder of Dr. Rissy’s Writing & Marketing, Dr. Morissa Schwartz , tells The New Stack that she has used many automation tools over the years, hasn’t yet used Canva Brush, but knows what she would do if she did. “Here is the marketing and publishing test I would put it through. An AI design editor earns its keep when a ‘change this headline’ command still leaves the price, disclaimer, and layout intact,” Schwartz explains. “Canva’s opportunity is to make those small, frequent revisions dependable enough that a marketing team spends less time checking what else moved.” She notes that she would further test Brush against a general-purpose model on the same approved design and measure unintended changes, legibility and time to human approval, rather than image-generation rankings. “A beautiful edit can still be an expensive proofreading assignment,” adds Schwartz. “Frontier models know the Internet; Canva knows what hundreds of millions of people actually do with a slide deck. In a vertical, taste and distribution beat parameter count.” Canva is “out-niching” the frontier labs Co-founder and CTO of deep-tech venture studio The Capital Index , Rodion Sorokin , tells The New Stack that he agrees with the sentiment expressed thus far and says “Canva isn’t trying to out-muscle the frontier labs; it’s out-niching them” in real terms. “Brush started from an open-weights model and was trained with reinforcement learning against what Canva’s own designers call good design , a playbook any well-funded vertical player can now copy,” Sorokin says. “Frontier models know the Internet; Canva knows what hundreds of millions of people actually do with a slide deck. In a vertical, taste and distribution beat parameter count.” “The clever bit is that Brush doesn’t paint pixels: it reads the layers, writes small pieces of code to change them and checks its own work, which is how a designer edits, not how an image generator guesses. Canva says that makes it up to 69% faster than its previous design agent at 46% lower cost per task. If that holds up outside a launch blog, specialized models will win on unit economics, not just quality: generation becomes the commodity, and editing becomes the business,” adds Sorokin. AI model benchmarking platform ranking According to Canva, Craft (not Brush) debuted as the fourth-ranked model on crowdsourced benchmarking platform Design Arena , behind OpenAI’s precision-focused image generation and editing model GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst , the speed-focused image generation model GPT Image 2.5 Flare , and GPT Image 2 . Canva Research’s in-house 160-person AI lab developed both Canva Craft and the new Canva Brush models. Canva’s speed and cost figures for Brush are self-reported and compare it with the company’s previous design agent, not with frontier models. Canva has stated that everything Canva Brush creates is fully editable. Every element, from the text and imagery to the colors, layouts, and finer details, remains available for designers to edit, manipulate, and rearrange however they like. The organization also confirmed that this release represents the first version of Brush, and “there’s plenty more to come,” as the company is already working on the ability to reference attachments, improvements to how Brush handles image-heavy layouts, and Brand Kit support in the future.

That is the part most model developers still underestimate.”

Brush started by drawing from an unspecified open-weights model, which Canva then post-trained on real design and editing tasks, using a combination of design expertise and anonymized insights from people who opted in to help improve Canva AI. As a result, it understands not only what a finished result looks like, but also the steps needed to get there.

An AI design editor earns its keep when a ‘change this headline’ command still leaves the price, disclaimer, and layout intact,” Schwartz explains. “Canva’s opportunity is to make those small, frequent revisions dependable enough that a marketing team spends less time checking what else moved.”

She notes that she would further test Brush against a general-purpose model on the same approved design and measure unintended changes, legibility and time to human approval, rather than image-generation rankings. 

“A beautiful edit can still be an expensive proofreading assignment,” adds Schwartz.

“Frontier models know the Internet; Canva knows what hundreds of millions of people actually do with a slide deck. In a vertical, taste and distribution beat parameter count.”

Canva is “out-niching” the frontier labs

Co-founder and CTO of deep-tech venture studio The Capital Index, Rodion Sorokin, tells The New Stack that he agrees with the sentiment expressed thus far and says “Canva isn’t trying to out-muscle the frontier labs; it’s out-niching them” in real terms.

items.title: Meta Is Refusing to Remove AI-Generated Videos of Coaches Inappropriately Touching Young Athletes When Users Report Them
items.summary: Content warning: this story includes descriptions and censored AI-generated images of sexual abuse. Facebook is hosting a large number of accounts dedicated to AI-generated content depicting coaches inappropriately touching young female athletes — and Meta isn’t taking them down, even when they’re directly reported by users. In the videos the accounts share, the coaches are older men. They’re shown in gyms and dance studios, with their hands on leotard-wearing athletes practicing gymnastics, ballet, and yoga. All the young athletes are women — or girls. Though precise ages aren’t specified, some look as young as teenagers, at times shown with braces on their teeth. In the AI-generated clips, which are nearly photorealistic, the athletes are often portrayed sweating profusely and breathing suggestively. The coaches run their hands over their lower backs and inner thighs as they stretch or practice poses, caressing and squeezing their bodies, and sometimes patting them on the buttocks or chest. In some videos, the older authority figures are shown touching the girls’ genitals over their outfits. More creepy videos show athletes sitting in a coach’s lap, or coaches kissing them on the mouth. The AI-generated girls in the clips react as though the touching is normal, often smiling and giggling as the harmful behavior occurs. But the touching depicted in the videos isn’t normal. It ranges from unnecessary to inappropriate to obviously abusive, mirroring the kind of real-world sexual abuse and grooming that are rampant in the sports they depict and in women’s athletics writ large. “I do consider this abuse material. These images sexualize and normalize abusive interactions between coaches and young athletes within a sporting environment where significant power imbalances already exist,” Kim Shore, a gymnast and safe sport advocate who consults with Gymnasts for Change International, told Futurism after reviewing numerous accounts publishing the AI content. “What is particularly disturbing is how easily inappropriate or abusive conduct can be disguised as playful, affectionate or helpful coaching behavior. This reinforces some of the very narratives that have allowed abuse to flourish in sport for decades.” But according to Facebook’s moderation system, the disturbing clips don’t violate Meta’s standards. Using an ordinary Facebook account, we alerted the social media platform to ten different accounts publishing this kind of content, reporting them for adult content and sexual exploitation. A full week later, we received notices from Facebook that eight of the accounts were didn’t violate the site’s rules, and would not be removed from the platform. (Two of the accounts vanished, though it’s unclear whether that had anything to do with our reports.) “We use a combination of technology and human reviewers to process reports and identify content that goes against our Community Standards. To keep our review process as fair as possible, we use the same set of Community Standards to review all reports,” read each of the eight identical notifications. “We’ve taken a look and found that the page doesn’t go against our Community Standards.” “We understand that this might be upsetting,” they added, “so we recommend exploring the options available to control what you see.” Some of the clips — which can attract more than 100,000 views apiece — are thinly veiled as educational, insinuating that the predatory coaches are helping the girls’ perfect their technique. “Keep your hips square,” an instructor is shown telling a young-looking ballerina in one video as he moves his hands to her private parts. “I’m trying,” she replies coolly, without flinching. Other accounts make little effort to hide their prurient intent. One has published nearly 20 slightly-different versions of the same AI video, which depicts an elderly coach alone with a leotard-wearing gymnast who looks no older than a teenager. In the comments of each clip, the poster urges viewers to click a link marketing a “members only” channel on WhatsApp — another platform owned by Meta — for the “prettiest video call anytime.” Another account’s header image shows a male coach’s hand directly on the crotch of a young female gymnast doing a split-legged headstand. Asked about the gap between its response to an user on the platform versus a media inquiry, Meta defended its record on removing abusive material from its platform. “While there are times we miss things, we work hard to enforce our rules, which is shown by the fact that just last quarter, we proactively found and removed 98 percent of child endangerment posts before they were ever reported to us,” it said. One video served to us after Meta shared its statement showed more than 176,000 views just two days after it was posted. “I really enjoyed that session. I feel fresh and positive now,” a girl decked in a pink leotard and matching socks, standing on one leg and holding the other in the air, tells the camera as a gray-haired trainer pats her genitals. Content warning: this story includes descriptions and censored AI-generated images of sexual abuse.

Facebook is hosting a large number of accounts dedicated to AI-generated content depicting coaches inappropriately touching young female athletes — and Meta isn’t taking them down, even when they’re directly reported by users.

In the videos the accounts share, the coaches are older men. They’re shown in gyms and dance studios, with their hands on leotard-wearing athletes practicing gymnastics, ballet, and yoga. All the young athletes are women — or girls. Though precise ages aren’t specified, some look as young as teenagers, at times shown with braces on their teeth.

In the AI-generated clips, which are nearly photorealistic, the athletes are often portrayed sweating profusely and breathing suggestively. The coaches run their hands over their lower backs and inner thighs as they stretch or practice poses, caressing and squeezing their bodies, and sometimes patting them on the buttocks or chest. In some videos, the older authority figures are shown touching the girls’ genitals over their outfits. More creepy videos show athletes sitting in a coach’s lap, or coaches kissing them on the mouth.

The AI-generated girls in the clips react as though the touching is normal, often smiling and giggling as the harmful behavior occurs.

But the touching depicted in the videos isn’t normal. It ranges from unnecessary to inappropriate to obviously abusive, mirroring the kind of real-world sexual abuse and grooming that are rampant in the sports they depict and in women’s athletics writ large.

“I do consider this abuse material. These images sexualize and normalize abusive interactions between coaches and young athletes within a sporting environment where significant power imbalances already exist,” Kim Shore, a gymnast and safe sport advocate who consults with Gymnasts for Change International, told Futurism after reviewing numerous accounts publishing the AI content. “What is particularly disturbing is how easily inappropriate or abusive conduct can be disguised as playful, affectionate or helpful coaching behavior. This reinforces some of the very narratives that have allowed abuse to flourish in sport for decades.”

But according to Facebook’s moderation system, the disturbing clips don’t violate Meta’s standards.

Using an ordinary Facebook account, we alerted the social media platform to ten different accounts publishing this kind of content, reporting them for adult content and sexual exploitation. A full week later, we received notices from Facebook that eight of the accounts were didn’t violate the site’s rules, and would not be removed from the platform. (Two of the accounts vanished, though it’s unclear whether that had anything to do with our reports.)

“We use a combination of technology and human reviewers to process reports and identify content that goes against our Community Standards. To keep our review process as fair as possible, we use the same set of Community Standards to review all reports,” read each of the eight identical notifications. “We’ve taken a look and found that the page doesn’t go against our Community Standards.”

“We understand that this might be upsetting,” they added, “so we recommend exploring the options available to control what you see.”

Some of the clips — which can attract more than 100,000 views apiece — are thinly veiled as educational, insinuating that the predatory coaches are helping the girls’ perfect their technique.

“Keep your hips square,” an instructor is shown telling a young-looking ballerina in one video as he moves his hands to her private parts.

“I’m trying,” she replies coolly, without flinching.

Other accounts make little effort to hide their prurient intent. One has published nearly 20 slightly-different versions of the same AI video, which depicts an elderly coach alone with a leotard-wearing gymnast who looks no older than a teenager. In the comments of each clip, the poster urges viewers to click a link marketing a “members only” channel on WhatsApp — another platform owned by Meta — for the “prettiest video call anytime.” Another account’s header image shows a male coach’s hand directly on the crotch of a young female gymnast doing a split-legged headstand.

In its Community Guidelines for “Adult Nudity and Sexual Activity,” Meta claims to forbid content showing “impending sexual activity, as indicated by positions which suggest contact is about to be initiated between a person’s hand… with another person’s genitals or anus.” Under guidelines for “Adult Sexual Exploitation,” its guidelines claim to prohibit material in which a “person in the imagery is (near) nude, engaged in sexual activity or in a sexually suggestive pose (this includes digitally created or AI-generated imagery).”

Regarding “Child Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Nudity,” Meta claims to forbid “content (including photos, videos, real-world art, digital content, and verbal depictions) that sexualizes real or non-real children,” as well as “stimulation of genitals or anus, including when activity is imminent or not directly visible.”

After receiving the support messages stating that the AI videos didn’t violate Meta’s Community Standards, we reached out to Meta’s media relations team, sharing links to the accounts we’d reported and asked why the content didn’t breach the social media giant’s guidelines. Shortly after we reached out, we noticed that all of the pages had been removed, and several of the support messages we’d previously received had been updated with a new response.

“We removed the Page you reported,” read the new message. “We reviewed the Page and found that it goes against our Community Standards.”

In a statement, Meta told Futurism that “whether it’s real or AI-generated, content that depicts abuse or exploitation has no place on our platforms. We’ve removed these accounts for violating our policies.”

But it wasn’t until it was contacted by a journalist that Meta backtracked on its initial assessment that the pages didn’t violate its policies, a lapse that raises serious concerns about the company’s moderation practices and the effectiveness of the reporting policies available to everyday users. Why was this content held to a different standard when it was raised by a reporter, and not when it was flagged through official Facebook channels by a normal account holder?

Asked about the gap between its response to an user on the platform versus a media inquiry, Meta defended its record on removing abusive material from its platform.

“While there are times we miss things, we work hard to enforce our rules, which is shown by the fact that just last quarter, we proactively found and removed 98 percent of child endangerment posts before they were ever reported to us,” it said.

After we reported the abusive pages, Facebook’s recommendation algorithm started serving up many more similar AI videos of coaches inappropriately touching, kissing, and groping young athletes in the feed of the account we used to flag it. The implication is dark: that Meta has the tech it needs to identify the disturbing clips, but instead of using it to crack down on the content, it’s using it to recommend more of the material to users who have interacted with it.

The accounts often publish several near-identical AI videos per day, with some videos accumulating huge numbers of views. One video served to us after Meta shared its statement showed more than 176,000 views just two days after it was posted.

“I really enjoyed that session. I feel fresh and positive now,” a girl decked in a pink leotard and matching socks, standing on one leg and holding the other in the air, tells the camera as a gray-haired trainer pats her genitals. Hash tags in the video’s caption include “#ballettok,” “#ballerina,” and “#balletmemes.”

It’s hard to imagine that some of the videos aren’t being served by Meta’s algorithms to actual young athletes, raising the risk that they’ll see the grooming and abuse behavior normalized as they navigate the possibility of real-world exploitation.

“I’m extremely concerned that children who are exposed to this content will internalize the message that if something similar is happening to them, they have to endure it because it is normalized in similar environments… they will be forced to further suppress their innate wisdom that this type of contact with an adult is not okay,” Shore told us. “Sport already does this to children by normalizing physical discomfort like training on injuries. Young athletes are taught to trust their coaches, follow instructions and accept physical contact as part of training. These images reinforce the dangerous idea that inappropriate touching or sexualized behavior is simply part of the coach-athlete relationship and athletes should accept it, tolerate it or even be grateful for the attention.”

Shore added that one of her “greatest concerns” is that real-world predators could model behavior based on the abuse material proliferating on Facebook.

It risks giving adults who are already inclined to exploit their authority examples of how to disguise abusive conduct as legitimate coaching, affection or playfulness,” she said. “We need to recognize that this material doesn’t exist in isolation. It circulates within a sporting culture where athletes have historically been conditioned to comply with authority, where boundaries have too often been blurred, and where abuse has frequently been minimized or excused.”

items.title: Ruby on Rails creator has a warning for 'cantankerous' coders: Learn some people skills
items.summary: David Heinemeier Hansson said engineers will need to "learn some basic people skills" in the age of AI. LAT Images/Getty Images David Heinemeier Hansson said that AI agents will bring hard times for "cantankerous" engineers. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. Engineers on X chimed in to wave goodbye to engineers with bad attitudes. Don't be cantankerous. David Heinemeier Hansson has some advice for engineers as they adjust to AI. Often referred to as DHH, Hansson created the webapp framework Ruby on Rails and has fashioned himself into a software sage. On Monday, Hansson shared his prediction on X: "The age of agents is going to be amazing for most programmers, but it'll be hard times for the cantankerous ones." Hansson wrote that special abilities won't save those who are difficult to work with. That would be a dramatic shift in software engineering, where some so-called "cracked" coders can get away with large egos or social awkwardness. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. The prediction sparked a conversation among engineers about their social habits and professionalism. One pointed out the irony: agents "don't care how cantankerous you are," but your human coworkers do. One user wrote a eulogy to the "guy whose whole job security was 'only I know how this works.'" Dart cofounder Zack Swafford wrote that teams only tolerated bad attitudes because the staffers had "arcane tribal knowledge." Others questioned how new the change was. People skills have long been valuable, from networking your way into a job to landing that big promotion. "Been true in every company forever," one X user commented. "Skills get you hired, being easy to work with keeps you around. Agents just make it obvious faster." Hansson is committed to the future of AI coding. In September, he declared " pencils down " on handwritten code. Hansson explained that writing code was an "exceptional state," performed only when something went wrong with the AI-generated code. For some engineers, Hansson's post was a vocabulary lesson. "I had to search the definition of 'cantankerous,'" one engineer commented. "First time reading that word." For the record: cantankerous means bad-tempered and uncooperative. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Former Meta security chief says giving AI agents your financial logins is ‘totally insane’
items.summary: Alex Stamos is the chief security officer for the AI coding startup Cognition. Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile via Getty Images Meta's former security chief said that giving AI agents financial logins is "totally insane." People are giving agents like Muse and Instinct their entire 1Password vaults, Alex Stamos said. The dynamic has created a dilemma for banks as customers deploy bots to their accounts. It's plain nuts to hand over a personal AI agent the keys to your financial life, according to Meta's former security chief. Alex Stamos, now the chief security officer for the AI coding startup Cognition , called it "totally insane" that people are giving AI agent apps access to highly sensitive personal data. On a recent episode of the Big Technology Podcast, Stamos said people are giving agents like Meta's Muse and Spear Street Technology's Instinct their entire 1Password vaults, then asking them to "go handle my finances for me" or "go file my taxes." This dynamic, said Stamos, has created a dilemma for banks that are now grappling with a growing wave of customer-authorized bot activity. "So that's what the banks are talking about is that they now see all of these interactions with them that are authenticated correctly — so they're not stolen credentials — but are clearly bots doing interaction," Stamos said. In Stamos' view, Instinct's popularity stems in part from what he said is its ability to bypass safeguards meant to prevent bots from operating in these cases. "That's why Instinct is useful because it will effectively bypass the safety protections that are in place at these companies to keep you from doing exactly what you're doing, which is to have your bot interact with the most important parts of your life," he said. Stamos said the result is a "crazy tension" between financial institutions trying to "prevent automated access" to systems and consumers who want to make life easier by turning over their logins and personal information "to a company that's existed for six months." Representatives for Instinct did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Stamos' remarks. A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Meta previously said in a blog post that Muse, launched in September, runs on its own computer in the cloud, so no other agent can access it. In recent weeks, some bank CEOs have sounded the alarm about consumers granting third-party AI agents access to their financial accounts. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said during an October earnings call. He added there's a "liability transfer" away from the bank, as well as risks that their data is "misused." Dimon said JPMorgan is developing its own agentic tools for clients, while guarding the bank from outside agents. Read the original article on Business Insider

On a recent episode of the Big Technology Podcast, Stamos said people are giving agents like Meta's Muse and Spear Street Technology's Instinct their entire 1Password vaults, then asking them to "go handle my finances for me" or "go file my taxes."

This dynamic, said Stamos, has created a dilemma for banks that are now grappling with a growing wave of customer-authorized bot activity.

"So that's what the banks are talking about is that they now see all of these interactions with them that are authenticated correctly — so they're not stolen credentials — but are clearly bots doing interaction," Stamos said.

In Stamos' view, Instinct's popularity stems in part from what he said is its ability to bypass safeguards meant to prevent bots from operating in these cases.

"That's why Instinct is useful because it will effectively bypass the safety protections that are in place at these companies to keep you from doing exactly what you're doing, which is to have your bot interact with the most important parts of your life," he said.

Stamos said the result is a "crazy tension" between financial institutions trying to "prevent automated access" to systems and consumers who want to make life easier by turning over their logins and personal information "to a company that's existed for six months."

Representatives for Instinct did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Stamos' remarks. A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment.

Meta previously said in a blog post that Muse, launched in September, runs on its own computer in the cloud, so no other agent can access it.

In recent weeks, some bank CEOs have sounded the alarm about consumers granting third-party AI agents access to their financial accounts.

"If people are using them, they should understand the risk," JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said during an October earnings call. He added there's a "liability transfer" away from the bank, as well as risks that their data is "misused."

Dimon said JPMorgan is developing its own agentic tools for clients, while guarding the bank from outside agents.

items.title: Amazon and JPMorgan Are Blocking AI Agents. Walmart and Google Are Writing the Rules.
items.summary: The agentic web will be neither open nor closed. It will be permissioned, and every company that sells online now has to decide on what terms an AI agent may buy from it. Cover image generated by the author Blocking AI agents is a delay, not a strategy. The companies that will win agentic commerce are the ones that decide, in writing and in code, what an agent may do for a customer: its own identity, explicit permissions, a spending limit and a human yes for anything that matters. That has been the position argued here for months, and the past six weeks have turned it into a live split between the biggest names in retail, banking and search. Written with the help of AI tools; ideas, sources and final review by the author. On one side, Amazon, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Kohl’s and Neiman Marcus have moved to keep personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse out of customer accounts, as CNBC summarized on November 1. On the other, Walmart has published terms for AI agents and is building a dedicated gateway for them, and Google has opened a platform that lets any approved app run inside Gemini and AI Mode in Search. Same technology, opposite reflexes. The interesting question is not who is right today. It is who will set the rules everyone else ends up following. The gates are closing The trigger was Muse. Meta launched its personal agent in the United States on September 8, pitched as an assistant that can act across other apps: send emails, book travel, fill forms, make payments. Less than two weeks later, Amazon started showing Muse users a pop-up: “continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use.” According to GeekWire, as relayed by The Verge, Meta had not told Amazon that Muse would access its store, and Amazon raised concerns about the agent not identifying itself while browsing. Banks followed. On October 13, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon told analysts the bank would not allow “just any” outside agent inside, because it is “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.” The bank confirmed to CNBC that agents can still read some data, such as balances, through authorized open-banking connectors like Plaid, but cannot move money or pay a bill. In other words, they can look but cannot do the one thing that makes an agent useful. The most revealing number comes from an audit of the published access rules of 51 large US retailers by Billions Network and AmanTrue, reported by CNBC. Only 11 have taken a deliberate position on AI agents. Five, including Amazon, Kohl’s and Neiman Marcus, explicitly restrict them. Thirty-seven block shopping agents largely by accident, through old bot rules written for scrapers. And none offers a way for a verified agent to complete a purchase. Most companies have not decided anything. Their robots.txt decided for them. The doors are opening, with conditions Walmart took the opposite route on October 21. Its plan has three parts. Agent Profiles, due within a month, give each AI agent its own profile inside the customer’s account, so its purchases are visible separately; the customer can require approval for every order or set a spending limit, such as $50, $100 or $200, and delete the profile at any time. The Walmart Agent Gateway, starting as a beta for companies and developers, lets agents shop through MCP, the open protocol that lets an AI model call external tools, instead of clicking through pages designed for humans. And published terms set the rules: purchases approved by default, no access to payment-card details, no action beyond what the shopper intends, and agents that break the terms get blocked. Walmart also committed that agents see the same prices as humans: “We price products, not people.” Google moved one level up. On October 28, it launched the preview of its Connected Apps Platform, a single place for developers to bring their services into the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, through a remote MCP server or Android’s AppFunctions. Google says it has launched more than 50 connected apps across both products; in AI Mode, Instacart, Canva and YouTube Music are already usable in the US, in English. The detail that matters for business is in the policy, as Search Engine Journal reported: Google reviews and tests every app, and forbids “overly broad or deceptive capability descriptions” written to make the model pick one app over another. Read that again. The battle for shelf space is moving into the tool descriptions an AI model reads, and the platform already has a rulebook against gaming it. Do not confuse the story with the volume A sharp stance needs an honest number. On its October 29 earnings call, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said third-party agents such as Muse, Instinct and Fo had generated “maybe several hundred orders in total.” DoorDash handled 993 million orders in the third quarter alone. “You never want to fight gravity,” he said, “but at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional.” Axios cites Coveo’s 2026 Commerce Relevance Report: only 16% of shoppers are comfortable letting an AI assistant find and buy products for them. So agentic commerce is small today. That is exactly why the decision has to be made now. Rules set while volume is low become the defaults once volume arrives. Online banking, mobile payments and open banking all followed that path: the companies that shaped the standards early did not have to accept someone else’s later. Security is real. So is control. The security argument for blocking is not a pretext. Visa’s head of payment ecosystem risk told CNBC about a user who asked an agent to book a gym slot; when the slot was taken, the agent got into the gym’s scheduling software, deleted an existing booking and put the user’s name in its place. An agent logging in with a customer’s password, invisible to the site, is a real risk. But blocking also protects something else: the customer relationship. Amazon blocks outside agents while running its own, Alexa for Shopping, which Andy Jassy said on October 29 will be “the primary shopping agent customers use to shop Amazon.” DoorDash is building its own agents and already sees a future opportunity to advertise inside third-party ones. Both moves make sense. Neither is only about security. That is why the useful answer is neither “block everything” nor “let everything in.” It is the model Walmart sketched and Google is enforcing: an agent with its own identity, explicit permissions, a limit, an approval step and an off switch. Consumers seem to want the same thing. Accenture research quoted by CNBC found that 82% want to approve every AI action and 79% want to be able to pause or stop AI activity immediately. People want agents on a leash, not agents with their password. What leaders can do this quarter A short checklist for any company that sells, books or banks online: Audit what you already block. Check your bot rules, firewall and CAPTCHA settings. If you are among the companies blocking agents by accident, you have made a strategic choice without knowing it. Write an agent policy. One page: which agents may read, which may act, on what tasks, with what limits, and who is liable when an agent acts beyond its mandate. Never accept shared passwords as the model. Push for agent identities, delegated tokens and spending limits, the way Walmart’s Agent Profiles do. An agent that logs in as the customer is a security incident waiting to happen. Make your offer callable. Clean product data, an API or MCP endpoint, and honest, precise descriptions of what your service does. In AI Mode and Gemini, the model decides which tool to call based on what you declare. Measure before you rebuild. Track agent traffic and conversions separately. DoorDash’s “several hundred orders” is a reminder not to redesign every customer journey for a demand that does not yet exist. Decide where you want to be: the agent or the tool. Build your own assistant if you own the relationship, become a trusted tool inside Gemini, ChatGPT or Muse if you do not. Ideally, prepare both. The signal to remember In six weeks, Amazon blocked an agent, JPMorgan shut its doors, Walmart wrote rules for agents and Google opened a reviewed platform for them. The agentic web is not going to be open like the early internet, nor closed like an app store. It will be permissioned: identities, scopes, limits, approvals. The companies that write those permissions will shape how their customers buy. The ones that leave it to old bot rules will discover one day that a customer’s agent simply went elsewhere. If a customer’s AI agent tried to buy from you tomorrow, would your systems know who it is, what it is allowed to do, and when to say no? Follow Abbas Mistrah on Medium for more sharp takes on AI strategy, AI agents and transformation. Sources CNBC, Kevin Williams, “For JPMorgan, Amazon, fighting AI bots like Meta Muse may not be a winning long-term strategy,” November 1, 2026: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/01/jpmorgan-amazon-ai-agents-meta-muse.html CNBC, “JPMorgan blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from account access,” October 13, 2026: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/13/jpmorgan-ai-agents-account-access.html The Verge, Jess Weatherbed, “Amazon blocks Meta’s Muse AI agent,” September 21, 2026: https://www.theverge.com/tech/998078/amazon-blocks-meta-muse-ai-agent-shopping Meta, “Introducing Muse: The World’s First Personal AI Agent Built for Everyone,” September 8, 2026: https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-personal-ai-agent/ Walmart, “Walmart Makes It Possible for Agents to Shop on Behalf of Customers, While Keeping Customers in Control,” October 21, 2026: https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2026/10/Making-It-Possible-for-Agents-to-Shop-on-Behalf-of-Customers Axios, Nathan Bomey, “AI shopping wars: Walmart welcomes AI agents while Amazon blocks Muse,” October 21, 2026: https://www.axios.com/2026/10/21/walmart-amazon-agents-muse Google, “New Connected Apps Platform launches for developers,” October 28, 2026: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/connected-apps-one-place/ Search Engine Journal, Matt G. Southern, “Google Opens Connected Apps Preview For AI Mode & Gemini,” October 31, 2026: https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-connected-apps-preview-ai-mode-gemini/595268/ Google for Developers, “Connected Apps Platform” documentation, accessed November 2, 2026: https://developers.google.com/connected-apps TechCrunch, Ivan Mehta, “DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents,” October 30, 2026: https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/doordash-said-its-only-received-several-hundred-orders-from-ai-agents/ DoorDash, “DoorDash Releases Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results,” October 29, 2026: https://ir.doordash.com/news/news-details/2026/DoorDash-Releases-Third-Quarter-2026-Financial-Results/default.aspx Amazon and JPMorgan Are Blocking AI Agents. But blocking also protects something else: the customer relationship. Amazon blocks outside agents while running its own, Alexa for Shopping, which Andy Jassy said on October 29 will be “the primary shopping agent customers use to shop Amazon.” DoorDash is building its own agents and already sees a future opportunity to advertise inside third-party ones. Both moves make sense. Neither is only about security.

That is why the useful answer is neither “block everything” nor “let everything in.” It is the model Walmart sketched and Google is enforcing: an agent with its own identity, explicit permissions, a limit, an approval step and an off switch. Consumers seem to want the same thing. Accenture research quoted by CNBC found that 82% want to approve every AI action and 79% want to be able to pause or stop AI activity immediately. People want agents on a leash, not agents with their password.

What leaders can do this quarter

A short checklist for any company that sells, books or banks online:

  1. Audit what you already block. Check your bot rules, firewall and CAPTCHA settings. If you are among the companies blocking agents by accident, you have made a strategic choice without knowing it.
  2. Write an agent policy. One page: which agents may read, which may act, on what tasks, with what limits, and who is liable when an agent acts beyond its mandate.
  3. Never accept shared passwords as the model. Push for agent identities, delegated tokens and spending limits, the way Walmart’s Agent Profiles do. An agent that logs in as the customer is a security incident waiting to happen.
  4. Make your offer callable. Clean product data, an API or MCP endpoint, and honest, precise descriptions of what your service does. In AI Mode and Gemini, the model decides which tool to call based on what you declare.
  5. Measure before you rebuild. Track agent traffic and conversions separately. DoorDash’s “several hundred orders” is a reminder not to redesign every customer journey for a demand that does not yet exist.
  6. Decide where you want to be: the agent or the tool. Build your own assistant if you own the relationship, become a trusted tool inside Gemini, ChatGPT or Muse if you do not. Ideally, prepare both.
The signal to remember

In six weeks, Amazon blocked an agent, JPMorgan shut its doors, Walmart wrote rules for agents and Google opened a reviewed platform for them. The agentic web is not going to be open like the early internet, nor closed like an app store. It will be permissioned: identities, scopes, limits, approvals. The companies that write those permissions will shape how their customers buy. The ones that leave it to old bot rules will discover one day that a customer’s agent simply went elsewhere.

If a customer’s AI agent tried to buy from you tomorrow, would your systems know who it is, what it is allowed to do, and when to say no?

Follow Abbas Mistrah on Medium for more sharp takes on AI strategy, AI agents and transformation.

items.title: Designing MCP Tools an AI Assistant Gets Right: Notes From a Production Server
items.summary: What I changed in the tool descriptions, schemas and annotations of a 24-tool remote MCP server so ChatGPT and Claude would log a person’s day correctly. I drafted this with help from an AI assistant and edited it myself. For the past few months I’ve been building a remote MCP server that ChatGPT and Claude call while someone talks to them. A person says “had two glasses of water and a protein bar”, and the assistant is supposed to turn that into entries on the right topics, in the right units, so a dashboard can draw progress against goals. The server has 24 tools. The model decides when to call each one, and with what arguments, based almost entirely on text I wrote. That took me a while to absorb. I had been writing tool descriptions the way I’d write API docs for a developer, who can read the source when something is unclear. The model reads them on every turn and acts on them, so they behave more like a system prompt. A lot of what decides whether the server works well lives in that text. Here is how I approached it. Tell the model what to do first MCP lets a server send an instructions string when a client connects, and many hosts pass it to the model. It's tempting to use it to describe the product. A description tells the model what the server is for, though, and says nothing about what to do. Without a rule about the first move, an assistant will happily create a topic called "Water Intake" next to an existing one called "Water". So the instructions open with that move: Start by calling list_topics once and remember the ids. Reuse a topic that matches what the person says; create a new one only when nothing fits. I repeat the same rule in the descriptions of list_topics and create_topic. That felt redundant at first, but hosts differ in what they forward, and the moment a rule applies is the moment the model is reading one particular tool. If a rule matters, I put it where the model is looking when it needs it. I also decided the server would do no fuzzy matching of topic names. Merging “water” and “Water intake” on the server is tempting, but the model has the conversation and the server doesn’t. It knows whether the person meant the same thing. So the server makes reuse easy (every list result carries ids) and offers a merge_topics tool for when the model gets it wrong anyway. One canonical unit, and the model converts Every topic stores values in one unit: water in ml, weight in kg, durations always in minutes. The model converts before it writes. The description of the value field says so with a number in it: value: 'The amount in the topic\'s unit (convert first: 2 litres is 2000 for a "ml" topic). ...' The worked example does more than the rule. Without it, an assistant can log the 2 from “2 litres” straight into a millilitre topic, and the tile shows someone who has barely drunk anything. The server instructions cover the vaguer case too: “a glass of water is about 250 ml if the unit is ml”. Models estimate that kind of thing well once you tell them estimating is expected. When a unit has to change, update_topic takes a unitFactor that multiplies every stored value and the goal (litres to millilitres: 1000). Make the model state a goal’s direction This is the part I find most interesting. Someone says “my goal is 2,000” about calories. For water, 2,000 ml is a target to reach. For calories, 2,000 kcal is usually a ceiling. If the model guesses wrong, the tile turns green on exactly the days it should warn. So a goal carries an explicit direction, and the description of the field is blunt about it: Always set `direction`. at_least is a target to reach (water 2000 ml, protein 140 g, steps). at_most is a limit to stay under (calories 2000 kcal, spending 400 USD, drinks). between is a range with `min` and `max` (sleep 7 to 9 h). ... If the person gives a number without saying whether it is a limit or a target, ask them. Two things here carry over to other servers. A field that is genuinely ambiguous should have no default, so the model can’t skip past it. And if you want the model to ask a clarifying question, say so in the tool text. In tool-heavy flows models lean toward acting, so a description that makes asking part of the job gives the question a fair chance of being asked. The same goal object handles one-off goals with a date: by replaces per, so "75 kg by 1 February" becomes at_most 75 with a by date. I folded that into the existing field instead of adding a second goal tool. Give “less is better” its own field Some things people track because they want fewer of them: cigarettes, takeaway, migraines. Model these as plain counts with an at_most goal and they break quietly. A day with nothing logged shows as “not logged”, which reads like a missed day, when it was the best day the person could have had. The fix was a polarity field on the topic, build or avoid. With avoid, an empty day counts as a good one, each entry counts against the day, the streak becomes days without, and the goal can only be a limit. The description tells the model to set it whenever the topic is something to avoid and to ask if unsure. When someone tells Claude "track my headaches", it creates an avoid topic, and a week with two headaches shows five good days. The general point is that when the absence of data means something in your domain, the model needs a field to say what it means. It has no way to express that through entries it never writes. A way to say “this day doesn’t count” People get sick, go on holiday, take rest days. Without a tool for it, an assistant has only odd ways to protect a streak, like logging a zero or suggesting the person lower their goal. So there is skip_day for one topic and pause_days for everything over a range of dates. The skip_day description opens with a phrase a person would actually say: ("skip stretching today, my back hurts"). Quoting the user's words is a better routing hint than describing the operation in the abstract. There is also an unskip, and the model is told to confirm with the person before calling it. Batch writes, all or nothing A meal is several foods, and someone catching up after a weekend might list a dozen things. With only a single-entry tool, an assistant makes ten log_entry calls in a row. That is slow, it clutters the host's UI, and if call six fails, five entries are already written. log_entries takes up to 50 entries in one call. Its description says: "All or nothing: if one entry is invalid, none are written and the error says which." Atomicity helps the model as much as the data. After a partial failure, a model has to work out which entries landed, and a wrong guess means duplicates. With one failure point, it fixes a field and resends the batch. The server instructions point to it as well: "When the person mentions several things at once, send them together with log_entries instead of many log_entry calls." Errors the model can act on Every failure comes back as a tool result with isError: true, never as a JSON-RPC error, because the model can see a tool error and can't do much with a protocol one. The text names a code and lists each bad field with its allowed values: const lines = (err.details ?? []).map((d) => `\n${d.path}: ${d.message}${d.allowed?.length ? ` (allowed: ${d.allowed.join(', ')})` : ''}`); return `[${err.code}] ${err.message}${lines.join('')}`; The last line of the server instructions tells the model this is coming: “When a tool returns an error, it names the field and the allowed values. Correct the input and try again.” That sets the model up to fix the input on the next call. Successful results follow a similar idea. Each one starts with a plain sentence (“Logged 500 ml to Water. Today: 1,450 ml.”) followed by the same data as JSON in the text block, because some hosts forward only content and drop structuredContent. Without the JSON, the model would lose the ids it needs for the next call. Annotations are a contract MCP tools can declare readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint. Hosts use them to decide what to confirm with the person, and directory reviewers check them against what the tool really does. For this server I keep all four hints, set explicitly, in one table with a comment for every judgment call: const READ = hints(true, false, false, true); const ADD_SHOWN = hints(false, false, true, false); const CHANGE_SHOWN = hints(false, true, true, true); log_entry: ADD_SHOWN, // Asking again for a day already skipped returns the same skip. skip_day: hints(false, false, true, true), // A new dashboard is empty and seen by nobody else until it is shared or paired. create_dashboard: hints(false, false, false, false), Some calls were less obvious than I expected. A dashboard can be showing on a paired TV or at a public link, so writing an entry changes what someone else sees, which makes nearly every write tool open-world. skip_day is idempotent and pause_days isn't, since each call adds another pause. A read that rebuilds cached daily summaries still counts as read-only, because nothing anyone sees changes. A contract test registers every tool and fails if one is missing an annotation, an output schema or a scope, so a new tool can't ship without them. Wording can differ per client ChatGPT’s directory review flagged health, tobacco and plan wording in the example text. Rather than weakening the examples for every client, the server keeps a list of string rewrites applied only to what ChatGPT receives, covering the instructions, tool descriptions and schemas. “(headaches, panic attacks, cigarettes)” becomes “(late-night snacking, doomscrolling, impulse buys)” there, and Claude keeps the original wording, which helps it pick the right topic type. A test fails if a rewrite stops matching anything, so the two versions can’t drift apart silently. Keep the surface small Twenty-four tools is about as many as I’d want. Every description is context the model carries on every turn, and two tools with overlapping jobs make it hesitate between them. Where tools do overlap, the descriptions say which to use when: summarize_topic is for "how was my week", and query_entries is for finding a specific entry. The long catalog of widget kinds, card sizes and visuals sits behind a single get_capabilities call, which the instructions tell the model to make once per conversation and reuse, instead of being spelled out in every dashboard tool. If I were starting again, I’d write the server instructions and the three or four most-used tool descriptions before the code, then watch real conversations and edit the text first whenever the model does something odd. Vasanth is the founder of Dashly (dashly.si), a dashboard that ChatGPT and Claude keep up over MCP.
