items.title: Voting in 2026 Is Getting an AI Slop 'I Voted' Sticker
items.summary: It’s a small pleasure, but receiving an “I Voted” sticker after casting my ballot is one of my favorite parts of the whole voting process. I slap the sticker on my chest and spend the rest of the day feeling like I accomplished a little something. I participated in democracy and everyone who sees me will know it. Artificial intelligence robbed me of that small joy this year and replaced it with a small horror. My “I Voted” sticker is AI-generated slop. Getting a little sticker when you vote has been a tradition in the US since the 1980s . It’s a symbol of the election cycle. People take selfies and post them or share them with friends. It’s a celebration of democracy and a small way to pressure people into going to the ballot box. The voting sticker has been subject to every kind of discourse imaginable. Are “I Voted” stickers worth the cost? Wondered Marketplace in 2020. A cemetery in New York has spent time and money tending to the grave of Susan B Anthony because voters coat it in stickers during voting season. In 2008, companies like Starbucks and Ben and Jerry’s ran afoul of election laws for offering free treats to people who showed their “I Voted” stickers. It’s appropriate but depressing that I got an AI slop “I Voted” sticker in 2026, the year it feels like the mainstream began to reckon with AI. My sticker is ugly. It’s a busy circular nightmare. “I Voted” is spelled out in small bronze text at the top of the ring. Bronze laurels encircle a bronze bald eagle that stretches atop the American flag. Below this is more text: “250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY” and "SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL.” Below that, another line reads — as best I can tell — “CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA.” I assume this was meant to say “CELEBRATING FREEDOM," but whoever churned out this slop wasn’t using the latest models and the fine detail is lost. I put the sticker on reluctantly, but I was not proud. I sent a photo of the offending sticker to journalist friends with my face cropped out. They immediately noticed it was AI-generated. I did not post my sticker online. I shared it with no one else. My democratic joy turned to shame. A few hours later, a friend sent me a selfie. He’d just left the voting booth. His sticker was beautiful, tasteful, a testament to the subtle art of the “I Voted” sticker. A red ring enclosed a blue field. The crescent and palmetto (symbols of South Carolina) sat elegantly behind a bold white “I VOTED.” His sticker catches the eye. Passers-by will know exactly what the sticker says. They know he voted. Anyone looking at my sticker will wonder how I spilled some bronze paint on my chest. I trembled with indignation. One town over from me they’re giving out the good stickers and I’m stuck with slop. First my town of 12,000 installs 33 Flock cameras and now this? I spent some time scrolling through social media to see other “I Voted” stickers. So many are so beautiful. Michigan runs a contest where students can submit their own idea for a sticker and the state will print up the winners . Kentucky , Albany , and several other places around the country do the same. Louisiana commissions local artists to produce gorgeous stickers . My mouth hung up in a jealous scowl as I stared at pictures of New Orleanians bedecked with a sticker showing a hand drawn trumpet blasting out “I Voted” alongside Mardi Gras beads. Only Denton, Texas (another place I’ve lived, weirdly) seems to also have AI-generated slop stickers . Denton’s sticker is, at least, personalized. The city’s court house is in the corner looking more or less correct. The “I Voted” is large and centered in the sticker itself. Like mine, the image is too busy. Too much text, too many fireworks, and the inclusion of the Liberty Bell clutters the whole thing up. The central message — “I Voted” — is bright white. It doesn’t sink into a busy bronze soup like on my sticker. Complaining about AI-slop “I Voted” stickers may seem trivial in a world where AIs are choosing targets in warzones and vibecoders are reverse-engineering every piece of software ever written. But these little things are important. These small annoyances pile up until things like ChatGPT flyers are so ubiquitous that you don’t notice them anymore. The AI drive-thru works well enough and one day you stop worrying about it so much. You get an ugly AI slop “I Voted” sticker and you slap it on or toss it out. Enough of these build up until you don’t notice that AI all around you. And then, one day, it’s all normal. Right now we’re figuring out where our AI lines are. Society is negotiating what the future will look like. We’re fighting data centers , figuring out how to burn tokens to keep our bosses happy, and learning what we will and won’t abide. Me? I draw the line at AI-generated “I Voted” stickers.
items.summary_html:
It’s a small pleasure, but receiving an “I Voted” sticker after casting my ballot is one of my favorite parts of the whole voting process. I slap the sticker on my chest and spend the rest of the day feeling like I accomplished a little something. I participated in democracy and everyone who sees me will know it. Artificial intelligence robbed me of that small joy this year and replaced it with a small horror. My “I Voted” sticker is AI-generated slop. 

Getting a little sticker when you vote has been a tradition in the US since the 1980s. It’s a symbol of the election cycle. People take selfies and post them or share them with friends. It’s a celebration of democracy and a small way to pressure people into going to the ballot box. 

The voting sticker has been subject to every kind of discourse imaginable. Are “I Voted” stickers worth the cost? Wondered Marketplace in 2020. A cemetery in New York has spent time and money tending to the grave of Susan B Anthony because voters coat it in stickers during voting season. In 2008, companies like Starbucks and Ben and Jerry’s ran afoul of election laws for offering free treats to people who showed their “I Voted” stickers.

It’s appropriate but depressing that I got an AI slop “I Voted” sticker in 2026, the year it feels like the mainstream began to reckon with AI.

My sticker is ugly. It’s a busy circular nightmare. “I Voted” is spelled out in small bronze text at the top of the ring. Bronze laurels encircle a bronze bald eagle that stretches atop the American flag. Below this is more text: “250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY” and "SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL.” Below that, another line reads — as best I can tell — “CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA.” I assume this was meant to say “CELEBRATING FREEDOM," but whoever churned out this slop wasn’t using the latest models and the fine detail is lost.

I put the sticker on reluctantly, but I was not proud. I sent a photo of the offending sticker to journalist friends with my face cropped out. They immediately noticed it was AI-generated. I did not post my sticker online. I shared it with no one else. My democratic joy turned to shame.

A few hours later, a friend sent me a selfie. He’d just left the voting booth. His sticker was beautiful, tasteful, a testament to the subtle art of the “I Voted” sticker. A red ring enclosed a blue field. The crescent and palmetto (symbols of South Carolina) sat elegantly behind a bold white “I VOTED.”

His sticker catches the eye. Passers-by will know exactly what the sticker says. They know he voted. Anyone looking at my sticker will wonder how I spilled some bronze paint on my chest. I trembled with indignation. One town over from me they’re giving out the good stickers and I’m stuck with slop. First my town of 12,000 installs 33 Flock cameras and now this? 

I spent some time scrolling through social media to see other “I Voted” stickers. So many are so beautiful. Michigan runs a contest where students can submit their own idea for a sticker and the state will print up the winners. Kentucky, Albany, and several other places around the country do the same. Louisiana commissions local artists to produce gorgeous stickers. My mouth hung up in a jealous scowl as I stared at pictures of New Orleanians bedecked with a sticker showing a hand drawn trumpet blasting out “I Voted” alongside Mardi Gras beads.

Only Denton, Texas (another place I’ve lived, weirdly) seems to also have AI-generated slop stickers. Denton’s sticker is, at least, personalized. The city’s court house is in the corner looking more or less correct. The “I Voted” is large and centered in the sticker itself. Like mine, the image is too busy. Too much text, too many fireworks, and the inclusion of the Liberty Bell clutters the whole thing up. The central message — “I Voted” — is bright white. It doesn’t sink into a busy bronze soup like on my sticker.

Complaining about AI-slop “I Voted” stickers may seem trivial in a world where AIs are choosing targets in warzones and vibecoders are reverse-engineering every piece of software ever written. But these little things are important. These small annoyances pile up until things like ChatGPT flyers are so ubiquitous that you don’t notice them anymore. The AI drive-thru works well enough and one day you stop worrying about it so much. You get an ugly AI slop “I Voted” sticker and you slap it on or toss it out. Enough of these build up until you don’t notice that AI all around you. And then, one day, it’s all normal.

Right now we’re figuring out where our AI lines are. Society is negotiating what the future will look like. We’re fighting data centers, figuring out how to burn tokens to keep our bosses happy, and learning what we will and won’t abide.

Me? I draw the line at AI-generated “I Voted” stickers.

items.title: The Rise of AI Orchestration: Connecting Intelligence with Real-World Execution
items.summary:
Why intelligent models still struggle to execute real-world tasks — and how orchestration connects LLMs, tools, memory, and workflows to make AI systems work. The Rise of AI Orchestration, with an orchestrator hub linked to LLM, tools, memory and APIs The Assistant That Knew Everything and Did Nothing Picture a Monday morning. You type one sentence to your AI assistant: “Pull last quarter’s top five customer complaints, draft a fix plan, and book a review with the team.” The reply arrives in seconds. It is a flawless essay on how to analyze customer complaints: clear headings, confident tone, even a tidy checklist. And not one complaint was read. No plan was filed. No meeting was booked. The intelligence was real. The execution was zero. That gap, between a model that can talk about work and a system that can do work, is one of the most important engineering problems in applied AI today. The discipline that closes it has a name: AI orchestration . This article takes you from “what does an LLM actually do?” to designing an orchestrated system you could ship. You will get one architecture diagram, working Python you can run in minutes, and an honest list of the places these systems break. The central idea: for most real-world AI features, the hard part is no longer the model. It is the loop around it: what the system may do, what it remembers, when it stops, and who checks its work. I make that case three ways: by tracing the idea to the agent research it grew, by building a complete orchestrator you can run, and by showing honestly where it breaks. Your reading map Level 1: why a smart model alone is a brain in a jar Level 2: what orchestration is, in one analogy Level 3: the four parts of every orchestrated system Level 4: six patterns that cover most real designs Build it: a working orchestrator in about 100 lines Level 5: reflection, guardrails, observability, humans in the loop Reality check: where it fails, and what I would do about it Level 1: The Brain in a Jar A large language model (LLM) does one thing: given text, it predicts the next piece of text. Do that at enormous scale and you get something that writes, reasons, translates, and explains. That is remarkable. It is also all the model does on its own. By default, an LLM has three hard limits: It cannot act. It cannot send an email, query your database, or click a button. It only produces text. It cannot see the present. Its knowledge is frozen at training time. It does not know today’s prices or this morning’s incident. It forgets. It holds only what fits in its context window. Close the conversation and the working memory is gone. Think of a brilliant consultant locked in a soundproof room, with no phone, no laptop, and no notes from yesterday. You can slide questions under the door and get wonderful answers back. But you would never call that consultant “your employee who gets things done.” Every useful AI product you have used has quietly solved these three limits. It gave the brain hands (tools), eyes (retrieval), and a notebook (memory), then added something to decide which one to use and when. That last part is orchestration. Level 2: What AI Orchestration Actually Is AI orchestration is the layer of software that decides what happens next: which model to call, which tool to run, what to remember, and when to stop. The best analogy is a symphony. Every musician in the orchestra is skilled, but without a conductor you get noise. The conductor does not play an instrument. They decide who plays, when, how loudly, and when the piece is finished. In an AI system: The musicians are the LLM, a search API, a code interpreter, a database, a calendar, a vector store. The score is the goal and the plan. The conductor is the orchestrator, the control loop that reads the situation and picks the next move. This idea is not new. LLM-powered agents framed the model as the agent’s “brain” surrounded by planning, memory, and tool use. What has changed since 2023 is that this stopped being a research sketch and became everyday infrastructure: tool calling is built into major model APIs, and open standards for connecting models to tools and data have appeared. A useful distinction. A chatbot answers. An agent acts. An orchestrated system coordinates one or many agents, tools, and checks so the work finishes reliably. Orchestration is what turns a clever answer into a completed task. Three cards showing the progression from chatbot that answers, to agent that acts, to orchestrated system that finishes. Level 3: The Anatomy of an Orchestrated System Strip away the branding and nearly every orchestrated AI system has the same four parts. The structure follows the agent breakdown in overview. Planning. Break a big goal into smaller steps. Techniques here include chain of thought (“think step by step”), Tree of Thoughts, which explores several reasoning paths, and React, which alternates between reasoning and acting. Memory. Short-term memory is whatever sits in the model’s context window. Long-term memory lives outside the model, usually as embeddings in a vector store that the system searches at query time. Tools. Functions the model can request: search, a calculator, a SQL query, an HTTP call, a code runner. The model does not run them; it asks, and your code runs them. The control loop. The conductor itself. It sends context to the model, reads what the model wants to do, runs the tool, feeds the result back, and repeats until the goal is met or a limit is hit. The diagram below shows how they connect. Follow the arrows clockwise and you are watching one full turn of the loop. Diagram of the orchestration loop: plan, ask the model, run the tool, remember, with guardrails around every step The goal enters the orchestrator, which cycles through the four steps, consulting memory and calling tools, until it returns an answer. The guardrails band applies to every pass. Level 4: Six Orchestration Patterns That Cover Most Designs Six orchestration patterns. You do not need a new architecture for every project. Most real systems are a combination of the six patterns below. 1. Prompt chain How it works: fixed steps, and each output feeds the next. Use it when: the task splits cleanly into stages (extract, then summarize, then format). Watch out for: one bad step poisons everything after it. 2. Router How it works: a model or rule classifies the request and sends it down a specialist path. Use it when: inputs vary a lot, such as billing, bugs and sales questions. Watch out for: misrouting sends the work to the wrong specialist. 3. Parallel fan-out How it works: independent sub-tasks run at once and the results are merged. Use it when: the sub-tasks don’t depend on each other. Watch out for: the merge step can hide disagreements. 4. Orchestrator and workers How it works: a planner decides the sub-tasks at run time and delegates them. Use it when: you can’t know the steps in advance. Watch out for: cost and latency grow fast. 5. Generate and critique How it works: one pass produces, another judges and sends back fixes. Use it when: quality matters more than speed. Watch out for: loops that never converge, so cap the rounds. 6. Human checkpoint How it works: the system pauses for a person before a risky action. Use it when: actions are costly or irreversible. Watch out for: approval fatigue, so gate only the risky steps. The rule I follow: use the simplest pattern that works, and add autonomy only when you can measure that it helps. A fixed chain you can debug in five minutes beats a clever planner you cannot explain. Build It: A Working Orchestrator in About 100 Lines Theory is cheap, so here is the Monday-morning task from the opening, solved. This is a complete orchestrator with the four parts from Level 3: tools, memory, a planner, and a control loop. It uses only the Python standard library, so you can paste it into a file and run it. One honest note: the planner here is a simple rule-based stand-in for an LLM. That is deliberate. It lets you see the orchestration working without an API key, and it proves a point worth remembering: the loop, the guardrails, and the memory are the same whether the “brain” is rules or a frontier model. """mini_orchestrator.py - a tiny, dependency-free orchestration loop.""" from collections import Counter from dataclasses import dataclass, field # ---------- 1. TOOLS: the "hands" ---------- COMPLAINTS = [ {"id": 1, "topic": "slow checkout"}, {"id": 2, "topic": "login failures"}, {"id": 3, "topic": "slow checkout"}, {"id": 4, "topic": "wrong invoice"}, {"id": 5, "topic": "slow checkout"}, {"id": 6, "topic": "login failures"}, {"id": 7, "topic": "missing refund"}, ]def fetch_complaints(quarter: str) -> list: return COMPLAINTS # in real life: a database or ticketing APIdef top_issues(complaints: list, n: int = 3) -> list: counts = Counter(c["topic"] for c in complaints) return [{"topic": t, "count": k} for t, k in counts.most_common(n)]def draft_plan(issues: list) -> str: return "
".join(f"- Fix '{i['topic']}' (x{i['count']})" for i in issues)def book_meeting(title: str, attendees: list) -> str: return f"Booked '{title}' with {', '.join(attendees)}"TOOLS = { "fetch_complaints": fetch_complaints, "top_issues": top_issues, "draft_plan": draft_plan, "book_meeting": book_meeting, } NEEDS_APPROVAL = {"book_meeting"} # risky actions wait for a human# ---------- 2. MEMORY: the notebook ---------- @dataclass class Memory: goal: str steps: list = field(default_factory=list) # (tool, args, result) def add(self, tool, args, result): self.steps.append((tool, args, result)) def result_of(self, tool): for t, _, r in reversed(self.steps): if t == tool: return r return None# ---------- 3. PLANNER: the "brain" (stand-in for an LLM) ---------- def rule_based_planner(mem: Memory) -> dict: if mem.result_of("fetch_complaints") is None: return {"action": "fetch_complaints", "args": {"quarter": "last"}} if mem.result_of("top_issues") is None: return {"action": "top_issues", "args": {"complaints": mem.result_of("fetch_complaints"), "n": 3}} if mem.result_of("draft_plan") is None: return {"action": "draft_plan", "args": {"issues": mem.result_of("top_issues")}} if mem.result_of("book_meeting") is None: return {"action": "book_meeting", "args": {"title": "Complaint fix review", "attendees": ["support", "eng"]}} return {"final": "Plan drafted and review booked:
" + mem.result_of("draft_plan")}# ---------- 4. CONTROL LOOP: the conductor ---------- def run(goal, planner, approve, max_steps=8): mem = Memory(goal) for step in range(1, max_steps + 1): decision = planner(mem) if "final" in decision: return decision["final"], mem name, args = decision["action"], decision["args"] if name not in TOOLS: # guardrail: allow-list mem.add(name, args, "ERROR: unknown tool") continue if name in NEEDS_APPROVAL and not approve(name, args): # human checkpoint mem.add(name, args, "DENIED by human") return "Stopped: a human declined the action.", mem try: result = TOOLS[name](**args) except Exception as exc: # errors become observations result = f"ERROR: {exc}" mem.add(name, args, result) preview = str(result)[:60].replace("
", " ") print(f"step {step}: {name} -> {preview}") return "Stopped: step limit reached.", mem # guardrail: budgetif __name__ == "__main__": answer, memory = run( goal="Top complaints -> fix plan -> review meeting", planner=rule_based_planner, approve=lambda name, args: True, # replace with a real prompt in production ) print("
FINAL:", answer) Run it and you get this trace (I ran this exact file before putting it in the article): step 1: fetch_complaints -> [{'id': 1, 'topic': 'slow checkout'}, {'id': 2, 'topic': 'lo step 2: top_issues -> [{'topic': 'slow checkout', 'count': 3}, {'topic': 'login fa step 3: draft_plan -> - Fix 'slow checkout' (x3) - Fix 'login failures' (x2) - Fix step 4: book_meeting -> Booked 'Complaint fix review' with support, eng FINAL: Plan drafted and review booked: - Fix 'slow checkout' (x3) - Fix 'login failures' (x2) - Fix 'wrong invoice' (x1) What to notice, because this is the whole game: The model never executes anything. It proposes an action; the loop validates it and runs it. Three guardrails cost five lines. An allow-list of tools, a human approval gate on the risky action, and a step budget so it cannot loop forever. Errors become observations. If a tool fails, the failure goes back into memory so the planner can adapt instead of crashing. Swapping in a real model. Replace rule_based_planner with a function that sends the goal and mem.steps to an LLM with your tool definitions, then converts its tool request into the same {"action": ..., "args": ...} dictionary (or {"final": ...} when it is done). Nothing else changes. Major model APIs support this style of tool calling; check your provider's current documentation for the exact request format. Level 5: From Demo to Production A demo that works once is not a system. These five habits are what separate the two. 1. Make it reflect After the first answer, run a second pass whose only job is to find what is wrong with it: a missing step, an unsupported claim, a failed check. Feed the critique back and try again, with a hard cap on rounds. when an LLM judged its own work in an expert domain, it missed flaws that human experts caught. A critic is not an oracle. Give it real checks (tests, schema validation, a lookup against a trusted source) wherever you can. 2. Layer your guardrails Before the model: validate and sanitize inputs. Around tools: allow-lists, typed arguments, and least-privilege credentials. If a tool only needs read access, give it only read access. After the model: check output format and policy before anything is shown or executed. Treat tool output as data, never as instructions. A web page or a document an agent reads can contain text written to hijack it. Content that arrives through a tool should never be allowed to change the goal. 3. Trace everything Every step should log what the planner saw, which tool it chose, the arguments, the result, the time, and the cost. When an agent misbehaves at 2 a.m., the trace is the only way to answer “why did it do that?” without guessing. In the code above, mem.steps is already a minimal trace. 4. Put humans where mistakes are expensive Do not ask for approval on everything; people stop reading prompts they see fifty times a day. Gate the few actions that are costly or irreversible: payments, deletions, external messages, production changes. Let the rest run. 5. Budget for cost, latency, and failure Each model call takes time and money, and orchestration multiplies calls. Set step limits and timeouts, cache repeated lookups, and use a smaller model for simple routing or extraction. Make steps safe to retry, so a network error halfway through does not book two meetings. Weng’s overview names the underlying constraints plainly: finite context length, difficulty with long-term planning, and an unreliable natural-language interface between the model and its tools [1]. Everything above is engineering built around those three facts. The Honest Part: Where Orchestration Breaks Most articles on this topic stop at the exciting part. Here is the part I would want a colleague to tell me before I built anything. Errors compound. Suppose each step in a ten-step workflow succeeds 95% of the time, and failures are independent. The whole run then succeeds about 60% of the time (0.95 to the tenth power is roughly 0.60). That is an illustration, not a measurement of any real system, but the shape is real: long chains punish small error rates. Shorter chains, validation after each step, and retries on cheap steps all help. Non-determinism makes testing hard. The same input can produce different tool choices on different runs. You cannot rely on a single passing test. Build a small set of realistic tasks, run each several times, and track pass rates over time. Autonomy has a price. The more freedom you give a planner, the harder it is to predict cost, latency, and behavior. Newer models and APIs have improved this considerably, but the lesson stands: earn autonomy step by step. Sometimes you do not need an agent. If the steps are known and fixed, a plain script or a prompt chain is cheaper, faster, and easier to debug. Reach for an orchestrator when the path genuinely depends on what the system discovers along the way. Security is part of the design, not a final review. Tools turn text into actions. Any text the system reads, from a web page to an email, is a possible way to steer it. Least privilege and approval gates are not optional extras. A Lesson I Learned Beyond the Model I used to think that if every component of an AI pipeline was working correctly, the final output should be reliable too Working on AI-powered product visualization challenged that assumption. There were situations where the pipeline appeared to be functioning as expected, yet the final results were inconsistent. Instead of looking at the model as the only source of the problem, I started examining the entire flow — how image inputs were processed, how information moved between stages, and how individual components influenced the final output. That experience changed the way I look at AI engineering. A model can perform well in isolation, but a real-world system has to work as a whole. I began paying closer attention to what happens before and after inference, because sometimes the problem isn’t the intelligence of the model; it’s how the system around it is engineered. That’s when I started seeing AI development differently: building a model is one challenge. Building a system you can trust is another. And that is also why orchestration interests me. It brings together the parts of AI engineering that are easy to overlook when we focus only on model performance: coordination, execution, validation, debugging, and reliability. . The Takeaway The next engineering challenge is making those capabilities useful in systems that can perform real work. A model can generate a plan. An orchestrated system can coordinate the tools, information, decisions, and checks required to carry it out. That difference matters. We don’t need every AI application to become fully autonomous. We need systems that understand their responsibilities, operate within defined boundaries, handle failures, and know when a human should take control. If there is one idea I want you to take away from this article, it is this: Intelligence decides what to do. Orchestration makes sure the right things get done, with the right controls in place. Start with a task you understand. Break it into steps. Identify the tools it needs. Build the simplest workflow that works. Then test its failure cases before giving it more autonomy. Because the real engineering challenge isn’t just making AI capable. It is making AI dependable. One question to leave you with: If you could delegate one repetitive task from your daily work to an AI system, what would it be — and which action would you never allow it to perform without human approval? This is the beginning of my exploration into the engineering behind intelligent systems, from understanding how AI works to discovering how we can build systems that reliably execute real-world tasks. References [2] J. Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (2022), NeurIPS 2022 [3] S. items.summary_html:
Why intelligent models still struggle to execute real-world tasks — and how orchestration connects LLMs, tools, memory, and workflows to make AI systems work.The Rise of AI Orchestration, with an orchestrator hub linked to LLM, tools, memory and APIsThe Assistant That Knew Everything and Did Nothing

Picture a Monday morning. You type one sentence to your AI assistant: “Pull last quarter’s top five customer complaints, draft a fix plan, and book a review with the team.”

The reply arrives in seconds. It is a flawless essay on how to analyze customer complaints: clear headings, confident tone, even a tidy checklist. And not one complaint was read. No plan was filed. No meeting was booked.

The intelligence was real. The execution was zero.

That gap, between a model that can talk about work and a system that can do work, is one of the most important engineering problems in applied AI today. The discipline that closes it has a name: AI orchestration.

This article takes you from “what does an LLM actually do?” to designing an orchestrated system you could ship. You will get one architecture diagram, working Python you can run in minutes, and an honest list of the places these systems break.

The central idea: for most real-world AI features, the hard part is no longer the model. It is the loop around it: what the system may do, what it remembers, when it stops, and who checks its work. I make that case three ways: by tracing the idea to the agent research it grew, by building a complete orchestrator you can run, and by showing honestly where it breaks.

Your reading map

  • Level 1: why a smart model alone is a brain in a jar
  • Level 2: what orchestration is, in one analogy
  • Level 3: the four parts of every orchestrated system
  • Level 4: six patterns that cover most real designs
  • Build it: a working orchestrator in about 100 lines
  • Level 5: reflection, guardrails, observability, humans in the loop
  • Reality check: where it fails, and what I would do about it
Level 1: The Brain in a Jar

A large language model (LLM) does one thing: given text, it predicts the next piece of text. Do that at enormous scale and you get something that writes, reasons, translates, and explains. That is remarkable. It is also all the model does on its own.

By default, an LLM has three hard limits:

  1. It cannot act. It cannot send an email, query your database, or click a button. It only produces text.
  2. It cannot see the present. Its knowledge is frozen at training time. It does not know today’s prices or this morning’s incident.
  3. It forgets. It holds only what fits in its context window. Close the conversation and the working memory is gone.

Think of a brilliant consultant locked in a soundproof room, with no phone, no laptop, and no notes from yesterday. You can slide questions under the door and get wonderful answers back. But you would never call that consultant “your employee who gets things done.”

Every useful AI product you have used has quietly solved these three limits. It gave the brain hands (tools), eyes (retrieval), and a notebook (memory), then added something to decide which one to use and when. That last part is orchestration.

Level 2: What AI Orchestration Actually Is

AI orchestration is the layer of software that decides what happens next: which model to call, which tool to run, what to remember, and when to stop.

The best analogy is a symphony. Every musician in the orchestra is skilled, but without a conductor you get noise. The conductor does not play an instrument. They decide who plays, when, how loudly, and when the piece is finished.

In an AI system:

  • The musicians are the LLM, a search API, a code interpreter, a database, a calendar, a vector store.
  • The score is the goal and the plan.
  • The conductor is the orchestrator, the control loop that reads the situation and picks the next move.

This idea is not new. LLM-powered agents framed the model as the agent’s “brain” surrounded by planning, memory, and tool use. What has changed since 2023 is that this stopped being a research sketch and became everyday infrastructure: tool calling is built into major model APIs, and open standards for connecting models to tools and data have appeared.

A useful distinction. A chatbot answers. An agent acts. An orchestrated system coordinates one or many agents, tools, and checks so the work finishes reliably. Orchestration is what turns a clever answer into a completed task.
Three cards showing the progression from chatbot that answers, to agent that acts, to orchestrated system that finishes.Level 3: The Anatomy of an Orchestrated System

Strip away the branding and nearly every orchestrated AI system has the same four parts. The structure follows the agent breakdown in overview.

  1. Planning. Break a big goal into smaller steps. Techniques here include chain of thought (“think step by step”), Tree of Thoughts, which explores several reasoning paths, and React, which alternates between reasoning and acting.
  2. Memory. Short-term memory is whatever sits in the model’s context window. Long-term memory lives outside the model, usually as embeddings in a vector store that the system searches at query time.
  3. Tools. Functions the model can request: search, a calculator, a SQL query, an HTTP call, a code runner. The model does not run them; it asks, and your code runs them.
  4. The control loop. The conductor itself. It sends context to the model, reads what the model wants to do, runs the tool, feeds the result back, and repeats until the goal is met or a limit is hit.

The diagram below shows how they connect. Follow the arrows clockwise and you are watching one full turn of the loop.

Diagram of the orchestration loop: plan, ask the model, run the tool, remember, with guardrails around every step

The goal enters the orchestrator, which cycles through the four steps, consulting memory and calling tools, until it returns an answer. The guardrails band applies to every pass.

Level 4: Six Orchestration Patterns That Cover Most DesignsSix orchestration patterns.

You do not need a new architecture for every project. Most real systems are a combination of the six patterns below.

1. Prompt chain
How it works: fixed steps, and each output feeds the next.
Use it when: the task splits cleanly into stages (extract, then summarize, then format).
Watch out for: one bad step poisons everything after it.

2. Router
How it works: a model or rule classifies the request and sends it down a specialist path.
Use it when: inputs vary a lot, such as billing, bugs and sales questions.
Watch out for: misrouting sends the work to the wrong specialist.

3. Parallel fan-out
How it works: independent sub-tasks run at once and the results are merged.
Use it when: the sub-tasks don’t depend on each other.
Watch out for: the merge step can hide disagreements.

4. Orchestrator and workers
How it works: a planner decides the sub-tasks at run time and delegates them.
Use it when: you can’t know the steps in advance.
Watch out for: cost and latency grow fast.

5. Generate and critique
How it works: one pass produces, another judges and sends back fixes.
Use it when: quality matters more than speed.
Watch out for: loops that never converge, so cap the rounds.

6. Human checkpoint
How it works: the system pauses for a person before a risky action.
Use it when: actions are costly or irreversible.
Watch out for: approval fatigue, so gate only the risky steps.

The rule I follow: use the simplest pattern that works, and add autonomy only when you can measure that it helps. A fixed chain you can debug in five minutes beats a clever planner you cannot explain.

Build It: A Working Orchestrator in About 100 Lines

Theory is cheap, so here is the Monday-morning task from the opening, solved. This is a complete orchestrator with the four parts from Level 3: tools, memory, a planner, and a control loop. It uses only the Python standard library, so you can paste it into a file and run it.

One honest note: the planner here is a simple rule-based stand-in for an LLM. That is deliberate. It lets you see the orchestration working without an API key, and it proves a point worth remembering: the loop, the guardrails, and the memory are the same whether the “brain” is rules or a frontier model.
"""mini_orchestrator.py - a tiny, dependency-free orchestration loop."""
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
# ---------- 1. TOOLS: the "hands" ----------
COMPLAINTS = [
    {"id": 1, "topic": "slow checkout"},
    {"id": 2, "topic": "login failures"},
    {"id": 3, "topic": "slow checkout"},
    {"id": 4, "topic": "wrong invoice"},
    {"id": 5, "topic": "slow checkout"},
    {"id": 6, "topic": "login failures"},
    {"id": 7, "topic": "missing refund"},
]def fetch_complaints(quarter: str) -> list:
    return COMPLAINTS  # in real life: a database or ticketing APIdef top_issues(complaints: list, n: int = 3) -> list:
    counts = Counter(c["topic"] for c in complaints)
    return [{"topic": t, "count": k} for t, k in counts.most_common(n)]def draft_plan(issues: list) -> str:
    return "
".join(f"- Fix '{i['topic']}' (x{i['count']})" for i in issues)def book_meeting(title: str, attendees: list) -> str:
    return f"Booked '{title}' with {', '.join(attendees)}"TOOLS = {
    "fetch_complaints": fetch_complaints,
    "top_issues": top_issues,
    "draft_plan": draft_plan,
    "book_meeting": book_meeting,
}
NEEDS_APPROVAL = {"book_meeting"}  # risky actions wait for a human# ---------- 2. MEMORY: the notebook ----------
@dataclass
class Memory:
    goal: str
    steps: list = field(default_factory=list)  # (tool, args, result)    def add(self, tool, args, result):
        self.steps.append((tool, args, result))    def result_of(self, tool):
        for t, _, r in reversed(self.steps):
            if t == tool:
                return r
        return None# ---------- 3. PLANNER: the "brain" (stand-in for an LLM) ----------
def rule_based_planner(mem: Memory) -> dict:
    if mem.result_of("fetch_complaints") is None:
        return {"action": "fetch_complaints", "args": {"quarter": "last"}}
    if mem.result_of("top_issues") is None:
        return {"action": "top_issues",
                "args": {"complaints": mem.result_of("fetch_complaints"), "n": 3}}
    if mem.result_of("draft_plan") is None:
        return {"action": "draft_plan",
                "args": {"issues": mem.result_of("top_issues")}}
    if mem.result_of("book_meeting") is None:
        return {"action": "book_meeting",
                "args": {"title": "Complaint fix review", "attendees": ["support", "eng"]}}
    return {"final": "Plan drafted and review booked:
" + mem.result_of("draft_plan")}# ---------- 4. CONTROL LOOP: the conductor ----------
def run(goal, planner, approve, max_steps=8):
    mem = Memory(goal)
    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        decision = planner(mem)
        if "final" in decision:
            return decision["final"], mem
        name, args = decision["action"], decision["args"]
        if name not in TOOLS:                                   # guardrail: allow-list
            mem.add(name, args, "ERROR: unknown tool")
            continue
        if name in NEEDS_APPROVAL and not approve(name, args):  # human checkpoint
            mem.add(name, args, "DENIED by human")
            return "Stopped: a human declined the action.", mem
        try:
            result = TOOLS[name](**args)
        except Exception as exc:                                # errors become observations
            result = f"ERROR: {exc}"
        mem.add(name, args, result)
        preview = str(result)[:60].replace("
", " ")
        print(f"step {step}: {name} -> {preview}")
    return "Stopped: step limit reached.", mem                  # guardrail: budgetif __name__ == "__main__":
    answer, memory = run(
        goal="Top complaints -> fix plan -> review meeting",
        planner=rule_based_planner,
        approve=lambda name, args: True,  # replace with a real prompt in production
    )
    print("
FINAL:", answer)

Run it and you get this trace (I ran this exact file before putting it in the article):

step 1: fetch_complaints -> [{'id': 1, 'topic': 'slow checkout'}, {'id': 2, 'topic': 'lo
step 2: top_issues -> [{'topic': 'slow checkout', 'count': 3}, {'topic': 'login fa
step 3: draft_plan -> - Fix 'slow checkout' (x3) - Fix 'login failures' (x2) - Fix
step 4: book_meeting -> Booked 'Complaint fix review' with support, eng
FINAL: Plan drafted and review booked:
- Fix 'slow checkout' (x3)
- Fix 'login failures' (x2)
- Fix 'wrong invoice' (x1)

What to notice, because this is the whole game:

  • The model never executes anything. It proposes an action; the loop validates it and runs it.
  • Three guardrails cost five lines. An allow-list of tools, a human approval gate on the risky action, and a step budget so it cannot loop forever.
  • Errors become observations. If a tool fails, the failure goes back into memory so the planner can adapt instead of crashing.

Swapping in a real model. Replace rule_based_planner with a function that sends the goal and mem.steps to an LLM with your tool definitions, then converts its tool request into the same {"action": ..., "args": ...} dictionary (or {"final": ...} when it is done). Nothing else changes. Major model APIs support this style of tool calling; check your provider's current documentation for the exact request format.

Level 5: From Demo to Production

A demo that works once is not a system. These five habits are what separate the two.

1. Make it reflect

After the first answer, run a second pass whose only job is to find what is wrong with it: a missing step, an unsupported claim, a failed check. Feed the critique back and try again, with a hard cap on rounds. when an LLM judged its own work in an expert domain, it missed flaws that human experts caught. A critic is not an oracle. Give it real checks (tests, schema validation, a lookup against a trusted source) wherever you can.

2. Layer your guardrails
  • Before the model: validate and sanitize inputs.
  • Around tools: allow-lists, typed arguments, and least-privilege credentials. If a tool only needs read access, give it only read access.
  • After the model: check output format and policy before anything is shown or executed.
  • Treat tool output as data, never as instructions. A web page or a document an agent reads can contain text written to hijack it. Content that arrives through a tool should never be allowed to change the goal.
3. Trace everything

Every step should log what the planner saw, which tool it chose, the arguments, the result, the time, and the cost. When an agent misbehaves at 2 a.m., the trace is the only way to answer “why did it do that?” without guessing. In the code above, mem.steps is already a minimal trace.

4. Put humans where mistakes are expensive

Do not ask for approval on everything; people stop reading prompts they see fifty times a day. Gate the few actions that are costly or irreversible: payments, deletions, external messages, production changes. Let the rest run.

5. Budget for cost, latency, and failure

Each model call takes time and money, and orchestration multiplies calls. Set step limits and timeouts, cache repeated lookups, and use a smaller model for simple routing or extraction. Make steps safe to retry, so a network error halfway through does not book two meetings.

Weng’s overview names the underlying constraints plainly: finite context length, difficulty with long-term planning, and an unreliable natural-language interface between the model and its tools [1]. Everything above is engineering built around those three facts.

The Honest Part: Where Orchestration Breaks

Most articles on this topic stop at the exciting part. Here is the part I would want a colleague to tell me before I built anything.

Errors compound. Suppose each step in a ten-step workflow succeeds 95% of the time, and failures are independent. The whole run then succeeds about 60% of the time (0.95 to the tenth power is roughly 0.60). That is an illustration, not a measurement of any real system, but the shape is real: long chains punish small error rates. Shorter chains, validation after each step, and retries on cheap steps all help.

Non-determinism makes testing hard. The same input can produce different tool choices on different runs. You cannot rely on a single passing test. Build a small set of realistic tasks, run each several times, and track pass rates over time.

Autonomy has a price. The more freedom you give a planner, the harder it is to predict cost, latency, and behavior. Newer models and APIs have improved this considerably, but the lesson stands: earn autonomy step by step.

Sometimes you do not need an agent. If the steps are known and fixed, a plain script or a prompt chain is cheaper, faster, and easier to debug. Reach for an orchestrator when the path genuinely depends on what the system discovers along the way.

Security is part of the design, not a final review. Tools turn text into actions. Any text the system reads, from a web page to an email, is a possible way to steer it. Least privilege and approval gates are not optional extras.

A Lesson I Learned Beyond the Model
I used to think that if every component of an AI pipeline was working correctly, the final output should be reliable too
Working on AI-powered product visualization challenged that assumption.
There were situations where the pipeline appeared to be functioning as expected, yet the final results were inconsistent. Instead of looking at the model as the only source of the problem, I started examining the entire flow — how image inputs were processed, how information moved between stages, and how individual components influenced the final output.
That experience changed the way I look at AI engineering.
A model can perform well in isolation, but a real-world system has to work as a whole. I began paying closer attention to what happens before and after inference, because sometimes the problem isn’t the intelligence of the model; it’s how the system around it is engineered.
That’s when I started seeing AI development differently: building a model is one challenge. Building a system you can trust is another.
And that is also why orchestration interests me.
It brings together the parts of AI engineering that are easy to overlook when we focus only on model performance: coordination, execution, validation, debugging, and reliability..
The Takeaway

The next engineering challenge is making those capabilities useful in systems that can perform real work.

A model can generate a plan. An orchestrated system can coordinate the tools, information, decisions, and checks required to carry it out.

That difference matters.

We don’t need every AI application to become fully autonomous. We need systems that understand their responsibilities, operate within defined boundaries, handle failures, and know when a human should take control.

If there is one idea I want you to take away from this article, it is this:

Intelligence decides what to do. Orchestration makes sure the right things get done, with the right controls in place.

Start with a task you understand. Break it into steps. Identify the tools it needs. Build the simplest workflow that works. Then test its failure cases before giving it more autonomy.

Because the real engineering challenge isn’t just making AI capable.

It is making AI dependable.

One question to leave you with:

If you could delegate one repetitive task from your daily work to an AI system, what would it be — and which action would you never allow it to perform without human approval?

This is the beginning of my exploration into the engineering behind intelligent systems, from understanding how AI works to discovering how we can build systems that reliably execute real-world tasks.
References

[2] J. Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (2022), NeurIPS 2022

[3] S. Yao et al., Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models (2023), arXiv

[4] S. Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (2023), ICLR 2023

[5] Anthropic, Building Effective Agents, Anthropic Research

[6] N. Shinn and B. Labash, Reflexion: An Autonomous Agent with Dynamic Memory and Self-Reflection (2023), arXiv

[7] Y. Shen et al., HuggingGPT: Solving AI Tasks with ChatGPT and its Friends in Hugging Face (2023), arXiv

items.title: Home Depot wants your AI agent to show some ID first
items.summary: Home Depot's CIO shares how she's thinking about AI agents, cybersecurity, and Anthropic's Mythos. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Have an AI agent? Need a hammer? Home Depot is thinking about how to make that palatable for the retailer. Angie Brown, the company's CIO, spoke to Business Insider about agents, the PHP cyber scramble, and AI fixes. She also talked about Home Depot's use of Anthropic's Mythos, and early attempts to join its Project Glasswing. Home Depot wants to roll out the welcome mat for your AI agent — so long as it's wearing a name tag and acting on your behalf. During a sit-down interview with Business Insider, Angie Brown , the company's executive vice president and chief information officer, said the retailer wants to support AI agents that can search and buy products on a customer's behalf. But Home Depot needs to be sure of two things first. "We want to know you're not a bot, and we actually want to know if it's you," she said. "That's something that Muse is working on right now, to self-identify." Her comments are the latest glimpse into how legacy retailers — and their tech staff — are thinking about the possible next generation of online shopping. Recently, several Silicon Valley companies have launched consumer-focused AI agents, such as Meta's Muse and Spear Street Technology's Instinct AI . They promise agents capable of scanning the internet, comparing products, filling carts, and buying items with little to no intervention from the person who sent them. Their rollout has been met with varying levels of resistance and buy-in from online retailers. Amazon barred Muse from shopping on its marketplace, saying the bots didn't properly identify themselves. Several other retailers — including Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora, and Shopify — have announced integrations or openness to AI agents. In October, Meta announced that it co-developed a personal agent protocol with Sierra AI to standardize AI agent identification. Brown said Home Depot is open to the idea of AI agents, but the retailer doesn't want to lose its connection with loyal customers. Frequent Home Depot shoppers, such as contractors and remodelers, are part of the company's Pro Rewards platform, where they're eligible for discounts. The retailer doesn't "want to lose contact with the customer," she said. "That's the next evolution," Brown added, confirming that Home Depot is in active conversations with Meta about how Muse should introduce itself to websites. "There's openness on both sides, because they want it to grow." Home Depot is already using AI to defend itself Brown said Home Depot is deploying AI amid a recent wave of cybersecurity worries. Last week, companies around the world raced to patch critical vulnerabilities in PHP , a programming language used in an estimated 70% of websites. The flaws were discovered with help from OpenAI and prompted US cybersecurity officials to urge affected organizations to update their systems or, in some cases, take them offline. Brown, whose remit includes Home Depot's cybersecurity, called the hours after the warning a "little hectic," but said the company's main website was not affected. "We had a couple of operating units — companies we've bought and things like that that are a little bit smaller — that had to plug a few vulnerabilities," she said, including an internal job application system that was taken down "in the middle of the day for about an hour to patch." Otherwise, she said, the company was largely spared from the sudden tech anxieties. Home Depot, Brown confirmed to Business Insider, has access to Anthropic's Mythos AI model, though the company wasn't granted early access via Project Glasswing, "despite our best efforts, and calling a lot of friends." Those slots were largely reserved for banks and cybersecurity firms, not major retailers. The Anthropic models "found a few things" for Home Depot to fix in its code — but the agents also found a few "false positives," Brown said. Home Depot, she said, has long ranked cybersecurity vulnerabilities, but AI is leading the company to rethink its desired time to deploy a fix. "The speed to fix a vulnerability has to be driven down to hours," she said. Update, November 2, 2026 — This story has been updated to reflect that Home Depot has not participated in Anthropic's Project Glasswing initiative. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Anthropic's amended IPO paperwork reveals soaring Q3 revenue and a stunning compute bill
items.summary: Anthropic's fresh S-1 updates complicate its profitability narrative. Oliver Contreras / AFP via Getty Images Anthropic filed an amended S-1 filing on Monday, giving investors a more recent picture of its financials. The update reveals Q3 revenue of nearly $17 billion and an overall operating loss for the period ending September 30. The company also disclosed $895 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments. Anthropic's revenue is soaring. So is the cost to keep Claude running. On Monday, the AI company filed an amended version of its S-1, the public filing that discloses its financials ahead of its much-anticipated initial public offering. The company filed the original paperwork last week. Monday's amendments include the third-quarter numbers that didn't make it into the initial filing: Anthropic generated nearly $17 billion in revenue during the period, a more than $5 billion increase from the prior quarter and roughly 12X year over year. But the compute required to power that growth weighed on the business. Anthropic swung back to a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter, after reporting $974 million in operating income in the second. Anthropic wrote in the filing that its Q3 operating loss was "primarily driven by $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments," which it said costs significantly more than comparable multiyear arrangements. The company also disclosed about $895 billion in committed spending on compute and infrastructure — nearly half of it expected by the end of 2030. Anthropic's fresh disclosure illustrates the often shifting economics of the AI race. While their increasingly capable AI products are spurring adoption, the frontier labs are also committing to enormous amounts of computing capacity — which can take years to build and come online — in an effort to meet anticipated demand. Anthropic's compute and infrastructure charges rose to $9.9 billion in the third quarter. That's a 4X increase in one year. Anthropic also reported $2 billion in non-cash charges related to its donation-matching program , where employees can pledge equity awards to charitable causes, and the company matches the pledge with nonvoting Class N shares. The company has not yet disclosed an IPO price range, number of shares, or the size of the offering. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Anthropic's fresh S-1 updates complicate its profitability narrative.

Oliver Contreras / AFP via Getty Images

  • Anthropic filed an amended S-1 filing on Monday, giving investors a more recent picture of its financials.
  • The update reveals Q3 revenue of nearly $17 billion and an overall operating loss for the period ending September 30.
  • The company also disclosed $895 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments.

Anthropic's revenue is soaring. So is the cost to keep Claude running.

On Monday, the AI company filed an amended version of its S-1, the public filing that discloses its financials ahead of its much-anticipated initial public offering. The company filed the original paperwork last week.

Monday's amendments include the third-quarter numbers that didn't make it into the initial filing: Anthropic generated nearly $17 billion in revenue during the period, a more than $5 billion increase from the prior quarter and roughly 12X year over year.

But the compute required to power that growth weighed on the business. Anthropic swung back to a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter, after reporting $974 million in operating income in the second.

Anthropic wrote in the filing that its Q3 operating loss was "primarily driven by $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments," which it said costs significantly more than comparable multiyear arrangements.

The company also disclosed about $895 billion in committed spending on compute and infrastructure — nearly half of it expected by the end of 2030.

Anthropic's fresh disclosure illustrates the often shifting economics of the AI race. While their increasingly capable AI products are spurring adoption, the frontier labs are also committing to enormous amounts of computing capacity — which can take years to build and come online — in an effort to meet anticipated demand.

Anthropic's compute and infrastructure charges rose to $9.9 billion in the third quarter. That's a 4X increase in one year.

Anthropic also reported $2 billion in non-cash charges related to its donation-matching program, where employees can pledge equity awards to charitable causes, and the company matches the pledge with nonvoting Class N shares.

The company has not yet disclosed an IPO price range, number of shares, or the size of the offering.

items.title: Anthropic Posts $17 Bn in Q3 Revenue, Swings to Operating Loss
items.summary: Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue in Q3 2026, up from $11.6 billion in the previous quarter. But it recorded an operating loss of $567 million. The company shared its July to September financials in updated filings ahead of its planned IPO. Revenue increased more than 12 times from approximately $1.4 billion year-on-year, but performance reversed from a $974 million profit in Q2 to a loss in Q3 Anthropic attributed the latest quarter’s operating loss partly to its reliance on short-term computing capacity. The company incurred $5 billion in expenses for short-term computing during Q3, which it said costs significantly more than capacity secured through multi-year agreements. It also recorded $2 billion in non-cash expenses related to its employee share-donation matching programme. The company’s amended filing also disclosed $33.2 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, compared with $2.5 billion in the same period last year. Its operating loss for the nine months stood at $1.26 billion. Its net loss reached $104 billion, including a $94.3 billion non-cash charge reflecting changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and other financing instruments. Anthropic filed its initial registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26. The filing also disclosed approximately $895.4 billion in committed spending on computing and infrastructure. Of this, around $447.5 billion is expected to fall due before the end of 2030, including $69.8 billion in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. These commitments reflect the long-term contracts Anthropic uses to secure computing capacity for model training and inference. Anthropic reported more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, up from more than 950 a year earlier. The company said successive model releases and increased usage contributed to revenue growth. However, price reductions on newer models and contractual discounts reduced revenue by about $600 million between Q2 and Q3.

items.title: Investors Are Getting Palpably Nervous About the AI Industry’s Financial Situation
items.summary: For years now, some of the biggest players in the AI space have been investing in smaller startups — which in turn use the same exact money to purchase services from the same large companies. Investors have watched this circular financing with quiet but growing trepidation. After all, as the Wall Street Journal points out , if the AI bubble were to pop, the consequences could be dire. Now, with fears over a sudden collapse are as palpable as ever, such a “tangled web of AI bets,” as the newspaper puts it, could spell disaster. The signs aren’t exactly hard to identify. Just last week, Google’s parent company Alphabet experienced the biggest drop in its market value in its history, wiping out well over half a trillion dollars in value . The accompanying crash likely didn’t just send jitters across tech markets. Since the AI industry is effectively propping up the entire US economy, its failure could have far-reaching consequences to a public that’s increasingly skeptical of its offerings . Since most of these companies’ fates are inextricably linked by circular financing, a major economic downturn or weakening demand could have cascading repercussions, especially considering much of the sector’s financing is based on debt. Beyond the tech industry’s very bad week, data center operators aren’t looking much better. Nvidia customer CoreWave, which analysts have dubbed the “ AI trade’s canary in the coal mine ,” has also seen its shares decline over months, raising plenty of flags . Despite the widespread unease, enormous data center expansion efforts are in full swing, major bipartisan backlash notwithstanding. It’s an unprecedented all-in that could jeopardize the entire economy if it were to collapse. Even beyond the US, the circular financing is starting to worry investors sweat in Asia. The Bank of Korea recently warned of a “semiconductor version of Dutch disease,” an economic concept describing a booming sector that overtakes all other tradable market segments. Yet the country is doubling down, with president Lee Jae Myung pledging today to “boldly invest in AI and future growth engines,” effectively doubling AI and chip spending for next year. Only time will tell whether that’ll be the right move as more and more investors get cold feet. More on the AI bubble: Stock Market Bloodbath Spikes Fears of AI Bubble Bursting
items.summary_html:
For years now, some of the biggest players in the AI space have been investing in smaller startups — which in turn use the same exact money to purchase services from the same large companies.

Investors have watched this circular financing with quiet but growing trepidation. After all, as the Wall Street Journal points out, if the AI bubble were to pop, the consequences could be dire. Now, with fears over a sudden collapse are as palpable as ever, such a “tangled web of AI bets,” as the newspaper puts it, could spell disaster.

The signs aren’t exactly hard to identify. Just last week, Google’s parent company Alphabet experienced the biggest drop in its market value in its history, wiping out well over half a trillion dollars in value.

The accompanying crash likely didn’t just send jitters across tech markets. Since the AI industry is effectively propping up the entire US economy, its failure could have far-reaching consequences to a public that’s increasingly skeptical of its offerings.

Since most of these companies’ fates are inextricably linked by circular financing, a major economic downturn or weakening demand could have cascading repercussions, especially considering much of the sector’s financing is based on debt.

Beyond the tech industry’s very bad week, data center operators aren’t looking much better. Nvidia customer CoreWave, which analysts have dubbed the “AI trade’s canary in the coal mine,” has also seen its shares decline over months, raising plenty of flags.

Despite the widespread unease, enormous data center expansion efforts are in full swing, major bipartisan backlash notwithstanding. It’s an unprecedented all-in that could jeopardize the entire economy if it were to collapse.

Even beyond the US, the circular financing is starting to worry investors sweat in Asia. The Bank of Korea recently warned of a “semiconductor version of Dutch disease,” an economic concept describing a booming sector that overtakes all other tradable market segments.

Yet the country is doubling down, with president Lee Jae Myung pledging today to “boldly invest in AI and future growth engines,” effectively doubling AI and chip spending for next year.

Only time will tell whether that’ll be the right move as more and more investors get cold feet.
