items.title: OpenAI AI Training Preferences in robots.txt: A Safe Rollout Guide for Web Teams
items.summary: OpenAI AI Training Preferences in robots.txt A shared AI-training signal is arriving. Treat it as a versioned content-use policy — not a magic bot block — and you can keep your site’s intent clear without breaking another path by accident. One website can have more than one AI-use decision. The useful first step is to name each one. A two-line change in robots.txt can feel wonderfully simple: publish a preference, solve an AI-policy question, move on. That is exactly why it deserves more care. On October 30, OpenAI said it plans to honor a shared robots.txt signal that lets site operators state a preference about the use of content for foundational generative-AI training. Google announced support for the same direction. The proposal is based on current IETF work and uses a policy token named __usage_ai-training. The important word is preference . The signal is about a particular use of content: changing the learned parameters of a generative model. It is not, by itself, a general instruction to crawl or not crawl. It does not settle search inclusion, user-triggered visits, CDN bot rules, historic collection, contract terms, or every future AI use case. That distinction is not a technical footnote. It is the difference between a policy that says what your organization meant and one that accidentally changes discovery, support, analytics, or the next person’s understanding of the system. Do not start with a line of syntax. Start with a sentence your team can defend: “We do or do not permit this part of the site to be used for generative-AI training.” This guide gives web developers, platform teams, and technical SEO leads a safe rollout path. It does not offer legal advice. Its aim is narrower and more practical: make the live policy, delivery path, and evidence match the decision. What changed — and what did not The IETF Internet-Draft describes a way to attach a content-use preference to paths using ordinary robots.txt group syntax. The shared token is __usage_ai-training. A disallow rule expresses a preference against AI training for a matching path; an allow rule expresses a preference in favor. That draft is work in progress, not a finished RFC. OpenAI says it will share implementation details as its rollout develops. Google says it intends to support the signal in early 2027. In other words: your policy design can begin now, but production behavior should be verified against each provider’s current documentation and observed rollout status before anyone claims the change is active everywhere. What has not changed is just as useful: Existing crawler rules remain separate. A rule for GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, Google-Extended, or another named product still carries its own documented meaning. Search is a different decision. OpenAI documents OAI-SearchBot for automated search crawling, while GPTBot concerns potential use in foundational-model training. Do not assume one rule answers both questions. User-requested retrieval is different again. OpenAI documents ChatGPT-User for visits initiated by a user or Custom GPT action; it is not automatic web crawling in the usual sense. A preference signal is not a firewall. It communicates intent to participating consumers. It does not stop a noncompliant client, a spoofed user agent, or a data source that never reads your file. This is good news for system design. You do not have to make one overloaded “AI yes/no” switch do every job. You can name the jobs and use the control that fits each one. Use a four-boundary rollout Most mistakes happen when an organization jumps from a policy meeting to a production file. A better pattern has four boundaries: intent, policy, delivery, and evidence. Each boundary asks a simple question, and each one catches a different kind of failure. 1. Intent: what use are you deciding about? Write the decision in plain language before opening a repository. “No AI” is too vague to implement well. Ask the content owner, legal or policy lead, product owner, and platform owner to decide separately: May public pages be used to train future generative models? May selected public assets, such as a press kit or API examples, be treated differently? Do we want automated discovery systems to access pages for search? Do we need to restrict high-volume traffic for capacity or security reasons? Are there contractual, regional, customer, or paid-content exceptions? Those answers might all be “yes,” all be “no,” or form a mix. A documentation site may decline training for most material while allowing a small media kit. A public support center may allow search discovery but choose a separate training preference. A SaaS dashboard should normally rely on authentication and application controls, not a public crawler policy, to protect customer data. Practical rule: give every answer an owner. “Marketing owns public content intent; platform owns delivery; security owns bot enforcement; SEO owns search-impact review” is far safer than “engineering will update robots.” 2. Policy: express the smallest correct preference Once intent is clear, use the narrowest rule that says it. The current draft’s whole-site opt-out pattern is straightforward: User-Agent: __usage_ai-training Disallow: / For a site that wants a broad training preference against use but wishes to carve out a public asset path, the draft provides this shape: User-Agent: __usage_ai-training Disallow: / Allow: /press-kit/ Do not copy these examples into production and then delete existing named-agent groups. The shared token is designed to be orthogonal to those groups. Keep a separate block for each existing policy that still matters. If your team already has a rule for GPTBot, preserve or deliberately revise it based on its own meaning. If you use Google-Extended, review it too: Google says the new shared opt-out will be interpreted as a Google-Extended disallow when Google-Extended is not explicitly specified, but your explicit configuration should still communicate your intent clearly. Also avoid an easy trap from ordinary crawler thinking. The draft says a wildcard group such as User-Agent: * does not express this new policy preference. The shared policy token needs its own group. A global block may affect conventional crawler access, but it is not a substitute for documenting a training preference. The policy file is only one stage. Keep training preference, discovery behavior, and release verification on separate tracks. 3. Delivery: make sure the live site serves the policy you reviewed A correct commit can still produce a wrong site. robots.txt is often assembled through a framework route, CMS plugin, static build, CDN edge rule, hostname redirect, or WAF setting. Each layer is an opportunity for drift. Start by finding the source of truth. Is the file committed in the repository? Generated from a CMS checkbox? Written by a framework handler? Overridden by a platform? Then map the public endpoints that matter: apex domain, www, preview host, alternate locale host, and any content subdomain. A policy that exists only on one hostname may not represent what you think it represents. Next, fetch the artifact like a client would. Do not rely only on a local file. curl -i https://example.com/robots.txt curl -sS https://example.com/robots.txt | sed -n '1,160p' # Follow the public redirect path too. curl -IL https://www.example.com/robots.txt Check the status code, redirect destination, content type, cache headers, and actual body. In CI, a lightweight assertion can catch accidental removal during a theme, CDN, or application deployment: curl -fsS https://example.com/robots.txt \ | grep -Fqx 'User-Agent: __usage_ai-training' curl -fsS https://example.com/robots.txt \ | grep -Fqx 'Disallow: /' That example is intentionally simple. In a real check, parse groups rather than grepping the whole file, because another group may contain a matching line with a different meaning. The point is to turn a sensitive policy into a release assertion, not a memory test. 4. Evidence: record what you decided and what you observed A policy needs a receipt. Store a short change record beside the configuration or in the ticket that introduced it. Include the decision owner, the exact paths covered, named-agent rules reviewed, delivery endpoints checked, review date, and a link to the provider documentation used at that time. Then track evidence that answers the questions you can actually answer. Web logs can show requests, bot verification status, paths, response codes, rate patterns, and whether a CDN blocked traffic. They cannot prove that every third party complied with a future-use preference. A snapshot of a provider’s documentation can show stated support, not the contents of a training corpus. That may sound modest. It is also honest and operationally useful. Your goal is not to promise perfect visibility into another organization’s systems. Your goal is to keep your own intent, controls, and escalation path clear. Do not collapse three different controls into one Teams commonly use “AI crawler” as if it were one thing. It is a category, not a control plane. Separate these cases in your runbook. Training preference This is the new shared signal’s job. It speaks to use of retrieved content for training generative models. It is a content-use policy. It is not a rate-limit setting, search command, or authentication boundary. Automated search discovery Discovery can have product-specific rules. OpenAI’s crawler documentation distinguishes OAI-SearchBot from GPTBot. If your publishing strategy values appearing in search-assisted answers, do not make a training-policy change without checking that the separate discovery policy still says what you intend. Conversely, allowing a search bot does not equal opting in to training. Traffic enforcement If the requirement is “this client must not reach this endpoint,” use enforcement controls: authentication, authorization, network filtering, a WAF, bot verification, rate limits, or a CDN rule. Validate claimed bots against providers’ published verification guidance where available. Blocking on a user-agent string alone is weak because user agents can be spoofed. Keeping these controls separate reduces two bad outcomes: a public policy being treated as a security mechanism, and a security rule being mistaken for a content-use preference. A deployment checklist your team can actually use Use this as a pull-request checklist or a short change ticket. It is deliberately small enough to survive real releases. Decision recorded: state the training preference in plain language and name the content owner. Scope reviewed: list domains, subdomains, path exceptions, locales, previews, and customer-only areas. Existing rules preserved: review GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, Google-Extended, and any other named groups instead of deleting them casually. New token isolated: add a dedicated __usage_ai-training group; do not assume a wildcard group carries the same meaning. Generated source checked: confirm whether the CMS, framework, CDN, or hosting platform can overwrite the file. Live artifact tested: fetch every production hostname after deployment and inspect redirects, body, and cache behavior. Security controls reviewed: keep access control, WAF, and rate limiting separate from the preference signal. Evidence saved: retain the diff, live fetch output, documentation links, owner, and next review date. For larger sites, add a policy test fixture. Give it a sample robots.txt with a broad disallow, a specific allow exception, legacy crawler groups, and a wildcard group. Assert that your parser and release tooling preserve each group. This catches an especially common failure: a “cleanup” change that flattens distinct policies into one block. Release confidence comes from checking the live artifact and its delivery path, not from trusting a local file. Handle the rollout as a change, not a one-time edit The shared signal is new. Provider support, documented semantics, and the IETF draft can change. That makes this a configuration with a review cycle, not an eternal snippet to paste into a theme. Set a calendar reminder tied to the rollout status of the providers you care about. Recheck the official documentation when OpenAI publishes implementation details, when Google begins support, when your CDN changes bot settings, and when an agency or plugin proposes a “helpful” robots update. Treat a platform migration, new domain, CMS redesign, or SEO audit as a trigger for the same review. A simple policy manifest can make that durable: policy: ai-training-preference owner: web-platform@example.com scope: public marketing and docs hosts intent: disallow generative-AI training except /press-kit/ separate_reviews: - automated search discovery - user-initiated fetches - bot enforcement and rate limits verified_live: 2026-11-01 next_review: provider-rollout-or-next-platform-change Keep that manifest as an internal record; it is not a proposed web standard. Its value is human: when a future teammate asks why a strange token exists, the answer is close to the code and connected to a decision. The durable lesson: policy should say one thing clearly The shared training-preference signal is useful precisely because it narrows a messy problem. You no longer have to maintain only a long list of vendor-specific names to express a broad training choice. But a broad choice still needs careful boundaries. Decide what use of content you mean. Express the smallest correct policy. Preserve separate crawler and discovery controls. Verify the live file through the real delivery stack. Record evidence without overstating what it can prove. That is how a tiny robots.txt change becomes a trustworthy web-platform policy rather than a mysterious line everyone is afraid to touch. FAQ What is __usage_ai-training? It is the shared policy token described by an IETF Internet-Draft for expressing a preference about use of website content in generative-AI training. It appears in a dedicated robots.txt group. The draft is work in progress, so check current provider documentation before relying on implementation behavior. Does an AI training preference block crawlers from visiting my site? No. The draft explicitly separates content-use preferences from crawler traffic management. Use named crawler groups if you want to express a crawler preference, and use authentication, a WAF, rate limits, or other enforcement controls when you need to restrict access. Can I block model training but still allow OpenAI search discovery? These are separate decisions. OpenAI documents GPTBot for potential foundational-model training use and OAI-SearchBot for automated search crawling. Review each relevant rule independently so your configuration matches your intended discovery policy. Should I remove existing GPTBot or Google-Extended rules? Not automatically. The shared signal is designed to coexist with existing controls, and providers can document their own precedence rules. Preserve existing groups until your team deliberately decides how each one should behave and verifies current provider guidance. Does this guarantee that my content will never appear in an AI response? No. A training preference is not a universal control over search, grounding, user-initiated fetches, prior collection, third-party datasets, or every AI product. Avoid guarantees. Document the specific use you are expressing a preference about and maintain separate controls for other goals. How do I verify the configuration after deployment? Fetch the public /robots.txt on every production hostname, inspect the redirect chain and final body, and save that evidence with the change record. Also check the CMS, CDN, and WAF layers that can rewrite or override the file. Revisit the test when a provider rollout or platform change occurs. items.summary_html:
OpenAI AI Training Preferences in robots.txt

A shared AI-training signal is arriving. Treat it as a versioned content-use policy — not a magic bot block — and you can keep your site’s intent clear without breaking another path by accident.

One website can have more than one AI-use decision. The useful first step is to name each one.

A two-line change in robots.txt can feel wonderfully simple: publish a preference, solve an AI-policy question, move on. That is exactly why it deserves more care.

On October 30, OpenAI said it plans to honor a shared robots.txt signal that lets site operators state a preference about the use of content for foundational generative-AI training. Google announced support for the same direction. The proposal is based on current IETF work and uses a policy token named __usage_ai-training.

The important word is preference. The signal is about a particular use of content: changing the learned parameters of a generative model. It is not, by itself, a general instruction to crawl or not crawl. It does not settle search inclusion, user-triggered visits, CDN bot rules, historic collection, contract terms, or every future AI use case.

That distinction is not a technical footnote. It is the difference between a policy that says what your organization meant and one that accidentally changes discovery, support, analytics, or the next person’s understanding of the system.

Do not start with a line of syntax. Start with a sentence your team can defend: “We do or do not permit this part of the site to be used for generative-AI training.”

This guide gives web developers, platform teams, and technical SEO leads a safe rollout path. It does not offer legal advice. Its aim is narrower and more practical: make the live policy, delivery path, and evidence match the decision.

What changed — and what did not

The IETF Internet-Draft describes a way to attach a content-use preference to paths using ordinary robots.txt group syntax. The shared token is __usage_ai-training. A disallow rule expresses a preference against AI training for a matching path; an allow rule expresses a preference in favor.

That draft is work in progress, not a finished RFC. OpenAI says it will share implementation details as its rollout develops. Google says it intends to support the signal in early 2027. In other words: your policy design can begin now, but production behavior should be verified against each provider’s current documentation and observed rollout status before anyone claims the change is active everywhere.

What has not changed is just as useful:

  • Existing crawler rules remain separate. A rule for GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, Google-Extended, or another named product still carries its own documented meaning.
  • Search is a different decision. OpenAI documents OAI-SearchBot for automated search crawling, while GPTBot concerns potential use in foundational-model training. Do not assume one rule answers both questions.
  • User-requested retrieval is different again. OpenAI documents ChatGPT-User for visits initiated by a user or Custom GPT action; it is not automatic web crawling in the usual sense.
  • A preference signal is not a firewall. It communicates intent to participating consumers. It does not stop a noncompliant client, a spoofed user agent, or a data source that never reads your file.

This is good news for system design. You do not have to make one overloaded “AI yes/no” switch do every job. You can name the jobs and use the control that fits each one.

Use a four-boundary rollout

Most mistakes happen when an organization jumps from a policy meeting to a production file. A better pattern has four boundaries: intent, policy, delivery, and evidence. Each boundary asks a simple question, and each one catches a different kind of failure.

1. Intent: what use are you deciding about?

Write the decision in plain language before opening a repository. “No AI” is too vague to implement well. Ask the content owner, legal or policy lead, product owner, and platform owner to decide separately:

  • May public pages be used to train future generative models?
  • May selected public assets, such as a press kit or API examples, be treated differently?
  • Do we want automated discovery systems to access pages for search?
  • Do we need to restrict high-volume traffic for capacity or security reasons?
  • Are there contractual, regional, customer, or paid-content exceptions?

Those answers might all be “yes,” all be “no,” or form a mix. A documentation site may decline training for most material while allowing a small media kit. A public support center may allow search discovery but choose a separate training preference. A SaaS dashboard should normally rely on authentication and application controls, not a public crawler policy, to protect customer data.

Practical rule: give every answer an owner. “Marketing owns public content intent; platform owns delivery; security owns bot enforcement; SEO owns search-impact review” is far safer than “engineering will update robots.”

2. Policy: express the smallest correct preference

Once intent is clear, use the narrowest rule that says it. The current draft’s whole-site opt-out pattern is straightforward:

User-Agent: __usage_ai-training
Disallow: /

For a site that wants a broad training preference against use but wishes to carve out a public asset path, the draft provides this shape:

User-Agent: __usage_ai-training
Disallow: /
Allow: /press-kit/

Do not copy these examples into production and then delete existing named-agent groups. The shared token is designed to be orthogonal to those groups. Keep a separate block for each existing policy that still matters. If your team already has a rule for GPTBot, preserve or deliberately revise it based on its own meaning. If you use Google-Extended, review it too: Google says the new shared opt-out will be interpreted as a Google-Extended disallow when Google-Extended is not explicitly specified, but your explicit configuration should still communicate your intent clearly.

Also avoid an easy trap from ordinary crawler thinking. The draft says a wildcard group such as User-Agent: * does not express this new policy preference. The shared policy token needs its own group. A global block may affect conventional crawler access, but it is not a substitute for documenting a training preference.

The policy file is only one stage. Keep training preference, discovery behavior, and release verification on separate tracks.

3. Delivery: make sure the live site serves the policy you reviewed

A correct commit can still produce a wrong site. robots.txt is often assembled through a framework route, CMS plugin, static build, CDN edge rule, hostname redirect, or WAF setting. Each layer is an opportunity for drift.

Start by finding the source of truth. Is the file committed in the repository? Generated from a CMS checkbox? Written by a framework handler? Overridden by a platform? Then map the public endpoints that matter: apex domain, www, preview host, alternate locale host, and any content subdomain. A policy that exists only on one hostname may not represent what you think it represents.

Next, fetch the artifact like a client would. Do not rely only on a local file.

curl -i https://example.com/robots.txt
curl -sS https://example.com/robots.txt | sed -n '1,160p'
# Follow the public redirect path too.
curl -IL https://www.example.com/robots.txt

Check the status code, redirect destination, content type, cache headers, and actual body. In CI, a lightweight assertion can catch accidental removal during a theme, CDN, or application deployment:

curl -fsS https://example.com/robots.txt \
  | grep -Fqx 'User-Agent: __usage_ai-training'
curl -fsS https://example.com/robots.txt \
  | grep -Fqx 'Disallow: /'

That example is intentionally simple. In a real check, parse groups rather than grepping the whole file, because another group may contain a matching line with a different meaning. The point is to turn a sensitive policy into a release assertion, not a memory test.

4. Evidence: record what you decided and what you observed

A policy needs a receipt. Store a short change record beside the configuration or in the ticket that introduced it. Include the decision owner, the exact paths covered, named-agent rules reviewed, delivery endpoints checked, review date, and a link to the provider documentation used at that time.

Then track evidence that answers the questions you can actually answer. Web logs can show requests, bot verification status, paths, response codes, rate patterns, and whether a CDN blocked traffic. They cannot prove that every third party complied with a future-use preference. A snapshot of a provider’s documentation can show stated support, not the contents of a training corpus.

That may sound modest. It is also honest and operationally useful. Your goal is not to promise perfect visibility into another organization’s systems. Your goal is to keep your own intent, controls, and escalation path clear.

Do not collapse three different controls into one

Teams commonly use “AI crawler” as if it were one thing. It is a category, not a control plane. Separate these cases in your runbook.

Training preference

This is the new shared signal’s job. It speaks to use of retrieved content for training generative models. It is a content-use policy. It is not a rate-limit setting, search command, or authentication boundary.

Automated search discovery

Discovery can have product-specific rules. OpenAI’s crawler documentation distinguishes OAI-SearchBot from GPTBot. If your publishing strategy values appearing in search-assisted answers, do not make a training-policy change without checking that the separate discovery policy still says what you intend. Conversely, allowing a search bot does not equal opting in to training.

Traffic enforcement

If the requirement is “this client must not reach this endpoint,” use enforcement controls: authentication, authorization, network filtering, a WAF, bot verification, rate limits, or a CDN rule. Validate claimed bots against providers’ published verification guidance where available. Blocking on a user-agent string alone is weak because user agents can be spoofed.

Keeping these controls separate reduces two bad outcomes: a public policy being treated as a security mechanism, and a security rule being mistaken for a content-use preference.

A deployment checklist your team can actually use

Use this as a pull-request checklist or a short change ticket. It is deliberately small enough to survive real releases.

  • Decision recorded: state the training preference in plain language and name the content owner.
  • Scope reviewed: list domains, subdomains, path exceptions, locales, previews, and customer-only areas.
  • Existing rules preserved: review GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, Google-Extended, and any other named groups instead of deleting them casually.
  • New token isolated: add a dedicated __usage_ai-training group; do not assume a wildcard group carries the same meaning.
  • Generated source checked: confirm whether the CMS, framework, CDN, or hosting platform can overwrite the file.
  • Live artifact tested: fetch every production hostname after deployment and inspect redirects, body, and cache behavior.
  • Security controls reviewed: keep access control, WAF, and rate limiting separate from the preference signal.
  • Evidence saved: retain the diff, live fetch output, documentation links, owner, and next review date.

For larger sites, add a policy test fixture. Give it a sample robots.txt with a broad disallow, a specific allow exception, legacy crawler groups, and a wildcard group. Assert that your parser and release tooling preserve each group. This catches an especially common failure: a “cleanup” change that flattens distinct policies into one block.

Release confidence comes from checking the live artifact and its delivery path, not from trusting a local file.

Handle the rollout as a change, not a one-time edit

The shared signal is new. Provider support, documented semantics, and the IETF draft can change. That makes this a configuration with a review cycle, not an eternal snippet to paste into a theme.

Set a calendar reminder tied to the rollout status of the providers you care about. Recheck the official documentation when OpenAI publishes implementation details, when Google begins support, when your CDN changes bot settings, and when an agency or plugin proposes a “helpful” robots update. Treat a platform migration, new domain, CMS redesign, or SEO audit as a trigger for the same review.

A simple policy manifest can make that durable:

policy: ai-training-preference
owner: web-platform@example.com
scope: public marketing and docs hosts
intent: disallow generative-AI training except /press-kit/
separate_reviews:
  - automated search discovery
  - user-initiated fetches
  - bot enforcement and rate limits
verified_live: 2026-11-01
next_review: provider-rollout-or-next-platform-change

Keep that manifest as an internal record; it is not a proposed web standard. Its value is human: when a future teammate asks why a strange token exists, the answer is close to the code and connected to a decision.

The durable lesson: policy should say one thing clearly

The shared training-preference signal is useful precisely because it narrows a messy problem. You no longer have to maintain only a long list of vendor-specific names to express a broad training choice. But a broad choice still needs careful boundaries.

Decide what use of content you mean. Express the smallest correct policy. Preserve separate crawler and discovery controls. Verify the live file through the real delivery stack. Record evidence without overstating what it can prove.

That is how a tiny robots.txt change becomes a trustworthy web-platform policy rather than a mysterious line everyone is afraid to touch.

FAQWhat is __usage_ai-training?

It is the shared policy token described by an IETF Internet-Draft for expressing a preference about use of website content in generative-AI training. It appears in a dedicated robots.txt group. The draft is work in progress, so check current provider documentation before relying on implementation behavior.

Does an AI training preference block crawlers from visiting my site?

No. The draft explicitly separates content-use preferences from crawler traffic management. Use named crawler groups if you want to express a crawler preference, and use authentication, a WAF, rate limits, or other enforcement controls when you need to restrict access.

Can I block model training but still allow OpenAI search discovery?

These are separate decisions. OpenAI documents GPTBot for potential foundational-model training use and OAI-SearchBot for automated search crawling. Review each relevant rule independently so your configuration matches your intended discovery policy.

Should I remove existing GPTBot or Google-Extended rules?

Not automatically. The shared signal is designed to coexist with existing controls, and providers can document their own precedence rules. Preserve existing groups until your team deliberately decides how each one should behave and verifies current provider guidance.

Does this guarantee that my content will never appear in an AI response?

No. A training preference is not a universal control over search, grounding, user-initiated fetches, prior collection, third-party datasets, or every AI product. Avoid guarantees. Document the specific use you are expressing a preference about and maintain separate controls for other goals.

How do I verify the configuration after deployment?

Fetch the public /robots.txt on every production hostname, inspect the redirect chain and final body, and save that evidence with the change record. Also check the CMS, CDN, and WAF layers that can rewrite or override the file. Revisit the test when a provider rollout or platform change occurs.

Sources
  • OpenAI: Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
  • IETF Internet-Draft: Machine-Readable Training Preference Signal
  • OpenAI: Overview of crawlers
  • Google Search Central: Supporting a shared AI training control for websites
  • Microsoft Bing Webmaster Tools: New AI preferences

items.title: Part XX — Delta Lake’s Transaction Log: Time Travel, VACUUM, and the Files That Never Die
items.summary: Your table never deletes anything. The Delta log is an append-only ledger, and every file you “removed” is still sitting on S3 until the log’s retention rules, the checkpoint cadence, and your VACUUM discipline all agree it can die. Misunderstand any one of the three and you get a $41,000-a-month storage bill — or worse, a restore that points at files which no longer exist. Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV | Part XV | Part XVI | Part XVII | Part XVIII | Part XIX | Part XX The $41,000-a-Month DELETE That Deleted Nothing The page came at 2:58 AM on a Tuesday, and it wasn’t from a pipeline. It was from FinOps, in Slack, with a screenshot: our S3 spend had crossed $41,000 for the month, up from $9,400 five months earlier, and the line was still climbing. The accused was bronze.clickstream — 412 terabytes, fourteen months of raw click events, roughly 2.1 billion rows a day landing through a Structured Streaming MERGE. Six months before that night, we had deleted 238 terabytes from that table. A GDPR erasure request had forced us to purge nine months of history containing raw PII. The DELETE ran for eleven hours, the row counts confirmed it, the auditors signed off. And the storage bill did not move. Not by a gigabyte. We did what every team does: we blamed VACUUM. Then we checked, and VACUUM had been running green every Sunday for a year. VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 168 HOURS, dry-run clean, a few hundred gigabytes reclaimed each time, job healthy. The 238 terabytes were simply still there, on S3, billing us $0.023 per GB-month, while the table insisted they were gone. At 3:40 AM, running on caffeine and indignation, the on-call engineer did the obvious thing. He disabled the retention safety check and ran the nuclear option: -- the 3:40 AM version of "have you tried turning it off and on again" VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 0 HOURS It worked. Forty-one thousand dollars a month of dead files evaporated in ninety minutes. We went back to sleep feeling like heroes. At 9:04 AM, finance ran the month-end close. Their reconciliation query reads the table TIMESTAMP AS OF the last day of the month — a time-travel read, thirty-one days back. It failed instantly with FileNotFoundException: a file referenced in the transaction log could not be found. The version they needed had been vacuumed out from under them at 4 AM. So had the training snapshot the ML team had pinned for a model refresh. Two teams, two broken reads, one very long incident review. So: what does DELETE actually delete in Delta Lake, what is VACUUM legally allowed to remove, and why did 238 terabytes of "deleted" data survive six months of weekly vacuums — while thirty-one-day-old files died the moment we got impatient? The Mechanic Underneath: The Table Is a Ledger, Not a Directory Forget the parquet files for a minute. A Delta table is not a directory of data files. A Delta table is _delta_log/ — a directory of JSON files, each one a commit, each commit a list of actions . The data files are just the payload the ledger points at. Every commit appends one file: 00000000000000000000.json, 00000000000000000001.json, and so on. Inside, the actions that matter: add : this parquet file is now part of the table (path, size, partition values, file statistics). remove : this parquet file is no longer part of the table — with a deletionTimestamp and a dataChange flag. The file itself is untouched. It becomes a tombstone . protocol : the minimum reader/writer versions this table requires. metaData : schema, partition columns, table properties. txn : the streaming application ID and version, for idempotent micro-batch commits. commitInfo : who committed, when, with what operation. The state of the table at version N is the replay of every action from 0 to N. Nothing is ever mutated in place. A DELETE doesn't delete rows — it writes new parquet files without those rows and logs remove actions against the old ones. An UPDATE, a MERGE, an OPTIMIZE: all rewrites, all tombstones. The old files sit on S3, fully intact, until something with the authority to forget them comes along. Because replaying millions of JSON files on every read would be absurd, Delta writes a checkpoint every 10 commits (controlled by delta.checkpointInterval): a parquet file summarizing the complete table state at that version, with _last_checkpoint pointing at the newest one. Reading version N means loading the nearest checkpoint at or below N and replaying only the JSON tail after it. That tail — the checkpoint cadence, the JSON retention, the replay cost — is where our second bill was hiding, as we'll see. This is the whole mental model: the log is the table, the files are just evidence, and forgetting is a scheduled, retention-gated operation — never an immediate one. Optimistic Concurrency: Every Commit Is a Conditional Write on a Version Number Writers don’t take locks. A writer reads the current version V, does its (possibly enormous) work against that snapshot, then attempts to write V+1.json as an atomic conditional put — it succeeds only if V is still the latest version. If another writer got there first, Delta runs conflict detection: two blind appends to different partitions can both commit (the loser retries against V+1); two MERGEs touching overlapping files cannot, and the loser gets a ConcurrentAppendException. This is why the streaming MERGE into bronze.clickstream and the Sunday OPTIMIZE could coexist without corrupting anything — and also why our incident had a blast radius instead of a corruption. The 4 AM vacuum didn't corrupt the log; it deleted evidence the log still referenced. The ledger was perfect. The files were gone. Optimistic concurrency protects the log's integrity, not the physical files' existence. Those are two different durability promises, and we had confused them. The protocol action deserves a paranoid glance too. minReaderVersion and minWriterVersion gate which engine versions may touch the table, and modern Delta adds named table features — deletion vectors, column mapping, liquid clustering, v2 checkpoints. Bumping the protocol is a one-way door: old readers are locked out permanently. It has nothing to do with our incident, but it's the same class of mistake — a metadata decision with physical consequences that you only discover at 9:04 AM. Time Travel Is Log Replay, Not a Backup TIMESTAMP AS OF and VERSION AS OF feel like backups. They are not. There is no snapshot stored anywhere. A time-travel read resolves your timestamp to a version number, loads the nearest checkpoint at or below it, and replays the JSON tail — the exact same machinery as a current read, just stopping earlier. The consequence is absolute: a time-travel read is only as durable as the log entries and the data files they reference. Keep the log for 30 days and you can time-travel 30 days — provided nobody vacuumed the files those old versions point at. Our finance query needed version history 31 days deep. Our vacuum at RETAIN 0 HOURS had deleted every file unreferenced by the current version, including every file the 31-day-old version needed. The ledger still described a table that could be reconstructed; the reconstruction was impossible. FileNotFoundException is the log telling the truth about files that no longer exist. VACUUM Can Only Delete What the Log Has Already Forgotten Here is the actual deletion pipeline, in order: A DELETE/MERGE/UPDATE logs remove actions with a deletionTimestamp. The files are now tombstones — logically dead, physically alive. Tombstones are protected for delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration (default: 7 days). This is not a suggestion; it's the table property VACUUM consults. VACUUM ... RETAIN N HOURS deletes data files that are referenced by no table version within the retention window — and only if they're older than the threshold. It also refuses RETAIN under 168 hours unless you explicitly disable spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled, because a query or a streaming micro-batch can legitimately take longer than you think. Now the root cause of the $41,000 bill: eighteen months earlier, a well-meaning predecessor had set two table properties “for audit safety”: 'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 365 days', 'delta.logRetentionDuration' = 'interval 365 days' Every tombstone the GDPR delete created was legally protected for a year. Our weekly VACUUM RETAIN 168 HOURS would list the 238 terabytes of dead files, check each one's deletionTimestamp against the one-year tombstone retention, and walk away. It ran green because it was doing exactly what the table told it to do: nothing. The retention property outranks your urgency. VACUUM obeys the log, not your FinOps dashboard. And the 3:40 AM RETAIN 0 HOURS? It bypassed the only guardrail standing between "delete unreferenced files" and "delete files that old-but-legitimate versions still reference." The default 168-hour floor exists precisely because time-travel readers, long-running queries, and concurrent writers can hold a logical reference to a version for days. Zero hours means zero patience for anyone reading the past. The Log Files Themselves Are the Second Bill While we were staring at the 238 terabytes, the _delta_log directory was running its own scam. bronze.clickstream commits roughly 3,400 times a day — streaming micro-batches, hourly OPTIMIZE runs, the occasional MERGE. With delta.logRetentionDuration set to 365 days, that is: 3,400 commits/day × 365 days ≈ 1.24 million JSON files sitting in _delta_log/. Every single read of that table — every dashboard refresh, every ad-hoc query — starts by listing _delta_log, reading _last_checkpoint, loading the checkpoint parquet, and replaying the JSON tail since the last checkpoint. Our tail was thousands of files long on a bad day. Query planning alone took 47 seconds before a single byte of data was touched, and S3 LIST requests — $0.005 per thousand — were a line item of their own. The ledger had become heavier than some of the tables it described. Checkpoints cap the replay, but they don’t cap the listing or the retention. The checkpoint interval (10) was fine; the 365-day log retention was the disease. A ledger you’re legally required to keep for a year is an archive, not a live table — and we were paying live-table prices to replay it on every query. The Fix, and What It Cost The naive fix is what we did at 3:40 AM. The engine-aware fix starts from the actual SLAs — how far back anyone is contractually allowed to read — and tiers every retention knob to match: # Naive: nuke everything unreferenced RIGHT NOW. # spark.conf.set( # "spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled", "false" # ) # disables the 7-day guardrail — the guardrail exists for time-travel readers # spark.sql("VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 0 HOURS") # Result: 238TB freed, then FileNotFoundException on every read older than "now". # Optimized: tier retention to the real SLAs, then vacuum honestly. spark.sql(""" ALTER TABLE bronze.clickstream SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 7 days', 'delta.logRetentionDuration' = 'interval 30 days' ) """) # finance needs 30-day time travel; GDPR needs 7-day tombstone expiry, not 365 # Always DRY RUN first, and read what it plans to delete: # spark.sql("VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 168 HOURS DRY RUN") spark.sql("VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 168 HOURS") Two companion decisions, both non-optional: Audit history moved out of the live table. The “audit safety” requirement was real, so we gave it a real answer: a monthly archived copy of the table in cheap storage, instead of a 365-day retention property strangling the production table. RESTORE discipline. RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF is metadata-only — it appends a new version re-adding old removed files. It can only resurrect files that still exist. Our runbook now states the restore horizon explicitly: 30 days, matching logRetentionDuration, verified by a monthly restore drill against a clone. The quantified results, thirty days later: S3 spend: $41,000/month → $12,400/month. The 238TB of GDPR tombstones plus ~40TB of orphaned log and compaction debris, gone — legally this time. _delta_log file count: 1.24M JSON files → ~102k. Thirty days of history at 3,400 commits/day. Query planning time: 47s → 3s on the standard dashboard queries. Same data, same cluster. Month-end close time-travel query: green , and covered by the monthly restore drill. The Catch: Retention Is a One-Way Door, and the Vacuum Doesn’t Know Your SLAs The honest counterweight, because the fix has sharp edges: Lowering retention is irreversible for old versions. The moment tombstones age past the new threshold and VACUUM runs, those versions are unrecoverable — RESTORE becomes a FileNotFoundException factory. We lowered 365 days to 30 only after the archive copy existed and the stakeholders signed the horizon in writing. VACUUM cannot delete files referenced within retention, full stop. A 30-day time-travel SLA means a minimum of 30 days of dead files sitting on S3. That is the price of the feature, not a bug in the tool. Budget for it. Never point S3 lifecycle rules at Delta data directories. Lifecycle policies delete by object age with no knowledge of the log. A lifecycle rule expiring “old” parquet files will happily delete files the current version references, and the table will corrupt silently until the next read. Retention belongs in Delta properties, not in bucket policies. The 168-hour floor is load-bearing. We now treat any request to vacuum below 7 days the way we’d treat a request to delete the backups: possible, documented, and requiring two sign-offs. A streaming MERGE micro-batch retrying against a transient failure can legitimately need files older than your impatience. Takeaways The log is the table: _delta_log/ defines every version; the parquet files are just evidence the ledger points at. Protect the ledger's integrity and the files' existence as two separate promises. DELETE is a rewrite, not an erasure: every DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE writes new files and tombstones the old ones. Storage is freed only when retention expires and VACUUM runs. VACUUM obeys the log, not your urgency: deletedFileRetentionDuration outranks your RETAIN clause. A 365-day tombstone retention makes weekly vacuums a ceremonial no-op. RETAIN 0 HOURS is a loaded gun: it deletes files that old-but-legitimate versions still reference. The 7-day guardrail exists because time-travel readers and long-running queries hold logical references for days. Time travel is only as durable as your retention: a 31-day-old read needs 31 days of log and 31 days of un-vacuumed files. Set logRetentionDuration from the restore SLA, not from vibes. The _delta_log is a cost center too: commit-heavy tables with long log retention accumulate millions of JSON files, and every reader pays the LIST-and-replay tax. Size logRetentionDuration to the readership, not the auditors — archive separately. In Delta Lake, nothing is ever deleted — it is only forgotten on a schedule. Make sure you’re the one writing the schedule. If this saved you a 3 AM pager incident, follow me on Medium for Twice a week for the next 3 Months of Advanced Data Engineering & AI. Let’s connect on LinkedIn and X . It was from FinOps, in Slack, with a screenshot: our S3 spend had crossed $41,000 for the month, up from $9,400 five months earlier, and the line was still climbing. The accused was bronze.clickstream — 412 terabytes, fourteen months of raw click events, roughly 2.1 billion rows a day landing through a Structured Streaming MERGE.

Six months before that night, we had deleted 238 terabytes from that table. A GDPR erasure request had forced us to purge nine months of history containing raw PII. The DELETE ran for eleven hours, the row counts confirmed it, the auditors signed off. And the storage bill did not move. Not by a gigabyte.

We did what every team does: we blamed VACUUM. Then we checked, and VACUUM had been running green every Sunday for a year. VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 168 HOURS, dry-run clean, a few hundred gigabytes reclaimed each time, job healthy. The 238 terabytes were simply still there, on S3, billing us $0.023 per GB-month, while the table insisted they were gone.

At 3:40 AM, running on caffeine and indignation, the on-call engineer did the obvious thing. He disabled the retention safety check and ran the nuclear option:

-- the 3:40 AM version of "have you tried turning it off and on again"
VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 0 HOURS

It worked. Forty-one thousand dollars a month of dead files evaporated in ninety minutes. We went back to sleep feeling like heroes.

At 9:04 AM, finance ran the month-end close. Their reconciliation query reads the table TIMESTAMP AS OF the last day of the month — a time-travel read, thirty-one days back. It failed instantly with FileNotFoundException: a file referenced in the transaction log could not be found. The version they needed had been vacuumed out from under them at 4 AM. So had the training snapshot the ML team had pinned for a model refresh. Two teams, two broken reads, one very long incident review.

So: what does DELETE actually delete in Delta Lake, what is VACUUM legally allowed to remove, and why did 238 terabytes of "deleted" data survive six months of weekly vacuums — while thirty-one-day-old files died the moment we got impatient?

The Mechanic Underneath: The Table Is a Ledger, Not a Directory

Forget the parquet files for a minute. A Delta table is not a directory of data files. A Delta table is _delta_log/ — a directory of JSON files, each one a commit, each commit a list of actions. The data files are just the payload the ledger points at.

Every commit appends one file: 00000000000000000000.json, 00000000000000000001.json, and so on. Inside, the actions that matter:

  • add: this parquet file is now part of the table (path, size, partition values, file statistics).
  • remove: this parquet file is no longer part of the table — with a deletionTimestamp and a dataChange flag. The file itself is untouched. It becomes a tombstone.
  • protocol: the minimum reader/writer versions this table requires.
  • metaData: schema, partition columns, table properties.
  • txn: the streaming application ID and version, for idempotent micro-batch commits.
  • commitInfo: who committed, when, with what operation.

The state of the table at version N is the replay of every action from 0 to N. Nothing is ever mutated in place. A DELETE doesn't delete rows — it writes new parquet files without those rows and logs remove actions against the old ones. An UPDATE, a MERGE, an OPTIMIZE: all rewrites, all tombstones. The old files sit on S3, fully intact, until something with the authority to forget them comes along.

Because replaying millions of JSON files on every read would be absurd, Delta writes a checkpoint every 10 commits (controlled by delta.checkpointInterval): a parquet file summarizing the complete table state at that version, with _last_checkpoint pointing at the newest one. Reading version N means loading the nearest checkpoint at or below N and replaying only the JSON tail after it. That tail — the checkpoint cadence, the JSON retention, the replay cost — is where our second bill was hiding, as we'll see.

This is the whole mental model: the log is the table, the files are just evidence, and forgetting is a scheduled, retention-gated operation — never an immediate one.

Optimistic Concurrency: Every Commit Is a Conditional Write on a Version Number

Writers don’t take locks. A writer reads the current version V, does its (possibly enormous) work against that snapshot, then attempts to write V+1.json as an atomic conditional put — it succeeds only if V is still the latest version. If another writer got there first, Delta runs conflict detection: two blind appends to different partitions can both commit (the loser retries against V+1); two MERGEs touching overlapping files cannot, and the loser gets a ConcurrentAppendException.

This is why the streaming MERGE into bronze.clickstream and the Sunday OPTIMIZE could coexist without corrupting anything — and also why our incident had a blast radius instead of a corruption. The 4 AM vacuum didn't corrupt the log; it deleted evidence the log still referenced. The ledger was perfect. The files were gone. Optimistic concurrency protects the log's integrity, not the physical files' existence. Those are two different durability promises, and we had confused them.

The protocol action deserves a paranoid glance too. minReaderVersion and minWriterVersion gate which engine versions may touch the table, and modern Delta adds named table features — deletion vectors, column mapping, liquid clustering, v2 checkpoints. Bumping the protocol is a one-way door: old readers are locked out permanently. It has nothing to do with our incident, but it's the same class of mistake — a metadata decision with physical consequences that you only discover at 9:04 AM.

Time Travel Is Log Replay, Not a Backup

TIMESTAMP AS OF and VERSION AS OF feel like backups. They are not. There is no snapshot stored anywhere. A time-travel read resolves your timestamp to a version number, loads the nearest checkpoint at or below it, and replays the JSON tail — the exact same machinery as a current read, just stopping earlier.

The consequence is absolute: a time-travel read is only as durable as the log entries and the data files they reference. Keep the log for 30 days and you can time-travel 30 days — provided nobody vacuumed the files those old versions point at. Our finance query needed version history 31 days deep. Our vacuum at RETAIN 0 HOURS had deleted every file unreferenced by the current version, including every file the 31-day-old version needed. The ledger still described a table that could be reconstructed; the reconstruction was impossible. FileNotFoundException is the log telling the truth about files that no longer exist.

VACUUM Can Only Delete What the Log Has Already Forgotten

Here is the actual deletion pipeline, in order:

  1. A DELETE/MERGE/UPDATE logs remove actions with a deletionTimestamp. The files are now tombstones — logically dead, physically alive.
  2. Tombstones are protected for delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration (default: 7 days). This is not a suggestion; it's the table property VACUUM consults.
  3. VACUUM ... RETAIN N HOURS deletes data files that are referenced by no table version within the retention window — and only if they're older than the threshold. It also refuses RETAIN under 168 hours unless you explicitly disable spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled, because a query or a streaming micro-batch can legitimately take longer than you think.

Now the root cause of the $41,000 bill: eighteen months earlier, a well-meaning predecessor had set two table properties “for audit safety”:

'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 365 days',
'delta.logRetentionDuration'         = 'interval 365 days'

Every tombstone the GDPR delete created was legally protected for a year. Our weekly VACUUM RETAIN 168 HOURS would list the 238 terabytes of dead files, check each one's deletionTimestamp against the one-year tombstone retention, and walk away. It ran green because it was doing exactly what the table told it to do: nothing. The retention property outranks your urgency. VACUUM obeys the log, not your FinOps dashboard.

And the 3:40 AM RETAIN 0 HOURS? It bypassed the only guardrail standing between "delete unreferenced files" and "delete files that old-but-legitimate versions still reference." The default 168-hour floor exists precisely because time-travel readers, long-running queries, and concurrent writers can hold a logical reference to a version for days. Zero hours means zero patience for anyone reading the past.

The Log Files Themselves Are the Second Bill

While we were staring at the 238 terabytes, the _delta_log directory was running its own scam. bronze.clickstream commits roughly 3,400 times a day — streaming micro-batches, hourly OPTIMIZE runs, the occasional MERGE. With delta.logRetentionDuration set to 365 days, that is:

3,400 commits/day × 365 days ≈ 1.24 million JSON files sitting in _delta_log/.

Every single read of that table — every dashboard refresh, every ad-hoc query — starts by listing _delta_log, reading _last_checkpoint, loading the checkpoint parquet, and replaying the JSON tail since the last checkpoint. Our tail was thousands of files long on a bad day. Query planning alone took 47 seconds before a single byte of data was touched, and S3 LIST requests — $0.005 per thousand — were a line item of their own. The ledger had become heavier than some of the tables it described.

Checkpoints cap the replay, but they don’t cap the listing or the retention. The checkpoint interval (10) was fine; the 365-day log retention was the disease. A ledger you’re legally required to keep for a year is an archive, not a live table — and we were paying live-table prices to replay it on every query.

The Fix, and What It Cost

The naive fix is what we did at 3:40 AM. The engine-aware fix starts from the actual SLAs — how far back anyone is contractually allowed to read — and tiers every retention knob to match:

# Naive: nuke everything unreferenced RIGHT NOW.
# spark.conf.set(
#     "spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled", "false"
# )  # disables the 7-day guardrail — the guardrail exists for time-travel readers
# spark.sql("VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 0 HOURS")
# Result: 238TB freed, then FileNotFoundException on every read older than "now".
# Optimized: tier retention to the real SLAs, then vacuum honestly.
spark.sql("""
  ALTER TABLE bronze.clickstream SET TBLPROPERTIES (
    'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 7 days',
    'delta.logRetentionDuration'         = 'interval 30 days'
  )
""")  # finance needs 30-day time travel; GDPR needs 7-day tombstone expiry, not 365
# Always DRY RUN first, and read what it plans to delete:
# spark.sql("VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 168 HOURS DRY RUN")
spark.sql("VACUUM bronze.clickstream RETAIN 168 HOURS")

Two companion decisions, both non-optional:

  • Audit history moved out of the live table. The “audit safety” requirement was real, so we gave it a real answer: a monthly archived copy of the table in cheap storage, instead of a 365-day retention property strangling the production table.
  • RESTORE discipline. RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF is metadata-only — it appends a new version re-adding old removed files. It can only resurrect files that still exist. Our runbook now states the restore horizon explicitly: 30 days, matching logRetentionDuration, verified by a monthly restore drill against a clone.

The quantified results, thirty days later:

  • S3 spend: $41,000/month → $12,400/month. The 238TB of GDPR tombstones plus ~40TB of orphaned log and compaction debris, gone — legally this time.
  • _delta_log file count: 1.24M JSON files → ~102k. Thirty days of history at 3,400 commits/day.
  • Query planning time: 47s → 3s on the standard dashboard queries. Same data, same cluster.
  • Month-end close time-travel query: green, and covered by the monthly restore drill.
The Catch: Retention Is a One-Way Door, and the Vacuum Doesn’t Know Your SLAs

The honest counterweight, because the fix has sharp edges:

  • Lowering retention is irreversible for old versions. The moment tombstones age past the new threshold and VACUUM runs, those versions are unrecoverable — RESTORE becomes a FileNotFoundException factory. We lowered 365 days to 30 only after the archive copy existed and the stakeholders signed the horizon in writing.
  • VACUUM cannot delete files referenced within retention, full stop. A 30-day time-travel SLA means a minimum of 30 days of dead files sitting on S3. That is the price of the feature, not a bug in the tool. Budget for it.
  • Never point S3 lifecycle rules at Delta data directories. Lifecycle policies delete by object age with no knowledge of the log. A lifecycle rule expiring “old” parquet files will happily delete files the current version references, and the table will corrupt silently until the next read. Retention belongs in Delta properties, not in bucket policies.
  • The 168-hour floor is load-bearing. We now treat any request to vacuum below 7 days the way we’d treat a request to delete the backups: possible, documented, and requiring two sign-offs. A streaming MERGE micro-batch retrying against a transient failure can legitimately need files older than your impatience.
Takeaways
  • The log is the table: _delta_log/ defines every version; the parquet files are just evidence the ledger points at. Protect the ledger's integrity and the files' existence as two separate promises.
  • DELETE is a rewrite, not an erasure: every DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE writes new files and tombstones the old ones. Storage is freed only when retention expires and VACUUM runs.
  • VACUUM obeys the log, not your urgency: deletedFileRetentionDuration outranks your RETAIN clause. A 365-day tombstone retention makes weekly vacuums a ceremonial no-op.
  • RETAIN 0 HOURS is a loaded gun: it deletes files that old-but-legitimate versions still reference. The 7-day guardrail exists because time-travel readers and long-running queries hold logical references for days.
  • Time travel is only as durable as your retention: a 31-day-old read needs 31 days of log and 31 days of un-vacuumed files. Set logRetentionDuration from the restore SLA, not from vibes.
  • The _delta_log is a cost center too: commit-heavy tables with long log retention accumulate millions of JSON files, and every reader pays the LIST-and-replay tax. Size logRetentionDuration to the readership, not the auditors — archive separately.

In Delta Lake, nothing is ever deleted — it is only forgotten on a schedule. Make sure you’re the one writing the schedule.

If this saved you a 3 AM pager incident, follow me on Medium for Twice a week for the next 3 Months of Advanced Data Engineering & AI. Let’s connect on LinkedIn and X.

Part XX — Delta Lake’s Transaction Log: Time Travel, VACUUM, and the Files That Never Die was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Why Peacock is making a huge bet on YouTube
items.summary: Today, I’m talking with Matt Strauss, who is now chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. This is Matt’s second time joining me on the show, and there’s been a whole lot of organizational and structural change at NBCU since the last time he and I spoke just two years ago — pure Decoder bait. First, about a month after Matt was on the show, Comcast spun off most of the NBCU cable channels into something called Versant. That’s when Matt’s title changed from heading up just the direct-to-consumer offering — meaning Peacock, plus some other streaming services — to heading up the whole thing, across all distribution. And now, Comcast is spinning off the NBCU business entirely into a whole new standalone company. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . That’s a lot to have going on all at once! And meanwhile, it’s only just this year that Peacock became an actual profitable business at all — and it’s still pretty far away from being anything like the juggernaut that Netflix is. But what NBCU has, and what Peacock has, that the rest of the streaming industry is still trying to wrap its head around, is live sports. Sports are huge. They held up the cable industry for years, they held up broadcast, and now they’re the big thing that could make streaming a winner for NBC. One thing before we start: You’ll hear me ask Matt about the red company and the blue company. That’s just my way of getting Matt to talk about Netflix and Skydance, the company that now owns both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. I think he did a good job playing along. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Matt Strauss, chairman of the NBCU Media Group. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Matt Strauss, you are the chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. Welcome back to Decoder . Thank you so much, Nilay. It’s great to be back. I am very excited to talk to you. There’s a lot going on in the media. It is a tumultuous time in Hollywood. I have to tell the audience that you and I are speaking minutes after Anthropic filed its S-1 , and all of humanity is going to be turned into AI. Who knows what entertainment we’ll be watching in the future? There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the very beginning of this. You have a new job since last time you were on the show. Last time, you were the head of Direct-to-Consumer — you were basically the head of Peacock and the other apps inside the family. Now you’re the chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group. What’s the new job? What does that mean? NBCUniversal Media Group is comprised of certain services within NBC. It’s the broadcast network, it’s Bravo, it’s Peacock, it’s NBC Sports. We also have NBC News and Telemundo. One of the things that we recognized, especially when we spun off some of our cable assets last year into Versant, was that the assets we had truly worked better together. NBC has been like a megaphone. Given the reach of NBC, it’s been incredibly strategic in growing Peacock, which is a bit ironic because I think so many people believed that broadcasting was a bit of a relic of the past in this digital world, but it’s actually proven to be the opposite. As things have gotten more fragmented, having a broadcast network is actually a superpower because we’re continuing to see ratings growth. That has been really helpful as we’ve been building out Peacock. But actually, Peacock was also finding new audiences, like cord cutters or people who maybe didn’t grow up watching NBC or some of our cable networks. So, Peacock’s also been really strategic in reaching and driving people back to NBC and Bravo. So, I think that flywheel is where we recognized that we needed to start operating differently. I’ve been a huge advocate of what I like to call “centers of excellence” in how I like to structure the business, which is, content first and platform second. How do we get maximum reach, maximum engagement? That really required us thinking differently about how we were running the business. Essentially, instead of having a programming group within broadcast and a programming group within streaming, we just collapsed the business. Now you’ve got one programming team, one marketing team, one product and technology team, one decision sciences and research team, and one advertising team. They’re all incentivized around continuing to grow the portfolio, get that maximum reach, maximum engagement, and drive top-line revenue. I think that structure, which we put in place about 18 months ago, is contributing to a lot of the success that we’re seeing now. Even if you look at 2026, NBC is the number one network in total viewers. We had an unbelievable early part of the year with “Legendary February,” which you might remember. That’s when we had the Super Bowl, the Milan Cortina Olympics, and the NBA All-Star Game. In 17 days, we reached over 225 million viewers. This summer, we had Love Island , which was the number one show of the summer for streaming. You had the World Cup, which was the number one Spanish-language sporting event in US history on Telemundo and Peacock. We had a show called The Five-Star Weekend , which was our number one scripted drama. Now, we’ve led ourselves into the fall, where we have Sunday Night Football, which has been the number one show for 15 consecutive years. We had a great kickoff with over 25 million viewers. We just had the NBA tip-off last week with the Knicks and the Sixers, which is the number one rated tip-off in NBA history. So, it does feel like we’re firing on all cylinders in how we’re trying to operate with this, again, content-first-platform-second mantra. But just to go one level deeper, a big part of this strategy is figuring out how do we move audiences across platforms. For example, when I mentioned that Love Island was the number one streaming show of the summer, 40 percent of those Love Island viewers also tuned in to watch the World Cup. So, migrating viewers back and forth across the portfolio is a critical part of how we see ourselves continuing to grow. But to effectuate that, you need to structure yourself in a way where people are incentivized along that vision. We’re still evolving as an organization, but I’m really proud of some of the milestones and accomplishments that we’ve made as a team. I love my job. I feel like I’ve got the best job in the industry at the moment. It is a tumultuous time in Hollywood, and you seem like one of the happiest people in the industry right at the second. That is very notable. You’re a Decoder pro, you brought up structure. I’m dying to ask you about the Decision Sciences Group. That’s the other question I ask everybody. But let me just back out for one second. You’re describing quite a lot of freedom in rethinking how something like NBCUniversal would work. You mentioned the Versant spin, so CNBC, MS Now, and a bunch of channels went that way. I’m on its networks all the time. I would describe the folks at Versant as feeling more free. They’re disconnected from the battleship that was Comcast and NBCUniversal. They can go try whatever they want to try. They’re energized by it in some ways. Then, Comcast looked at NBCUniversal and said, “We’re going to spin off that off as well. We’re going to be the cable business and NBCUniversal will be the entertainment business, and now you’re in charge of that.” You’re like a 20-year Comcast veteran. I think you got your start doing cable boxes. Yep. I started in 2004 at Comcast. Just tell me about that process. We spun off CNBC and MS Now into Versant. Now we’re looking at this company. We ought to spin off NBCUniversal as well. Just tell me about how that came about. What was that moment like? Did you all sit in a boardroom? Did it come down from on high? How did that happen? Well, that decision really was made by Brian Roberts and Mike Cavanagh. Candidly, I was not in the room when that decision was made, but I think if you were to ask people at NBCUniversal, it makes strategic sense. Do you feel that same sense of freedom? You know what? I think that there’s an energy. When people show up here, they feel very passionate about what they do. They believe in our strategy, they believe in our portfolio. Look at NBCUniversal more broadly. Before, I was describing the Media Group, but that is one piece of the broader company. You have Universal Pictures and Universal Television, which have obviously been having an unbelievable summer with The Odyssey and Obsession . You’ve got Universal’s theme parks and experiences. We opened up Epic Universe last year. We opened up a kids theme park in Texas. We announced we’re going to open up a theme park in the UK . We have Sky, which was part of the company but more squarely sat within Comcast Cable. Now that’s going to migrate over to the new NBCUniversal as part of this restructure. Then, you have these media assets, which I spoke about earlier. So, you’ve got this unbelievable portfolio. I think that people here really believe in our growth and that if we’re a separate company, it’s going to allow us to move faster. It’s going to let us have more clarity around where we want to make capital allocations and decisions. There are a few areas that really play to our strengths as an organization. One of them is live sports and live events. That’s always been a part of NBCUniversal that we’re really known for. If you just look at the sports portfolio that we have, Nilay, we’ve got NFL, NBA, MLB, the Big Ten Conference, the Premier League. We’ve got the Olympics with the IOC. You’ve got this unbelievable portfolio of sports content, and that’s a strategic asset when we’re partnering with the leagues because we believe in broadcast. We believe in broad reach. We’re not trying to put everything exclusively on a streaming platform. In 2026, we’ve demonstrated across almost every single sport that we can actually continue to grow ratings and reach new audiences, which is something that’s becoming more and more complicated. Can I ask about that? Because you also run Peacock, which is a paid streamer where you can access sports. When you say grow ratings on broadcast, are more people putting up antennas to watch sports over the air? No. What I mean… By the way, about 20 percent of TV households in this country do still use over-the-air antennas as— Oh, we have lots of listeners who are going to tell you that’s the best picture quality you can get. Yeah. It is amazing picture quality, especially if you live in the right look angle where you could pick up the signal. It comes back to what I said earlier about managing as a portfolio. We don’t think of it as a broadcast business sitting next to a streaming business. We really position ourselves as a digital-first company trying to get that maximum reach. When we look at the ratings, we’re combining what you would think of as more traditional ratings for linear television with streaming and all of our digital platforms. Whether that’s DVR or TV Everywhere, we aggregate it into one platform. When you look at it through that lens, which is just audience, we’ve actually demonstrated that across almost every sport — NFL, NBA, or MLB — the total viewers that we are reaching now are, in some cases, the highest they’ve been in decades. Even the Super Bowl, which we had earlier this year on NBC, reached about 137 million viewers at its peak, and that’s across all of our platforms. That Super Bowl was the highest-rated live event in NBC’s 100-year anniversary, which is this year. It’s kind of counterintuitive, but what we’re showing is that when we start operating as one, we can reach new audiences and we can aggregate them. We are demonstrating that not just across sports. There’s even something like the Thanksgiving Day Parade, which has been an institution on NBC for 99 years. This past Thanksgiving Day Parade was the highest-rated parade we have had in the company’s history. So, there’s a renaissance happening around live. In a world of instant gratification, on demand, and watching what you want when you want, the fact that you’re now seeing more and more viewers wanting the collective consciousness of social viewing, things that still matter in today’s society, that actually plays to our strengths. And we’re seeing that manifest itself with higher ratings. But as I mentioned, it’s also a big part of our strategy. It was a big part of our Peacock strategy, which was a bit of an anomaly when we launched Peacock six years ago. It’s also a huge part of what I think NBC does well, which is that we create these big tentpole events and we’re able to shine a light on them and get huge audiences that are continuing to show up, even in a world of fragmentation and cord-cutting. It’s interesting that you’ve described it as content first and platform second, and then you’re describing your approach to ratings as agnostic to distribution. You’re just sort of combining everything and saying, “This is the number of people we reached.” Well, take something like the Milan Cortina Olympics. This is an interesting example. If you were to look at that Winter Olympics, we had roughly 3,200 hours of content. There’s no way we can make all of that available on one network. There’s no way to daypart 3,200 hours. If you remember what we did with the Paris Olympics, we made the decision to make every event available live. When you make it all available live, we put it all on Peacock. This was a very controversial decision because the question has always historically been that if people tune in to watch this live during the day on Peacock, are they going to tune in to watch NBC primetime? Are we going to cannibalize our ratings or are we going to grow the ratings? This is where we really tested this strategy. If we’re truly indifferent, then what should happen is that we should be able to expand the funnel during the day, get more people into the Olympics, and try to create an experience that we’re very proud of. We really do believe, whether it was the Gold Zone or Multiview, that we were able to surprise and delight viewers and make it really easy to navigate and find all of the choices on Peacock. But then what happened was that people were tuning in to watch NBC during primetime because there’s a difference between what NBC does and what Peacock does. NBC was more about storytelling. It was more about, “Let’s talk about what happened today. What about the backstory of the athletes? How’s Mike Tirico going to address his perspective on things?” When you combine these two things together — putting all the content on Peacock and then having the primetime show — this Winter Olympics had about a 96 percent higher rating. About 25 million viewers were tuning in to watch the Milan Cortina Olympics, which was about 96 or 97 percent higher than Beijing. On the digital side, it was double the digital minutes of every other Winter Olympics combined. We also doubled the advertising revenue. You’ve got to be willing to break some glass. This is going to seem so obvious, but it starts with the consumer. It starts with, “How do we approach the consumer and give them the best experience?” And if you build it, they will come. The only reason I’m using the Olympics as an example is because if you were to look at the past, this was a real pain point where we didn’t make everything available on streaming or it was confusing for some viewers to figure out how to navigate all of the choices. We really, as an organization, decided to put our shoulder behind this, and I think the results ultimately speak for themselves. But again, it ladders back up to this vision of really starting to manage as one portfolio. If you can drive that maximum reach and engagement, that’s also going to be where you’ll get the best monetization. The Verge team in particular was addicted to Gold Zone , which was the whip-around coverage of every medal event. It was very fun. Let me ask you about this. A big Decoder trope is that your distribution fundamentally affects what you make, right? That the medium is essentially the message, and I know what a YouTuber makes because they’re on YouTube, and I know what a TikToker makes because they’re on TikTok. I could stretch this all the way back and say I know what broadcast TV looks like because the medium of broadcast TV has fundamentally shaped the content that gets made there. I know what cable shows on Bravo look like, and they’re not the same thing and they haven’t been for a while.
