Preparing Video Input for YOLO26 Object Detection and Tracking

For this lesson, you can use any traffic or pedestrian video. The pipeline is designed to work with standard Common Objects in Context (COCO) classes (e.g., person, car, bus, and truck).

If you do not already have a video, here are some easy options:

  • record a short clip with your phone
  • use a public traffic or street video
  • download a sample video from a public benchmark or a YouTube clip that clearly shows moving objects

For best results:

  • use a clip lasting 20 to 40 seconds
  • ensure objects actually cross the counting line
  • avoid scenes that are either extremely crowded or almost empty

For the examples in this lesson, a traffic video where vehicles move horizontally across the frame is the easiest choice because line-crossing events are easy to see and validate.

Running YOLO26 Object Detection on Video

You already ran YOLO26 on static images in Lesson 1. Now you need a detector wrapper that is built for a video loop.

The goal here is not theoretical elegance. The goal is a clean interface.

Before looking at the detector wrapper, let us define the shared data structures that the entire pipeline uses. In video_analytics/common/utils.py, you will define Detection and Track as simple dataclasses:

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Tuple


Point = Tuple[int, int]


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Detection:
    xyxy: Tuple[float, float, float, float]
    confidence: float
    class_id: int
    class_name: str


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Track:
    track_id: int
    xyxy: Tuple[float, float, float, float]
    confidence: float
    class_id: int
    class_name: str

    @property
    def centroid(self) -> Point:
        x1, y1, x2, y2 = self.xyxy
        return int((x1 + x2) / 2.0), int((y1 + y2) / 2.0)

Detection carries the per-frame detections from the model. Track contains the same detection fields plus a track_id and a computed centroid property that the analytics layer uses for line-crossing tests.

In video_analytics/models/detector.py, you will create a small wrapper around Ultralytics YOLO:

from typing import List

from ultralytics import YOLO

from ..common import Detection
from ..config import DetectionConfig


class YOLO26Detector:
    def __init__(self, config: DetectionConfig) -> None:
        self.config = config
        self.model = YOLO(config.model_path)

    def detect(self, frame) -> List[Detection]:
        result = self.model.predict(
            source=frame,
            conf=self.config.confidence,
            imgsz=self.config.image_size,
            device=self.config.device,
            verbose=False,
        )[0]

        boxes = result.boxes
        if boxes is None or len(boxes) == 0:
            return []

This wrapper does 3 useful things for you:

  • Centralizes model configuration
  • Hides the raw Ultralytics result object from the rest of the pipeline
  • Converts detections into a consistent internal structure

That last part matters. When the detector returns simple Detection objects, the tracker and analytics modules stay clean.

In the same file, we extract bounding boxes, confidences, class IDs, and class names, then normalize them into our internal Detection dataclass:

xyxy = boxes.xyxy.cpu().numpy()
confidences = boxes.conf.cpu().numpy()
class_ids = boxes.cls.cpu().numpy().astype(int)
names = result.names

detections: List[Detection] = []
for box, confidence, class_id in zip(xyxy, confidences, class_ids):
    detections.append(
        Detection(
            xyxy=(float(box[0]), float(box[1]), float(box[2]), float(box[3])),
            confidence=float(confidence),
            class_id=int(class_id),
            class_name=str(names[int(class_id)]),
        )
    )

At this point, the detector stage is done. For each frame, we now have a list of objects that YOLO26 thinks are present.

Adding ByteTrack Multi-Object Tracking

Detection alone is not enough for analytics, so the next step is adding the ByteTrack algorithm.

We are using ByteTrack here because it is a strong practical fit for real-time video analytics pipelines. It is widely used, works well in detection-based MOT pipelines, and provides stable IDs without turning the lesson into a tracking theory lecture.

We are also using ByteTrack instead of a simpler centroid tracker for a reason:

  • it handles occlusion and brief disappearances better than naive centroid matching
  • it uses detection confidence during association
  • it maintains a lost-track buffer that helps in busy scenes

That makes the ByteTrack multi-object tracking approach a much better fit for real-world people counting and vehicle counting pipelines where IDs need to stay stable under noise and partial visibility.

In video_analytics/models/tracker.py, you will wrap ByteTrack as follows:

from typing import Iterable, List

import numpy as np
import supervision as sv

from ..common import Detection, Track
from ..config import TrackingConfig


class ByteTrackTracker:
    def __init__(self, config: TrackingConfig, frame_rate: float) -> None:
        self.tracker = sv.ByteTrack(
            track_activation_threshold=config.activation_threshold,
            lost_track_buffer=config.lost_track_buffer,
            minimum_matching_threshold=config.minimum_matching_threshold,
            frame_rate=max(int(frame_rate), 1),
        )

    def update(self, detections: Iterable[Detection]) -> List[Track]:
        detections = list(detections)
        if not detections:
            empty = sv.Detections.empty()
            self.tracker.update_with_detections(empty)
            return []

The nice thing about wrapping it this way is that video_analytics/pipeline.py does not need to know anything about supervision.Detections or tracker internals.

Inside update, you convert the detection list into a tracker-friendly format:

sv_detections = sv.Detections(
    xyxy=xyxy,
    confidence=confidence,
    class_id=class_id,
    data={"class_name": metadata},
)
tracked = self.tracker.update_with_detections(sv_detections)

Then you convert the tracker output into Track objects that carry:

  • track ID
  • bounding box
  • confidence
  • class ID
  • class name

That gives us exactly what the analytics layer needs.

One small but important detail is the empty-detection path above. When YOLO26 misses everything in a frame, you still forward an empty Detections object into ByteTrack so tracks age naturally instead of collapsing immediately.

Real-World Challenge: Tracker Imperfections

Tracking is not perfect.

In real-world scenes:

  • objects may be temporarily lost
  • track IDs may switch
  • occlusions can break continuity

That matters because analytics depends on track identity. If a person disappears for a few frames and returns with a new ID, the pipeline may count them twice.

In production systems, common mitigation strategies include:

  • minimum track length thresholds
  • track smoothing
  • time-based filtering
  • re-identification models for harder scenes

This lesson keeps the implementation lightweight, but it is important to understand that tracking quality directly affects analytics quality in any people counting software or vehicle counting system.

Building the Analytics Layer for People Counting and Vehicle Counting

This is the most important part of the lesson.

We are not just showing tracked boxes. We are extracting business-level events from a stream of detections.

The main event in this lesson is line crossing, but the same analytics layer also supports class-filtered counting, multiple named lines, and optional zone occupancy, making it work as both a people counting system and a vehicle counting system.

The Idea

We define a virtual line across the frame. For each tracked object, we store its previous observed centroid and compare it with its current centroid.

If the centroid moves from one side of a configured line to the other, we count that as a crossing event.

The implementation is not limited to a single demo line. The analytics configuration can:

  • Restrict counting to selected classes (e.g., person or a combination of car, bus, and truck)
  • Handle multiple named counting lines in the same scene
  • Track optional zone occupancy for a rectangular region of interest

Before going further, note the coordinate convention we are using. OpenCV frames follow the standard image coordinate system:

  • the origin is at the top-left corner
  • x increases to the right
  • y increases downward

That convention affects both line direction and the sign of the crossing test. The "in" and "out" labels depend on the order of the line endpoints and the change in the centroid’s side-of-line value. Verify these labels against the intended direction of travel for your camera view.

This logic lives in video_analytics/analytics/engine.py:

@dataclass(slots=True)
class LineCrossingCounter:
    name: str
    line_start: Point
    line_end: Point
    allowed_classes: Optional[set[str]] = None
    previous_centroids: Dict[int, Point] = field(default_factory=dict)
    counted_track_ids: set[int] = field(default_factory=set)
    total_count: int = 0
    in_count: int = 0
    out_count: int = 0

The key state we store is:

  • Previous centroid per track ID for each counting line
  • Which track IDs have already been counted on each line
  • Total, in, and out counters per line
  • Optional occupancy count inside a configured zone

To determine whether a crossing happened, we compute which side of the line the object was on before and after:

previous_side = side_of_line(previous_centroid, self.line_start, self.line_end)
current_side = side_of_line(current_centroid, self.line_start, self.line_end)

if previous_side == 0:
    previous_side = current_side

if previous_side * current_side < 0:
    direction = "in" if previous_side < current_side else "out"
    self.counted_track_ids.add(track.track_id)

That is the heart of the line-crossing logic.

Once a track is counted, we add its ID to a counted_track_ids set so the same object is not counted repeatedly.

That design choice is deliberate. In this implementation, each track is counted only once per line. That works well for entry and exit counting use cases.

If your scene allows the same object to cross the same line multiple times, then you would want a more advanced per-track state machine instead of the simpler count-once logic used here.

The zone occupancy counter follows a simpler pattern. Instead of tracking crossings, it counts how many tracked objects currently have their centroid inside a rectangular region. In video_analytics/analytics/engine.py:

@dataclass(slots=True)
class ZoneOccupancyCounter:
    name: str
    top_left: Point
    bottom_right: Point
    allowed_classes: Optional[set[str]] = None
    occupancy_count: int = 0

    def update(self, tracks: List[Track]) -> None:
        current_count = 0
        for track in tracks:
            if self.allowed_classes is not None and track.class_name.lower() not in self.allowed_classes:
                continue

            centroid_x, centroid_y = track.centroid
            if self.top_left[0] <= centroid_x <= self.bottom_right[0] and self.top_left[1] <= centroid_y <= self.bottom_right[1]:
                current_count += 1
        self.occupancy_count = current_count

    def stats(self) -> Dict[str, int | str]:
        return {
            "name": self.name,
            "occupancy": self.occupancy_count,
        }

This is a per-frame snapshot, not cumulative. Every call to update recalculates the count from scratch based on which tracks are currently inside the zone. That makes it suitable for real-time occupancy monitoring where the question is “how many objects are in this region right now?”

Combined with class filters and optional zone occupancy, this is what makes the pipeline feel like a real application rather than a visualization demo.

Here is the core track drawing function:

def draw_tracks(frame, tracks: Iterable[Track]) -> None:
    for track in tracks:
        x1, y1, x2, y2 = as_int_tuple(track.xyxy)

def draw_stats(frame, stats: Dict[str, int], fps: float) -> None:
    lines = stats.get("lines", [])
    zone = stats.get("zone")
    panel_height = 90 + (len(lines) * 22) + (24 if zone else 0)
    cv2.rectangle(frame, (10, 10), (360, 10 + panel_height), PANEL_COLOR, -1)
    cv2.putText(frame, f"Total Count: {stats['total']}", (20, 38), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.7, TEXT_COLOR, 2)
    cv2.putText(frame, f"In: {stats['in']}  Out: {stats['out']}", (20, 64), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.65, TEXT_COLOR, 2)
    cv2.putText(frame, f"FPS: {fps:.2f}", (20, 90), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.65, TEXT_COLOR, 2)

In the current refactor, that panel can expand as the scene configuration gets richer. A simple run may show aggregate totals only, while a multi-line or zone-enabled run can also show per-line counts and occupancy. That makes the overlay useful both for demos and for validating system behavior during development.

The line drawing function is similarly straightforward:

def draw_line(frame, line_start: Point, line_end: Point, label: str | None = None) -> None:
    cv2.line(frame, line_start, line_end, LINE_COLOR, 2)
    if label:
        label_anchor = (line_start[0] + 12, max(24, line_start[1] - 12))

def draw_events(frame, events: Iterable[Tuple[str, str, str]]) -> None:
    y_offset = 130
    for class_name, line_name, direction in list(events)[-4:]:

Video I/O: The VideoStream and VideoWriter Classes

Before moving on to performance tuning, let us look at the video I/O layer that makes the pipeline work with both webcam feeds and recorded files.

The VideoStream class in video_analytics/io/video.py wraps OpenCV’s VideoCapture and handles frame reading, resizing, and optional frame skipping in one place:

class VideoStream:
    def __init__(self, config: VideoConfig) -> None:
        self.config = config
        self.capture = cv2.VideoCapture(parse_source(config.source))
        if not self.capture.isOpened():
            raise RuntimeError(f"Could not open video source: {config.source}")

    @property
    def fps(self) -> float:
        fps = self.capture.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)
        return fps if fps and fps > 0 else 30.0

    @property
    def frame_size(self) -> Tuple[int, int]:
        width = int(self.capture.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH))
        height = int(self.capture.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT))
        if self.config.frame_width and width > 0:
            scale = self.config.frame_width / width
            return self.config.frame_width, int(height * scale)
        return width, height

    def frames(self) -> Generator[Tuple[int, any], None, None]:
        frame_index = 0
        while True:
            grabbed, frame = self.capture.read()
            if not grabbed:
                break
            if self.config.frame_skip and frame_index % (self.config.frame_skip + 1) != 0:
                frame_index += 1
                continue
            if self.config.frame_width:
                height, width = frame.shape[:2]
                scale = self.config.frame_width / float(width)
                frame = cv2.resize(frame, (self.config.frame_width, int(height * scale)))
            yield frame_index, frame
            frame_index += 1

    def release(self) -> None:
        self.capture.release()

A few details worth noting. The fps property falls back to 30.0 when the backend reports 0 or nothing. That happens more often than you would expect with webcams and some video containers. The frames() generator yields (frame_index, frame) tuples, which lets the pipeline track frame positions without maintaining a separate counter. Resizing and frame skipping are both handled inside this generator, so the rest of the pipeline always receives ready-to-process frames.

The companion VideoWriter class handles output recording:

class VideoWriter:
    def __init__(self, output_path: Optional[str], fps: float, frame_size: Tuple[int, int]) -> None:
        self.writer = None
        if output_path:
            fourcc = cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*"mp4v")
            self.writer = cv2.VideoWriter(output_path, fourcc, fps, frame_size)

    def write(self, frame) -> None:
        if self.writer is not None:
            self.writer.write(frame)

    def release(self) -> None:
        if self.writer is not None:
            self.writer.release()

If you pass --output output.mp4 on the command line, the pipeline records every rendered frame to disk. If you do not, the writer stays inactive and performs no video encoding or disk writes. That guard pattern keeps the code clean without needing separate “record” and “no-record” code paths.

Performance Optimization for Real-Time Object Detection

Real-time video analytics systems are rarely bottlenecked by a single operation. Their performance depends on how efficiently detection, tracking, analytics, and rendering work together.

This codebase uses 4 practical optimization techniques to balance throughput, latency, and detection quality. Rather than repeating the implementation details covered earlier, we will focus on how these techniques affect the overall pipeline.

It is also useful to think about latency as a pipeline rather than a single number:

End-to-end latency = detection + tracking + analytics + rendering

In most practical runs:

  • Detection: often the most computationally expensive stage, particularly when running a deep learning model on every frame
  • Tracking: generally lightweight compared with neural network inference, although its cost depends on the tracker and the number of tracked objects
  • Analytics: typically adds little overhead when it consists of simple operations such as counting objects or updating statistics
  • Rendering: a bottleneck when every frame must be annotated and displayed in real time

The goal is not simply to maximize detector throughput. It is to maintain an acceptable balance between processing speed, detection quality, and the responsiveness of the complete application.

Frame Resizing

We resize frames before inference to reduce compute cost and stabilize throughput.

That happens in video_analytics/io/video.py:

if self.config.frame_width:
    height, width = frame.shape[:2]
    scale = self.config.frame_width / float(width)
    frame = cv2.resize(frame, (self.config.frame_width, int(height * scale)))
FPS Calculation

We keep a rolling FPS estimate with FPSMeter in video_analytics/common/utils.py so the overlay reflects actual runtime performance.

In video_analytics/io/video.py, we also fall back to 30.0 FPS when the backend does not report a valid value. That is especially useful for webcams and inconsistent capture backends.

Optional Frame Skipping

If the incoming stream is heavier than the machine can handle in real time, frame skipping provides a simple way to trade temporal resolution for throughput.

That logic also lives in video_analytics/io/video.py:

if self.config.frame_skip and frame_index % (self.config.frame_skip + 1) != 0:
    frame_index += 1
    continue
CPU vs MPS

On macOS, the most useful deployment toggle is the device argument.

  • Use device cpu for stable central processing unit (CPU)-only baselines
  • Use device mps on Apple Silicon when available

That makes the pipeline practical both for benchmarking and for day-to-day prototyping.

One more engineering note: the detector wrapper currently uses model.predict(...)[0] for clarity. For higher-throughput streaming systems, we can also explore streaming-oriented inference patterns (e.g., stream=True), but the current version is easier to teach and debug.

Table 1: Comparing pipeline responsiveness under CPU and MPS execution on macOS.

MPS delivers approximately 3.7 times the throughput of CPU execution under the tested settings. Timing each pipeline stage separately would establish how much of this improvement comes from model inference.

In practice, this means real-time performance is achievable on Apple Silicon with Metal Performance Shaders (MPS), while CPU-only execution may struggle to keep up with higher-resolution streams.

Running the Real-Time Video Analytics Pipeline

The runnable entry point starts in video_analytics/cli.py, while the frame-processing loop lives in video_analytics/pipeline.py. The root-level main.py remains as a thin convenience wrapper. This is the part where our OpenCV object tracking Python code comes together.

These modules do 4 things:

  • Parse CLI arguments
  • Build the pipeline configuration
  • Instantiate the detector, tracker, analytics layer, and video stream
  • Run the real-time frame loop

The command-line interface (CLI) itself is intentionally thin:

def main() -> None:
    args = parse_args()
    config = build_config(args)
    run_pipeline(config)

The heavier orchestration happens inside video_analytics/pipeline.py:

video_stream = VideoStream(config.video)
detector = YOLO26Detector(config.detection)
tracker = ByteTrackTracker(config.tracking, frame_rate=video_stream.fps)

frame_width, frame_height = video_stream.frame_size
analytics, resolved_lines = build_analytics_engine(config, frame_width, frame_height)

The build_analytics_engine function bridges our configuration and the live analytics objects. It resolves normalized line positions (e.g., line_y=0.5) into actual pixel coordinates using the frame dimensions, then creates 1 LineCrossingCounter per configured line and optionally a ZoneOccupancyCounter:

def build_analytics_engine(config, frame_width, frame_height):
    allowed_classes = set(config.analytics.class_allowlist) if config.analytics.class_allowlist else None
    resolved_lines = config.analytics.resolve_lines(frame_width, frame_height)
    line_counters = [
        LineCrossingCounter(
            name=line_name,
            line_start=line_points[0],
            line_end=line_points[1],
            allowed_classes=allowed_classes,
        )
        for line_name, line_points in resolved_lines
    ]

    zone_counter = None
    if config.analytics.zone is not None:
        zone_counter = ZoneOccupancyCounter(
            name=config.analytics.zone.name,
            top_left=config.analytics.zone.top_left,
            bottom_right=config.analytics.zone.bottom_right,
            allowed_classes=allowed_classes,
        )

    return AnalyticsEngine(line_counters=line_counters, zone_counter=zone_counter), resolved_lines

The result is an AnalyticsEngine that the frame loop can call with a simple analytics.update(tracks) on every iteration.

The actual frame loop ties everything together:

fps_meter = FPSMeter()
event_log: deque[tuple[str, str, str]] = deque(maxlen=4)
writer = VideoWriter(config.video.output_path, video_stream.fps, (frame_width, frame_height))

try:
    for _, frame in video_stream.frames():
        detections = detector.detect(frame)
        tracks = tracker.update(detections)
        events = analytics.update(tracks)
        for event in events:
            event_log.append((event.class_name, event.line_name, event.direction))

        fps = fps_meter.update()
        draw_tracks(frame, tracks)
        for line_name, line_points in resolved_lines:
            draw_line(frame, line_points[0], line_points[1], line_name)
        if config.analytics.zone is not None:
            draw_zone(frame, config.analytics.zone.top_left, config.analytics.zone.bottom_right, config.analytics.zone.name)
        draw_stats(frame, analytics.stats(), fps)
        draw_events(frame, event_log)

        writer.write(frame)

        if config.video.display:
            cv2.imshow("YOLO26 Video Analytics", frame)
            if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord("q"):
                break
finally:
    writer.release()
    video_stream.release()
    cv2.destroyAllWindows()

Each iteration reads 1 frame, pushes it through detection, tracking, and analytics, renders the overlay, and optionally writes to disk. The finally block ensures resources are cleaned up even if the loop exits early.

That split is useful because argument parsing, configuration, and runtime execution stay separate.

Here is the command to run it on a webcam:

cd yolo26_video_analytics
python main.py --source 0 --device mps --frame-width 960

If you want the pipeline configured specifically for people counting, use the preset:

cd yolo26_video_analytics
python main.py --preset people --source 0 --device mps

Those presets are defined in video_analytics/config.py. Here is what they look like:

def people_counting_preset() -> PipelineConfig:
    return PipelineConfig(
        detection=DetectionConfig(confidence=0.3),
        tracking=TrackingConfig(activation_threshold=0.3),
        video=VideoConfig(frame_width=960),
        analytics=AnalyticsConfig(
            lines=(AnalyticsLineConfig(name="entry-line", line_y=0.55),),
            class_allowlist=("person",),
        ),
    )


def traffic_counting_preset() -> PipelineConfig:
    return PipelineConfig(
        detection=DetectionConfig(confidence=0.35),
        tracking=TrackingConfig(activation_threshold=0.35),
        video=VideoConfig(frame_width=1280),
        analytics=AnalyticsConfig(
            lines=(
                AnalyticsLineConfig(name="northbound", line_y=0.42),
                AnalyticsLineConfig(name="southbound", line_y=0.68),
            ),
            class_allowlist=("car", "motorcycle", "bus", "truck"),
        ),
    )

The people preset turns the pipeline into people counting software with a single counting line at 55% of the frame height, filtering for person only. The traffic preset turns it into a vehicle counting system with 2 named lines at 42% and 68%, restricted to vehicle classes. Both adjust confidence thresholds slightly higher than the default to reduce noise in their target scenarios.

And here is a file-based example:

cd yolo26_video_analytics
python main.py \
    --source assets/videos/traffic.mp4 \
    --preset traffic \
    --model assets/models/yolo26n.pt \
  --device cpu \
  --frame-width 1280 \
  --output runs/traffic_count.mp4

If you need more control, you can expose the line explicitly:

python main.py --source assets/videos/traffic.mp4 --line-points 100,320,1180,320

Or configure multiple named lines and a class filter:

python main.py \
    --source assets/videos/traffic.mp4 \
    --multi-line-points "entry:0,280,1280,280|exit:0,520,1280,520" \
    --class-filter person \
    --device mps

And if you want to monitor occupancy inside a region of interest:

python main.py \
    --preset people \
    --source assets/videos/traffic_clip.mp4 \
    --zone-points 300,180,980,680 \
    --device mps
Example Output (video demo)

When the system is running, we should see:

  • stable bounding boxes
  • stable track IDs
  • 1 or more labeled counting lines depending on the configuration
  • total, in, and out counts in the top-left
  • per-line counts when multiple lines are enabled
  • optional zone boundaries and occupancy if configured
  • FPS updating live

That is the moment the system stops feeling like a model demo and starts feeling like an analytics application.

Figure 6: Annotated output video from the YOLO26 analytics pipeline, visualizing object detections, multi-object tracking IDs, labeled line-crossing logic, and real-time dashboard counts. (source: GIF by the author). Real-World Applications of People Counting and Vehicle Counting Systems

This real-time video analytics pipeline structure is widely reusable.

Traffic Analytics

Count vehicles crossing a road segment or entering an intersection.

Use the traffic preset with --class-filter car,bus,truck,motorcycle to restrict counting to vehicle classes. With 2 named lines (e.g., northbound and southbound), you can measure crossings at 2 locations. Verify how each line’s "in" and "out" labels correspond to traffic direction. Detecting congestion requires additional analytics (e.g., speed or occupancy measurements).

Retail Analytics

Count customers entering or leaving a store zone.

Point a ceiling-mounted camera at the entrance, set a horizontal counting line at the doorway, and use --class-filter person. This implementation counts each track only once per line. If the same track enters and later exits across the same line, the return crossing is not counted. Use the zone occupancy counter to report the number of tracked people currently inside a configured region. Pair this with zone-based occupancy counting if we also want to know how many people are standing in a specific aisle or checkout area.

Surveillance and Security

Track movement across a perimeter or virtual gate.

Because ByteTrack assigns persistent IDs, we can log which tracks crossed a boundary and in which direction. The overlay displays the 4 most recent crossing events. To support later review, extend the pipeline to save events to a file or database.

Industrial Monitoring

Count items moving across a conveyor or crossing a checkpoint.

The same line-crossing logic that counts people and vehicles also works for packages, parts, or any other object the YOLO26 model can detect. We only need to adjust the class allowlist and line position to match the specific setup.

The important part is not the line itself. The important part is that once detection, tracking, and analytics are separated cleanly, we can swap the event logic for many other use cases.

What Can Go Wrong in Your Real-Time Video Analytics Pipeline

While building and running this pipeline, a few practical issues can show up:

  • No output video generated: OpenCV does not create directories automatically. If we save to a path (e.g., runs/traffic_count.mp4), ensure the runs/ folder already exists.
  • Low FPS or lag: Reduce the frame width, enable frame skipping, or switch between cpu and mps to find a better runtime balance.
  • Incorrect counts: Line placement matters. If the line is too close to the frame edge or objects only partially cross it, the counts may be inconsistent.
  • Track ID switches: In crowded scenes or under occlusion, the tracker may reassign a new ID, which can lead to duplicate counts.

These are not signs that the code is fundamentally broken. They are normal challenges in real-world video analytics systems.

Summary

In this lesson, we moved beyond standalone object detection and built a complete real-time video analytics pipeline from scratch. Instead of thinking about one model in isolation, we learned to reason about a multi-stage system where detection, tracking, analytics, and visualization all need to work together cleanly.

We deployed YOLO26 as the detection backbone, wrapped ByteTrack for multi-object tracking, built a line-crossing analytics engine for people counting and vehicle counting, and connected everything through a modular pipeline that runs on both CPU and MPS. We used dataclasses to define clean interfaces between stages, and we kept configuration separate from runtime logic so the same codebase could serve a traffic counting preset, a people counting preset, or a fully custom setup.

The central idea of this lesson was the separation between detection and analytics. Detection alone can count objects within a frame, but counting unique objects or line-crossing events over time requires tracking and additional analytics. We need stable track IDs across frames before we can ask whether an object crossed a line or entered a zone. ByteTrack provided those IDs, and the analytics layer consumed them to produce directional counts, per-line totals, and optional zone occupancy.

Through the step-by-step build, we saw each layer added incrementally. We started with raw YOLO26 detections on video, added ByteTrack to get persistent IDs, layered in the LineCrossingCounter and ZoneOccupancyCounter for event-driven analytics, and finished with an OpenCV overlay that shows boxes, IDs, counts, and FPS in real time. We also explored practical performance controls including frame resizing, frame skipping, and the CPU vs MPS device toggle.

By the end of this lesson, we did not just detect objects in a video. We built a reusable pattern for real-time video analytics that separates concerns cleanly enough to swap the detector, change the tracker, or replace the analytics logic without rewriting the pipeline. That pattern applies equally well to traffic analytics, retail occupancy monitoring, security perimeter tracking, and industrial conveyor counting.

items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.summary: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. Tags: census , surveys , ai , generative-ai , llms

I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.

First, the updated chart

Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.

I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:

For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):

In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services".

Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.

The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here. Here's a copy of the file I used.

You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF.

The changing language of the questions

As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.

From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence

When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)

The BTOS about page explains what happened:

Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434.

The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.

Is this going to affect the survey?

The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.

The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI".

I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though.

Tags: census, surveys, ai, generative-ai, llms

items.title: Windows 11 upgrades stall amid ‘chipflation’ and ‘RAMageddon’
items.summary: Microsoft ended mainstream Windows 10 support a year ago, but PC upgrades to Windows 11 have ground to a halt, analysts said. Relief may not come until 2028 or even 2029, as high CPU prices, which analysts call “chipflation,” and high memory prices, widely known as the “RAMpocalypse” or “RAMageddon,” keep PC prices up. PC prices were already high, and recent steps like Intel raising CPU prices are increasing the base cost of PCs, said Dean McCarron, principal analyst at Mercury Research. “When prices are higher, demand goes down. It causes a deferred upgrade cycle,” McCarron said. Microsoft’s Windows revenue from PC makers fell 27% in its latest quarter, missing expectations, the company’s chief financial officer Amy Hood said on the company’s earnings call last week. Last year’s rush to upgrade from Windows 10 boosted PC demand, but sales have since slowed , Hood said. PC makers, which pay Microsoft for a Windows license on each PC sold, are also still sitting on unsold stock, Hood said. StatCounter numbers also show a steady number of PC users hanging on to Windows 10 throughout most of 2026. In September, Windows 10 was still running on 27.7% of Windows PCs worldwide, slightly up from 26.45% in February. That coincided with the PC market crash due to high RAM prices, uncertainty around tariffs, and the Iran war. Windows 11’s share of Windows PCs jumped from about half in October 2025 to 72.57% in February after mainstream Windows 10 support ended, then dipped to 71.5% in September. ( Windows 10 extended security updates are available for both businesses — for a hefty fee — and consumers.) For enterprises, upgrades are more complicated than making decisions based on price alone, said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research. Companies in a Windows 10 end-of-support replacement cycle face a conundrum: whether to invest in expensive AI PCs , Shah said. “All these trends are deflating the demand slowing down the replacement cycle,” Shah said. Buyers are being prudent about what to buy and when, waiting for better deals and lower prices, which won’t happen anytime soon, Shah said. A rush to buy PCs ahead of memory-driven price increases boosted PC shipments by 3.2% in the first quarter of 2026 , according to Counterpoint. But PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter and 21% in the third quarter . Commercial PC replacements and Windows migrations provided some stability to the market, but “was insufficient to offset the broader market contraction,” Shah said. “We…expect a 27% YoY decline in Q4 2026, highlighting the tough market.” Analysts were split on when PC prices will stabilize, but they agreed it won’t be 2027. Memory prices will remain inflated as long as most of the supply is directed to data centers feeding the AI boom, Mercury’s McCarron said. Intel in its recent earnings call telegraphed that its PC chip business will remain soft through the rest of 2026 and into 2027. Its lowest-cost PC chip, Wildcat Lake, is sold out. Supply constraints for memory and PC parts may last through 2029, said Steven Dickens, principal analyst at Hyperframe Research. “PC vendors are combating this through restricted configurations and bundles,” Dickens said. AI isn’t yet driving PC upgrades, which are mostly following a typical cycle, Dickens said. But high-end machines capable of running LLMs on-device are starting to shift the market. “We are seeing power user devices for local LLM deployment becoming a material part of the mix and changing the unit price average as a result,” Dickens said. At some point, enterprises will have to upgrade PCs, and the market will also turn around, McCarron said. If a soft PC market goes on for too long, “it will turn into a larger boom perhaps a year later,” McCarron said. “It’ll result in a larger PC upgrade cycle down the road,” McCarron said. “It’s like compressing a spring. The longer you hold it down, the harder it snaps back.”

“All these trends are deflating the demand slowing down the replacement cycle,” Shah said.

Buyers are being prudent about what to buy and when, waiting for better deals and lower prices, which won’t happen anytime soon, Shah said.

A rush to buy PCs ahead of memory-driven price increases boosted PC shipments by 3.2% in the first quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint. But PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter and 21% in the third quarter.

Commercial PC replacements and Windows migrations provided some stability to the market, but “was insufficient to offset the broader market contraction,” Shah said. “We…expect a 27% YoY decline in Q4 2026, highlighting the tough market.”

Analysts were split on when PC prices will stabilize, but they agreed it won’t be 2027. Memory prices will remain inflated as long as most of the supply is directed to data centers feeding the AI boom, Mercury’s McCarron said.

Intel in its recent earnings call telegraphed that its PC chip business will remain soft through the rest of 2026 and into 2027. Its lowest-cost PC chip, Wildcat Lake, is sold out.

Supply constraints for memory and PC parts may last through 2029, said Steven Dickens, principal analyst at Hyperframe Research.

“PC vendors are combating this through restricted configurations and bundles,” Dickens said.

AI isn’t yet driving PC upgrades, which are mostly following a typical cycle, Dickens said. But high-end machines capable of running LLMs on-device are starting to shift the market.

“We are seeing power user devices for local LLM deployment becoming a material part of the mix and changing the unit price average as a result,” Dickens said.

At some point, enterprises will have to upgrade PCs, and the market will also turn around, McCarron said. If a soft PC market goes on for too long, “it will turn into a larger boom perhaps a year later,” McCarron said.

“It’ll result in a larger PC upgrade cycle down the road,” McCarron said. “It’s like compressing a spring. The longer you hold it down, the harder it snaps back.”

items.title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
items.summary: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%. That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work. Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it. HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships. Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice. Build for adoption, not rationing Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code. As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them. items.summary_html:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.

This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process.

—Grace Huckins

Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths

Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes.

Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign.

Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths.

—Sara Kiley Watson

This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble
Big AI bills and weak earnings have spooked investors. (BBC)
+ The Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since June on Friday. (NBC News)
+ OpenAI has cut its funding target by $10 billion. (CNBC)
+ What even is the AI bubble? (MIT Technology Review)

2 Hackers have hit Ukraine and Russia’s emergency alert apps
Kyiv residents were warned of “nuclear danger.” (NBC News)
+ Russia’s app said nuclear warheads had been launched. (CNN)
+ Ukraine has blamed Russia, which hasn’t yet accused anyone. (BI)
+ AI will transform cyber warfare. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Binance users withdrew $3.6 billion after the largest ever crypto hack
The funds moved when the exchange reopened on Sunday. (Guardian)
+ Binance says it’s covered $6 billion of the stolen $6.3 billion. (Reuters $)
+ But the industry’s response has undermined its “decentralized” image. (Gizmodo)

4 An AI agent injected drugs into a live mouse’s brain
It chose the gene therapy and controlled the needle itself. (Wired $)
+ We need real-time tracking of AI agents. (MIT Technology Review)

5 Data centres have made utilities a flashpoint in the midterms
Americans are angry over rising electricity bills. (Reuters $)
+ Virtual power plants could help. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Apple has overtaken Nvidia as the world’s most valuable company
Investors are favouring its restraint on AI spending. (Bloomberg $)
+ But critics say it’s entering its “slop era.” (404 Media)

7 Supermarket fridges have overheated in a new wave of cyberattacks
Stores in Belgium, Sweden, and Luxembourg were hit. (Politico)

8 The first chocolate bars made from lab-grown cocoa are here
Startups are cultivating chocolate to tackle a cocoa shortage. (WSJ $)

9 Hackers hijacked digital billboards in multiple countries to show porn
They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.(Gizmodo)

10 A new 3D map reveals instability in interstellar space
The discovery could help explain why stars form so inefficiently. (Quanta)

Quote of the day

“It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.”

—Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society.

One more thing

Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent

Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away. He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function. But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play. 

Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility. And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve. Read the full story.

—Peter Barrett

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ A miniaturist has built a delightful diorama of the world’s creepiest living room.
+ The year’s best dog photos have been announced, and they’re very good boys and girls.
+ At the Green Zone golf club, you tee off in Sweden and putt in Finland, an hour in the future.
+ Astronomers say they’ve found the real celestial arrangement that inspired van Gogh’s The Starry Night.

items.title: Previewing the Debate Over Frontier AI Regulation
items.summary: If Democrats take control of at least one chamber of Congress and pick up a few governorships in the midterms, proposals to regulate frontier AI labs could get a more serious hearing. So I wanted to look at some of the ideas being discussed, particularly those that would change how labs develop and release models. A quick disclosure: my P(doom) , the odds I’d put on AI causing a catastrophe, is on the low side. I’m also cautious about new regulation. My default is to use existing laws to govern AI applications within specific sectors and industries. I’ve tried to approach these proposals with an open mind, but you may see some skepticism leak into my comments. Subscribe to our weekly newsletter Pausing RSI Requires Defining It First Some of the more ambitious proposals would pause recursive self-improvement (RSI) or even prohibit the development of “superintelligence.” I’ve written before about the distinction between an AI system making a bounded improvement and one that improves the process used to generate further improvements. That distinction matters if we’re going to regulate RSI. Does using a coding agent to improve a training pipeline count? What if the agent runs experiments and selects the best results? Without a clear, enforceable definition, I’m not sure what a ban would actually prohibit. Some proposals seem more practical, at least in principle. Requiring labs to evaluate internal models before using them to develop their successors is one example. But who sets the criteria, and who decides whether a model is safe enough for that work? I’m not sure a lab’s own assessment would be sufficient. I’m less convinced by proposals requiring three to nine months of public deployment before a model can be used for internal research. Public use may not reveal the risks of giving a model access to a lab’s research tools and training systems. Coordinated slowdowns also raise questions about competition, while short delays to complete safety testing seem like a reasonable compromise. Locking Down the Training Environment Of all the proposals, those involving training security strike me as the least controversial. Much of this is basic hygiene. Recent incidents involving frontier AI agents have shown why labs need to do a better job containing their own systems. OpenAI recently described its approach to securing frontier model training , including cutting off live internet access, adding multiple layers of isolation, and using its strongest models to test those defenses. In September, an internal model exploited a network misconfiguration to gain limited access to the internet. OpenAI paused some training while it strengthened its safeguards. This seems like an area where concrete security requirements make sense. I’d also support requiring labs to monitor for unauthorized agent activity, report serious incidents involving internal models, and regularly reassess their security controls. Researchers need realistic environments to test dangerous capabilities, particularly in cybersecurity, but that doesn’t justify unrestricted access to external systems. There are legitimate questions about how much incident information should be made public, especially when disclosure could help attackers. Still, these measures seem more practical and enforceable than some of the broader restrictions on model development. Who Tests the Frontier Labs? Security measures are only as good as the tests used to validate them. I like the idea of giving independent evaluators meaningful access to frontier labs, including internal models and safety procedures, not just models released to the public. Anthropic has already started giving researchers from METR, a nonprofit evaluator, employee-like access. Routine stress testing, safety plans that meet meaningful standards, and cooperation among international safety institutes also seem reasonable to me. Government agencies will struggle to hire enough people who understand these systems, and relying on labs to grade their own work isn’t sufficient. One idea I’ve heard is to encourage private testing firms, similar to credit rating agencies in finance. But that model has a well-known weakness. Before the financial crisis, rating agencies were paid by the banks whose securities they rated, and plenty of shaky mortgage-backed securities ended up with top grades. I’d rather see something closer to Underwriters Laboratories, with independent standards and a long tradition of testing how products fail. I recently recommended a book on test engineering, and I think AI teams have a lot to learn from that discipline. Credible independent assessments could also help CTOs compare models and insurers assess risk. Who Pays When Things Go Wrong? Holding specific decision-makers accountable and protecting employees who raise safety concerns seem reasonable to me. Liability is more complicated. When an AI application causes harm, how do we distinguish a problem with the underlying model from mistakes made by the company deploying it? Mandatory insurance is an interesting idea, and independent testing could help insurers assess risk. But someone still needs to figure out how to price risks that are difficult to measure and for which we have little historical data. Without that, I’m not sure how an insurance market would work. Other proposals would make voluntary safety commitments binding or prohibit labs from supplying AI for certain uses, including military applications and workplace surveillance. I’m skeptical that blanket restrictions on which customers private AI companies can serve would gain much traction. Regulating specific applications is one thing, but prohibiting entire categories of customers is another. I also don’t think labs should get to write their own rules, although regulators will need their technical input. The proposals discussed above may struggle to become law, but I wouldn’t be surprised if some became litmus tests in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary.

Pausing RSI Requires Defining It First

Some of the more ambitious proposals would pause recursive self-improvement (RSI) or even prohibit the development of “superintelligence.” I’ve written before about the distinction between an AI system making a bounded improvement and one that improves the process used to generate further improvements. That distinction matters if we’re going to regulate RSI. Does using a coding agent to improve a training pipeline count? What if the agent runs experiments and selects the best results? Without a clear, enforceable definition, I’m not sure what a ban would actually prohibit.

Some proposals seem more practical, at least in principle. Requiring labs to evaluate internal models before using them to develop their successors is one example. But who sets the criteria, and who decides whether a model is safe enough for that work? I’m not sure a lab’s own assessment would be sufficient. I’m less convinced by proposals requiring three to nine months of public deployment before a model can be used for internal research. Public use may not reveal the risks of giving a model access to a lab’s research tools and training systems. Coordinated slowdowns also raise questions about competition, while short delays to complete safety testing seem like a reasonable compromise.

Locking Down the Training Environment

Of all the proposals, those involving training security strike me as the least controversial. Much of this is basic hygiene. Recent incidents involving frontier AI agents have shown why labs need to do a better job containing their own systems. OpenAI recently described its approach to securing frontier model training, including cutting off live internet access, adding multiple layers of isolation, and using its strongest models to test those defenses. In September, an internal model exploited a network misconfiguration to gain limited access to the internet. OpenAI paused some training while it strengthened its safeguards. This seems like an area where concrete security requirements make sense.

I’d also support requiring labs to monitor for unauthorized agent activity, report serious incidents involving internal models, and regularly reassess their security controls. Researchers need realistic environments to test dangerous capabilities, particularly in cybersecurity, but that doesn’t justify unrestricted access to external systems. There are legitimate questions about how much incident information should be made public, especially when disclosure could help attackers. Still, these measures seem more practical and enforceable than some of the broader restrictions on model development.

Who Tests the Frontier Labs?

Security measures are only as good as the tests used to validate them. I like the idea of giving independent evaluators meaningful access to frontier labs, including internal models and safety procedures, not just models released to the public. Anthropic has already started giving researchers from METR, a nonprofit evaluator, employee-like access. Routine stress testing, safety plans that meet meaningful standards, and cooperation among international safety institutes also seem reasonable to me.

Government agencies will struggle to hire enough people who understand these systems, and relying on labs to grade their own work isn’t sufficient. One idea I’ve heard is to encourage private testing firms, similar to credit rating agencies in finance. But that model has a well-known weakness. Before the financial crisis, rating agencies were paid by the banks whose securities they rated, and plenty of shaky mortgage-backed securities ended up with top grades. I’d rather see something closer to Underwriters Laboratories, with independent standards and a long tradition of testing how products fail. I recently recommended a book on test engineering, and I think AI teams have a lot to learn from that discipline. Credible independent assessments could also help CTOs compare models and insurers assess risk.

Who Pays When Things Go Wrong?

Holding specific decision-makers accountable and protecting employees who raise safety concerns seem reasonable to me. Liability is more complicated. When an AI application causes harm, how do we distinguish a problem with the underlying model from mistakes made by the company deploying it? Mandatory insurance is an interesting idea, and independent testing could help insurers assess risk. But someone still needs to figure out how to price risks that are difficult to measure and for which we have little historical data. Without that, I’m not sure how an insurance market would work.

Other proposals would make voluntary safety commitments binding or prohibit labs from supplying AI for certain uses, including military applications and workplace surveillance. I’m skeptical that blanket restrictions on which customers private AI companies can serve would gain much traction. Regulating specific applications is one thing, but prohibiting entire categories of customers is another. I also don’t think labs should get to write their own rules, although regulators will need their technical input. 

The proposals discussed above may struggle to become law, but I wouldn’t be surprised if some became litmus tests in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary.

items.title: Apple Intelligence with Alibaba comes to China in December
items.summary: After many months of discussion , Apple has figured out a way to bring Apple Intelligence to China, working with Alibaba’s Qwen model on some features. Apple Intelligence will soon be made available as a developer beta and will ship to Chinese customers in December with iOS 27.3. China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology approved the use of Alibaba AI models with the iPhone in October 2026. Confirming the complexity of bringing these tools to China, Apple also received clearance in July from the Cyberspace Administration of China. Apple watchers are at liberty to reflect that the news comes at the best possible time for the company, which continues to grow smartphone market share in China. Apple Intelligence gets behind the iPhone Duo The promise of integrated AI support in the form of Apple Intelligence can only boost interest in the company’s recently introduced iPhone Duo . Recent Counterpoint Research data claims iPhone sales increased 29% year on year in China in the three weeks following launch of the 18 Pro series devices. Initial stock of the devices sold out in hours. China is also the world’s biggest market for foldable devices, which prompted some enterprising individuals to attempt to resell purchased iPhone Duos for far above their store price — scalpers have since reduced prices , because even in iPhone-crazy China, people weren’t willing to pay so much. While it’s a big step for Apple AI in China, it’s not quite the great leap Apple may have wanted to put in place. Siri AI sits this one out Siri AI is not supported and won’t be “anytime soon,” according to market speculation . While little is said about the reasons for that, it seems probable that political pressure in both the US and China may be partly to blame, as both nations see control of the means of AI production as essential for the future success of their differing ideologies. Apple has had to allow the Chinese government to approve ongoing updates to the suite. Chinese users can use Alibaba’s Qwen in Siri, writing tools, and visual intelligence, including functions related to text and image understanding. They don’t get Image Playground, but can expect: Writing tools Clean Up in Photos Notification summaries Email summaries and smart replies Priority Notifications Visual Intelligence Live Translation Text to Siri Qwen if you want to Apple and Alibaba also promise to maintain privacy. Customers will be able to choose if they wish to proceed with making a request through Qwen. Alibaba also said it would not use these requests for model training, though it isn’t yet clear if requests are going to Private Cloud Compute in Apple’s Chinese AI deployment. Will the introduction of Apple Intelligence in China make a difference? It probably already is, as months of ever stronger speculation mean most Chinese consumers knew Apple AI was coming to their iPhones even as they purchased them before the announcement took place. While the initial sales rush on Apple’s new devices among Chinese consumers has slowed, the news may help generate fresh enthusiasm for the iPhone in China. That’s great for Apple, but not such great news for some smaller smartphone vendors, who continue to be hammered by vicious increases in memory and other component prices. A critical catalyst at a critical time Speaking almost two years ago when industry observers had anticipated an Apple Intelligence launch in China would take place earlier, Morgan Stanley then suggested the Alibaba partnership would be “a critical catalyst for Apple’s competitive standing in China.” Other than painful price increases, not much has changed, and the introduction can only help consolidate the iPhone’s appeal in China. That’s good for Apple’s customers there, and great news for Apple’s investors everywhere else. It may even do something to retain a little US soft power. In the background, we see the continued economic pressure wrought by fast-increasing memory prices. This has driven smartphone makers to raise prices, which has itself driven a 21% year on year decline in sector sales . Apple and Samsung have proved more resilient to these price hikes than others, which means the added appeal generated by the launch of Apple Intelligence in the world’s second-largest economy is likely to make a highly significant difference to its market share in the short term, as well as shoring up share in future replacement cycles. Now please subscribe to my daily, human-curated Apple-related news headline feed at The Core , or follow me on BlueSky , LinkedIn , or Mastodon .

Apple watchers are at liberty to reflect that the news comes at the best possible time for the company, which continues to grow smartphone market share in China. 

Apple Intelligence gets behind the iPhone Duo

The promise of integrated AI support in the form of Apple Intelligence can only boost interest in the company’s recently introduced iPhone Duo. Recent Counterpoint Research data claims iPhone sales increased 29% year on year in China in the three weeks following launch of the 18 Pro series devices. While it’s a big step for Apple AI in China, it’s not quite the great leap Apple may have wanted to put in place. 

Siri AI sits this one out

Siri AI is not supported and won’t be “anytime soon,” according to market speculation. While little is said about the reasons for that, it seems probable that political pressure in both the US and China may be partly to blame, as both nations see control of the means of AI production as essential for the future success of their differing ideologies. Apple has had to allow the Chinese government to approve ongoing updates to the suite.

Chinese users can use Alibaba’s Qwen in Siri, writing tools, and visual intelligence, including functions related to text and image understanding. They don’t get Image Playground, but can expect:

  • Writing tools
  • Clean Up in Photos
  • Notification summaries
  • Email summaries and smart replies
  • Priority Notifications
  • Visual Intelligence
  • Live Translation
  • Text to Siri
Qwen if you want to 

Apple and Alibaba also promise to maintain privacy. Customers will be able to choose if they wish to proceed with making a request through Qwen. Alibaba also said it would not use these requests for model training, though it isn’t yet clear if requests are going to Private Cloud Compute in Apple’s Chinese AI deployment.

Will the introduction of Apple Intelligence in China make a difference? It probably already is, as months of ever stronger speculation mean most Chinese consumers knew Apple AI was coming to their iPhones even as they purchased them before the announcement took place. 

While the initial sales rush on Apple’s new devices among Chinese consumers has slowed, the news may help generate fresh enthusiasm for the iPhone in China. That’s great for Apple, but not such great news for some smaller smartphone vendors, who continue to be hammered by vicious increases in memory and other component prices.

A critical catalyst at a critical time

Speaking almost two years ago when industry observers had anticipated an Apple Intelligence launch in China would take place earlier, Morgan Stanley then suggested the Alibaba partnership would be “a critical catalyst for Apple’s competitive standing in China.” 

Other than painful price increases, not much has changed, and the introduction can only help consolidate the iPhone’s appeal in China. That’s good for Apple’s customers there, and great news for Apple’s investors everywhere else. It may even do something to retain a little US soft power.

In the background, we see the continued economic pressure wrought by fast-increasing memory prices. This has driven smartphone makers to raise prices, which has itself driven a 21% year on year decline in sector sales. 

Apple and Samsung have proved more resilient to these price hikes than others, which means the added appeal generated by the launch of Apple Intelligence in the world’s second-largest economy is likely to make a highly significant difference to its market share in the short term, as well as shoring up share in future replacement cycles.
