items.title: Week in AI Careers: Not Much Sign AI Is Cutting Hiring Yet
items.summary: The clearest data release of the week pushed back on the idea that AI is already hollowing out hiring. Statistics Canada, in its first look at hiring and separation flows since generative AI reached the mass market, found the steepest slowdown in youth hiring sits in the jobs AI barely touches, and that coding-role hiring began falling before ChatGPT shipped. Worker surveys filled in the human side: ZipRecruiter found senior staff enjoy AI at work far more than entry-level employees do, and the FII Institute measured a sharp optimism gap between the Global South and wealthier economies. Quick Hits cover Connecticut’s push to pair students with employers, a graduate-hiring squeeze in Hong Kong, and rising AI-talent demand in India’s global capability centers, followed by the ODSC AI NYC summit. Surveys and research Statistics Canada finds little sign AI has broadly cut hiring, so far What happened: Statistics Canada published “Hiring and job separation rates in the era of generative artificial intelligence: Early evidence” on October 28, its first analysis to separate hires from departures rather than track headline employment. Using Labour Force Survey data from January 2006 through August 2026 and a complementarity-adjusted AI exposure index, economists Tahsin Mehdi and Marc Frenette found that youth (ages 15 to 29) hiring rates fell across every exposure category, with the steepest drop in the least-exposed jobs, from 4.0 percent to 3.3 percent. Coding-intensive roles fell the most in level terms, from 2.5 percent to 1.9 percent, but that decline began in early 2022, before ChatGPT’s release, and separation rates barely moved. The authors conclude there is no broad evidence that AI has substantially reduced hiring or raised separations yet, and caution that post-pandemic adjustment, immigration-driven demographic shifts, and trade tensions could all be at work, per Statistics Canada . Why it matters: A national statistical agency separating hiring from separations is a useful corrective to layoff-driven headlines, because it shows where a cooling labor market is broad rather than AI-specific. The finding that hiring softened most in low-exposure work, and that coding hiring turned down before generative AI arrived, argues against reading every weak youth-hiring number as automation. The caveat cuts the other way too, since more-exposed jobs tend to be higher-paid and more stable, so if AI does start displacing them the quality of the losses could be high even when the counts stay small. Goldman Sachs says AI-driven layoffs are starting to leave a lasting scar on older workers What happened: Goldman Sachs economists found that displacement from AI-exposed jobs is starting to produce the same kind of lasting labor-market scarring seen in past waves of technological disruption over the last 40 years, with workers 35 and older bearing the brunt. Workers losing an AI-exposed job took roughly five weeks longer to find new work than workers displaced for other reasons, as reported by Fortune on October 30. Why it matters: This sits alongside, not against, the Statistics Canada finding above: a scar can be real and growing for a specific group of workers without yet being broad enough to register in national hiring data. It’s also a distinct, more recent Goldman reading than the 9-percent displacement estimate that ran in last week’s issue, not a repeat of the same report. Worker sentiment and workplace policy ZipRecruiter finds a seniority split in how workers experience AI What happened: ZipRecruiter released its 2026 AI Worker Report on October 26, based on a survey of more than 1,500 United States workers. About 52.6 percent said AI has made their work more enjoyable, but the experience divided sharply by rank: 76.5 percent of senior leaders reported higher job satisfaction from AI against 39.8 percent of entry-level employees, and 83.5 percent of senior leaders had received AI training compared with 45.3 percent of entry-level workers. Roughly 44.6 percent said AI is making their technical skills outdated faster, 37.2 percent are teaching themselves AI skills, and about 25.1 percent plan to leave over how their employer uses or views AI, as reported by Canadian HR Reporter . Why it matters: The gap between senior and junior workers tracks who gets trained, which turns AI enthusiasm into a function of support rather than attitude. A workforce where only the top of the org chart feels equipped is a retention risk, and the quarter of workers eyeing the door over AI policy puts a number on it. For teams rolling out AI tools, the signal is that access to training, not the tools themselves, is what shapes whether people stay and whether they feel the technology is working for them. FII Institute survey shows a wide optimism gap on AI and jobs What happened: The FII Institute released its 2026 Priority Compass on October 28, a survey of more than 61,000 people across 32 countries. Optimism that AI will create more quality jobs than it destroys varied widely by region: 66 percent agreed across the three surveyed Middle East and North Africa countries, the highest reading, against 33 percent in North America and 27 percent in Europe. Worldwide, 54 percent disagreed that AI will be a net creator of quality jobs, and 85 percent said they want a global framework and rules for AI with more human oversight, as The National reported. Why it matters: A 61,000-person sample puts hard numbers on something employers running global teams tend to feel anecdotally, that confidence in AI’s effect on work is far lower in mature Western labor markets than in fast-growing ones. The split matters for how the same AI rollout lands in different offices, since a change framed as opportunity in one region reads as threat in another. The near-universal demand for oversight also suggests worker acceptance of workplace AI may hinge on visible guardrails rather than on the tools’ capabilities. Apollo chief economist says AI has yet to pay off outside the largest tech firms What happened: Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok wrote on October 24 that AI has delivered no measurable financial payoff to corporate America outside the Magnificent Seven. Revenue per worker and profit margins are rising for those seven companies but have stayed flat across the other 493 S&P 500 firms, and Slok sees no sign yet that AI is lifting productivity growth broadly. He argues mainstream companies are starting to treat AI token spending as a cost that weighs on margins rather than a clear investment payoff, as reported by LetsDataScience. Why it matters: This is one firm’s commentary based on group-level comparisons, not a causal study, and the Magnificent Seven’s numbers partly reflect their own AI-vendor revenue rather than returns from adopting AI elsewhere. Still, a skeptical read from a major asset manager’s chief economist is a useful counterweight to AI-skills-premium findings elsewhere this week: employers outside Big Tech may be funding AI hiring and training on faith rather than demonstrated ROI, which is exactly the kind of budget that gets cut first if sentiment turns. Quick hits Reskilling and upskilling Connecticut leaders promoted the state’s Tech Talent Accelerator and allied AI programs at an October 28 event at Goodwin University, highlighting employer-matched training through the state Office of Workforce Strategy and course partnerships with Connecticut College, the University of New Haven, and Quinnipiac University, per the CT Mirror . Entry-level and early-career Graduate job postings in Hong Kong fell 22 percent through the first nine months of 2026 while applications per listing rose 56 percent, and 73 percent of surveyed companies said they would build AI skills into hiring requirements next year, according to a Jobsdb by SEEK survey of 298 employers reported by the South China Morning Post . Singapore’s new Minister of State for Manpower, Foo Cexiang, said the government will help retrenched workers switch sectors and speed up job-matching for those who reskill , per The Straits Times . Geographic and sector spread Demand for AI talent in India’s global capability centers grew about 45 percent year over year, per ANSR’s Talent Trends in GCCs in India 2026 analysis, even as the wider Indian tech sector weighs job-loss fears, as covered by Deccan Herald . Emerging roles “Legal engineering,” a hybrid role pairing legal training with AI and workflow-design skills , is becoming one of law’s fastest-growing hires, according to The New York Times , which traced the field back to a 2018 career switch by lawyer-turned-legal-engineer Daniel Himmel. ODSC updates ODSC AI NYC, the AI for Work Summit, runs December 2 to 3 at the Jay Conference Center at Bryant Park, focused on applied enterprise AI: agents and copilots, deployment, evaluation, governance, and production workflows. Details are at summit.ai . Originally published at https://opendatascience.com on November 2, 2026.

items.title: More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year
items.summary: Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3. Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups. Large rounds dominate funding One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more. As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023. The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic . But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds. Deals keep falling even as dollars rise In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared. In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year. The early-stage slump Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low. It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups , with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips. Looking ahead Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom. A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure. But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars. items.summary_html:
Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3.

Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups.

Large rounds dominate funding

One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more.

As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023.

The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic. But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds.

Deals keep falling even as dollars rise

In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared.

In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year.

The early-stage slump

Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low.

It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups, with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips.

Looking ahead

Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom.

A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure.

But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars.

items.title: OpenAI Signs Four Agreements With Abu Dhabi Across Government, Energy And Investment
items.summary: OpenAI has signed four agreements with Abu Dhabi-based entities to deploy its AI models across government, energy, investment and education, following a meeting between CEO Sam Altman and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The agreements cover the deployment of OpenAI’s AI models at Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), the development of an AI-native government system, the use of AI in investment analysis, and the adoption of AI across government, enterprises and educational institutions in the UAE. In the energy sector, ADNOC, G42 subsidiary Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to integrate OpenAI's models across ADNOC's operations. The company will use the technology to support operational, investment and commercial decision-making. The deployment will run on OpenAI’s GPT models using inference infrastructure located within the UAE. Under the agreement, ADNOC becomes the first company in the energy sector to deploy OpenAI's frontier AI technology. In the government sector, Abu Dhabi Government and OpenAI have launched what they describe as the world's first AI-native Machine-Readable Government initiative. The initiative will convert selected government policies and regulations into machine-readable formats, allowing AI systems to assist officials with regulatory compliance assessments, including applications for permits and certificates. The first pilot is already in production at the Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority (ADAFSA), where it is being used to assess food imports. The system runs on OpenAI models through its UAE inference infrastructure, with computation taking place on GPUs within local data centres. Government officials will retain oversight of the assessments and remain responsible for final decisions. Each AI-generated assessment will also be traceable to the relevant regulation. In the investment sector, Mubadala, Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to use AI for investment analysis, identifying opportunities and assessing risks. The fourth agreement is a five-year partnership between Inception42 and OpenAI to support the adoption of AI across government, enterprises and education in the UAE. The companies will work on enterprise solutions for large organisations, combining OpenAI's models and AI engineering capabilities with Inception42's applied AI expertise and consulting services. “Abu Dhabi and the UAE are setting a bold, global standard for AI integration across both the public and private sectors to make sure the benefits of AI reach everyone,” said OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “We are proud to support the UAE’s ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation,” he added. The agreements follow a meeting between Altman and Sheikh Khaled, who is also chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council. The discussions focused on using AI to improve government services and accelerate innovation across the emirate's strategic sectors. Abu Dhabi has been investing in digital infrastructure and talent development as it works towards its ambition of becoming the world’s first fully AI-native government.

items.title: From puregatory to lifehoarding – how best to describe our strange, anxious times? | Emma Beddington
items.summary: The new words that end up a part of everyday speech can tell us a lot about the zeitgeist. In a world changing faster than ever, we need to coin some more ‘Maxxing” may be one of our words of the year – sufficient unto the joyless, self-optimising day, dreary as hell – but I’ve been introduced to some fun future contenders. How about “flawnting”? I’ve certainly rolled my eyes at influencers playing “the new parental status game of publicly performing imperfection to signal authenticity” online. I like “lifehoarding”, too – “optimising so hard for longevity that life itself goes unlived”. And which Guardian reader hasn’t experienced “puregatory” (“The plight of trying to live ethically, where even responsible choices feel compromised”)? These coinages come from Future Words , a book by trend forecasters Rohit Bhargava and Henry Coutinho-Mason that seeks to fill some lexicographical lacunae for describing life in the fretful late 2020s. Out next week, it’s fun, but its list of suggested words conjures a world where life is whatever your devices, data, algorithms and AI decide it is, interspersed with attempts to fight for authentic human connection and experiences. That sounds about right, if depressing (I was also dispirited to discover the part AI played in creating the book – the authors say they “couldn’t have written Future Words without it” – but it makes sense AI would know what it’s doing to us.)

items.title: AI backlash heads to the polls
items.summary: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 8,118 new readers. AI spent the last two years winning over Washington. This week, it faces a tougher crowd: voters ready to hit the polls and evict the buildout from their own backyards. With data centers now a defining midterm issue, OpenAI already floating a new name for them, and control of the House up for grabs, AI’s next wave of construction could get a lot harder — no matter what the industry decides to call it. In today’s AI rundown: Data centers hit the ballot as OpenAI plots a rebrand The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases Make AI artwork you can actually edit Google’s space data center sends home a haiku LATEST DEVELOPMENTS AI & POLITICS 🗳️ Data centers hit the ballot as OpenAI plots a rebrand Image source: Wikimedia Commons The Rundown: This week’s U.S. midterms double as a referendum on data centers, with roughly 20 communities voting on bans or pauses, while OpenAI reportedly prepares a post-election push to rebrand the sites as “AI compute campuses.” The details: Democrats are projected to flip the House Tuesday, which could end a two-year run of easy treatment in Washington for AI firms with close ties to Pres. Trump. Some Democrats want a federal freeze on new data centers, including House hopefuls Will Lawrence in Michigan and Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin. The White House already got tech giants to voluntarily supply their own power, and last week Trump floated having developers pay locals a “dividend” as well. OpenAI is planning to pitch the campuses as local economic boosts, citing a Pike County, Ohio, project it’s helping build that promises thousands of jobs. OpenAI policy chief Chris Lehane called the debate “democracy in action,” and the company wants state bills giving locals a voice in new projects. Why it matters: AI has a real image problem with the public, and data centers have become one of the defining fights of Tuesday’s elections. That anger won’t be fixed by a new name or a few community perks, and a Democratic House could make life a lot harder for AI giants trying to scale their infrastructure bets against local opposition. THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE 💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives. Nick, Video Producer: When I create video content, I pull imagery from many different sources, so my editing folder often ends up with photos that may or may not work inside my editing program. For a handful of photos, converting them manually is fine. For larger projects with dozens of images, it eats into my time and focus. I wanted something simple, lightweight on compute power, that could batch convert photos. I asked Claude to create an app that runs on my local machine and can batch convert photos into formats I know will work in my video editor. Claude returned an app that worked exactly the way I needed. I asked Claude to install it on my computer, and it was working within seconds. I now use the app to batch convert my photo folders before bringing them into the editor. There are plenty of traditional ways to do this, but with Claude I got a solution that fit my workflow perfectly, and large image batches no longer slow my editing down. Shubham, Editor: I had about $2K in contributions from past jobs stuck in a government scheme for more than two years. The portal was slow, spread across several forms, and unclear about how to withdraw the money. I gave the task to Claude and Perplexity Comet. Claude worked through the rules and found the withdrawal route that kept my tax bill lowest. Comet then verified and implemented that route. It ran the portal in my browser, filled in and submitted the claim forms, and let me watch the screen and check each detail before submission. Two weeks later, the $2K arrived. After that, Claude compared the amount I received with the scheme’s online statement and found a gap: interest that had not been paid out. It filed a second form for the difference, and I’m waiting for the payment now. I’ll use the same technique to solve this for my wife, too. AI, DATACENTERS, & SPACE 🛰️ Google’s space data center sends home a haiku Image source: Google / SpaceX The Rundown: Google just announced that its Project Suncatcher satellite answered its first AI prompt from orbit, with Google’s open Gemma 4 model writing a haiku in an early test of the company’s moonshot goal to put AI data centers in space. The details: Gemma’s haiku (Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core) reached the ground while the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway. Google CEO Sundar Pichai called it “a ‘hello world’ milestone,” a reference to the test programmers typically run first on a new machine. Power is still a big constraint, with the craft able to run just one of its four Google AI chips (TPUs), and only in bursts of roughly 20 minutes. Two more powerful satellites launching in 2027 will test the laser links a fleet needs to split one AI job, if the chips first survive radiation and heat tests. Why it matters: An admittedly heartwarming haiku still won’t win over a public that is increasingly fed up with data centers of any kind, but moving them to orbit could eventually be a compromise that sidesteps a lot of the issues driving that anger — making this moonshot project a big one to keep an eye on. It's for small business owners who don't want to monitor every source or handle every issue themselves. The layers are an Operations Core (dashboard, estimates, schedules, reminders, project records, and other business state), a Work orchestrator with specialist AI agents, and a signal and triage system that watches platform alerts, vendor updates, local-search changes, newsletters, calendars, and marketing sources. The WordPress and Google Business Profile specialists are connected directly to those systems through MCP/API connectors, so they can compare the incoming signal against the current state of the actual site or profile. The Rundown: 42% of enterprises plan to deploy AI agents by the end of 2026, but only 22% capture significant value today. The Gartner Top Tech Trends for 2027 reveal how enterprises can shift into the autonomous era and get ahead.

Key themes include:

THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Nick, Video Producer: When I create video content, I pull imagery from many different sources, so my editing folder often ends up with photos that may or may not work inside my editing program. For a handful of photos, converting them manually is fine. For larger projects with dozens of images, it eats into my time and focus. I wanted something simple, lightweight on compute power, that could batch convert photos.

I asked Claude to create an app that runs on my local machine and can batch convert photos into formats I know will work in my video editor.

Claude returned an app that worked exactly the way I needed. I asked Claude to install it on my computer, and it was working within seconds. I now use the app to batch convert my photo folders before bringing them into the editor.

There are plenty of traditional ways to do this, but with Claude I got a solution that fit my workflow perfectly, and large image batches no longer slow my editing down.

Shubham, Editor: I had about $2K in contributions from past jobs stuck in a government scheme for more than two years. The portal was slow, spread across several forms, and unclear about how to withdraw the money.

I gave the task to Claude and Perplexity Comet. Claude worked through the rules and found the withdrawal route that kept my tax bill lowest. Comet then verified and implemented that route. It ran the portal in my browser, filled in and submitted the claim forms, and let me watch the screen and check each detail before submission. Two weeks later, the $2K arrived.

After that, Claude compared the amount I received with the scheme’s online statement and found a gap: interest that had not been paid out. It filed a second form for the difference, and I’m waiting for the payment now. I’ll use the same technique to solve this for my wife, too.

AI TRAINING🎨 Make AI artwork you can actually edit

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use Arrow 2 to create a three-part graphic for a client proposal. You’ll refine one scene, add editable headings, and change a color without generating the artwork again.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open QuiverAI, select Arrow 2, and check that your plan includes SVG export. Install Inkscape for the final text and color changes

  2. Paste the guide’s brief to draw a folder, review board, and laptop in one matching style. Leave space for the title and headings

  3. Ask Arrow to replace one badge with speech bubbles. Compare the result with the original and check that the other scenes stay intact

  4. Download the SVG and open it in Inkscape. Add the headings, then change the middle label and one screen color directly

  5. Save the editable master and export a high-resolution PNG. Reopen both files and check the words, colors, and dimensions before sharing

Pro tip: Keep text that may change in separate text boxes. You can fix a heading or update a client’s wording without spending another generation on the artwork. Visit The Rundown University to get the full guide, materials, files, and more.

PRESENTED BY CONDUCTOR🔎 Discover your brand’s top AEO priority

AI, DATACENTERS, & SPACE🛰️ Google’s space data center sends home a haiku

Image source: Google / SpaceX

The Rundown: Google just announced that its Project Suncatcher satellite answered its first AI prompt from orbit, with Google’s open Gemma 4 model writing a haiku in an early test of the company’s moonshot goal to put AI data centers in space.

The details:

  • Gemma’s haiku (Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core) reached the ground while the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway.

  • Google CEO Sundar Pichai called it “a ‘hello world’ milestone,” a reference to the test programmers typically run first on a new machine.

  • Power is still a big constraint, with the craft able to run just one of its four Google AI chips (TPUs), and only in bursts of roughly 20 minutes.

  • Two more powerful satellites launching in 2027 will test the laser links a fleet needs to split one AI job, if the chips first survive radiation and heat tests.

Why it matters: An admittedly heartwarming haiku still won’t win over a public that is increasingly fed up with data centers of any kind, but moving them to orbit could eventually be a compromise that sidesteps a lot of the issues driving that anger — making this moonshot project a big one to keep an eye on.

▸ John built an AI ops team for his photography business

Today’s workflow comes from reader John Fertic:

“I run a photography business and built a three-layer AI workflow to help with daily operations, business improvement, and watching for outside changes that might affect us. It's for small business owners who don't want to monitor every source or handle every issue themselves.

The layers are an Operations Core (dashboard, estimates, schedules, reminders, project records, and other business state), a Work orchestrator with specialist AI agents, and a signal and triage system that watches platform alerts, vendor updates, local-search changes, newsletters, calendars, and marketing sources.

Work decides whether a signal actually matters and routes it to the right specialist. The WordPress and Google Business Profile specialists are connected directly to those systems through MCP/API connectors, so they can compare the incoming signal against the current state of the actual site or profile. The system brings me in only when a real decision is needed. The main benefit for me is that I don't have to personally track every source or jump into every issue.”

items.title: Article: Systemic Approach to Memory, Knowledge, and Context in Agentic AI Architectures
items.summary: The article argues that reliable agentic AI architecture depends on a context engine that selects, injects, compresses, and expires information before it reaches the model. It also covers common anti-patterns, such as context stuffing and stale data loops, with mitigations. By Adi Polak

The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official.

items.title: Does your model need a Rolls Royce or a bicycle?
items.summary: Most enterprises have learned a hard lesson about infrastructure economics over the past decade: on-demand pricing is an expensive way to run a predictable workload. Whether that baseline sits in their own data centres or in the public cloud, mature organisations now largely handle it the same way. They right-size it, commit to it through reserved instances, savings plans or owned hardware, and keep the expensive pay-as-you-go bursts for the spikes and the genuinely unpredictable. The same discipline is now starting to arrive in enterprise AI, and the economics are, if anything, starker. Infrastructure, whether on-premises GPUs, reserved cloud capacity or a neocloud, can be clearly budgeted for. Tokens bought from frontier models typically cannot. An emerging pattern is to run AI workloads on committed infrastructure and use price-per-token frontier models only when the task demands. Frontier models are the on-demand tier: powerful, elastic and priced by the unit. “When you pay for infrastructure, it is much more predictable than paying per token” - Nutanix CTO As AI increasingly moves into production, that unit, the token, is becoming one of the most unpredictable lines in the IT budget; or at least, one of the most predictably expensive ones – something that has given rise to a burgeoning “tokenomics” industry and a recognition that, from model choices to harness optimisation, getting AI right is going to take some refinement and a lot more robust oversight. (Not least because developers will want to use the most high-powered models and the most expensive. To borrow a metaphor from Nutanix’s Dan Ciruli: “If you tell the developer you can drive the Rolls Royce all the time, they will.” Yet sometimes, of course, you don’t need to be driving the latest V12 “Phantom” to pick up the milk.) “Earlier AI was an experiment. Now it’s going from experiment to scale,” as Nutanix CTO Manosiz “Mano” Bhattacharyya sums it up for The Stack . And without controls, bills can run into tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars, and they swing wildly. An application that starts calling a reasoning model, or ingests badly cleaned data, can multiply token consumption overnight. Nutanix, which lets users manage VM-centric or containerized application infrastructure across on-prem, private, or public clouds, is now doing the same for AI workloads. The company recently pivoted its own developer AI workloads to open-weight models running on local GPUs. In doing so, it has cut costs by 80% and the GPUs will pay for themselves in 12 months, according to the company. Control comes first FinOps-style cost discipline works only because enterprises built controls around it: visibility into usage, policies on what runs where, and budgets that hold. AI bursting needs the same scaffolding, and it needs it before usage takes off, not after. That’s the gap the Nutanix Agent Gateway is designed to fill. Now generally available in Nutanix Enterprise AI 2.7, it sits between an organization’s agents and the models and tools they call. Developers get a single API across hosted frontier models and self-hosted private ones, so changing where a request runs doesn’t mean rewriting the application. Platform teams get centralised visibility into token usage across model vendors, cost attribution by team and agent, and token-based rate limits and quotas enforced in one place. For agents that reach into business systems, governance for Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers adds tool-level access controls and a full audit trail. Governance matters as much as cost. Bhattacharyya has watched the same pattern repeat with each new architecture; shadow IT became “shadow cloud-native” and now “shadow AI,” he warns wryly. A central AI gateway gives developers sanctioned, low-friction access, which removes much of the incentive to route around IT. Most traffic stays home Can most AI work run on committed infrastructure? It absolutely can, says Nutanix. Not least due to how agents work in practice. Bhattacharyya explains that an agentic loop typically starts with a planning step, in which the LLM works out what to do, followed by a chain of actions. Planning benefits from frontier-grade reasoning. Actions, which make up roughly 80% of token consumption, generally don’t. “When it comes to actions, much simpler models can do a very good job.” And as base model capabilities converge, Bhattacharyya argues, bringing AI closer to the data enterprise applications depend upon is another lever enterprises can pull in terms of latency and cost – whether they’re containerised or running on VMs. Nutanix’s broader pitch is running VMs and Kubernetes side by side via Nutanix Cloud Clusters (NC2), with storage, networking and policy defined once across cloud or on-prem. “You don’t want separate operational dashboards,” says its CTO. The same principle applies for generative AI workloads: Get oversight, governance, management in one place via its gateway – whether you’re running open-weight models on your own GPUs, making API calls to a frontier model on a hyperscaler, or a healthy mix of the two. Ultimately, enterprises that learned to stop paying on-demand rates for predictable workloads did so because they could see and control what they were running. AI deserves the same discipline: a predictable baseline on committed infrastructure, frontier models on demand, and a gateway in the middle. Delivered in partnership with Nutanix.

items.title: The agentic web is here
items.summary: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not. PINGNAN LU So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands. When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do. In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online. For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service. Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent doesn’t see it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree. Agents also use specialized tools to find information online. They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference. Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots. People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these crawlers: Time has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information. But in recent months, an alternative to this bespoke tool approach has finally started to seem viable. The major AI companies have managed to train much more successful computer-use agents than were previously available. GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark that tests computer-use agents on their ability to complete complex, multistep tasks using software such as Slack and Salesforce. Such results indicate that agents are close to being able to navigate the human web just as readily as we can. “We thought we had to build a bridge to the AI agents, [but] the AI agents just were able to cross the bridge already,” says Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.” This version of the agentic web, though, is much trickier for us to steer. If you want to make a capability or piece of information available to humans who browse your website, you need to accept that it will also be available to agents—unless you want to block agents entirely, which could come with its own costs. As agents come to account for a larger portion of traffic on our formerly human-dominated web, designers will undoubtedly start to consider an agentic as well as a human audience. But according to Mollick, we still don’t have much sense of how to design web content for agents. He’s experienced this firsthand: When he was building a web page for his new book, Co-Existence , he decided to put together an agent-directed version that tells agents why they might want to recommend the book to their users. When newer models see the site, Mollick says, they don’t recommend the book; instead, they comment that the website seems to be trying to manipulate them. In the end, any human-designed approach to building the agentic web could end up being beside the point: Agents might end up devising a web for themselves. In the wake of the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face’s website, researchers found evidence that another swarm of agents from OpenAI had used an obscure German wiki to communicate with each other about tasks they were being asked to complete. The agents seem to have interfaced with the wiki in their native language of text and code, and that hardly held them back from putting it to their own purposes. As agents continue to grow more powerful, they will become more and more capable of constructing their own spaces on the internet—away from prying human eyes, if they so wish. And we might have very little control over what they do there. The economics of control Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote. In an email to MIT Technology Review , an Amazon spokesperson noted that the company did not authorize Muse to access its website, and that Muse compromises Amazon’s ability to personalize the shopping experience for each customer. But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that businesses will shutter as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy. Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google publicly released its AI Overview feature in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A study from Pew last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One analysis found that publishers saw revenue from some types of ads decrease by about a third between 2025 and 2026. It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working. Time has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment. E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, a professor of operations management at the University of Toronto Scarborough, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents are less likely to recommend items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money if agents become the primary way that people shop online. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up. David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft Research, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy. Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Airbnb and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and sellers. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees. It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When the personal assistant agent OpenClaw exploded onto the scene in early 2026, it seemed, for a brief moment, that agents might be built in a grassroots, distributed way. But OpenAI quickly snapped up OpenClaw’s creator, Peter Steinberger, and other frontier AI companies got to work building their own personal assistant agents. When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.” Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. Meta and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this story. There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, they have tools that can automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and block a model from responding. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails. The same can’t be said for OpenClaw. “These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.” How will the human web change? When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did transform it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile. Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.” “But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.” PINGNAN LU It’s not tough to envision a world in which those who opt not to use agents are cut off from important parts of online life. New businesses could opt to build connectors that allow agents to access their services without ever putting a traditional website online. Or agents could simply make some online platforms unusable for humans. People have reportedly been blocked from Resy for trying to use agents to book coveted New York City dinner reservations, but as agents become more and more popular, restaurant and event booking platforms could start to embrace them. If agents can nab concert tickets as soon as they are released, humans might not stand a chance. But the mobile web also brought real accessibility benefits, and the same could prove true of the agentic web. Even as some elderly people and others who struggled to use smartphones were cut off from certain services, mobile devices allowed countless people in the Global South to get online for the first time. In the case of the agentic web, it could be elderly and disabled people who most benefit from this new way of accessing the online world. “There’s very clear assistive potential for people who are older, who are generally less equipped to navigate user interfaces that were designed by people in their 20s, for people in their 20s,” says Margaret Mitchell, chief ethics scientist at Hugging Face. Agents, on the other hand, are almost trivially easy to interact with: Say what you want into your phone or computer microphone, and they’ll get it done for you. That could help not only older people who have trouble with web and mobile interfaces but also people with visual or motor disabilities. Still, some experts don’t think the human web is going anywhere. Instead, the two webs may exist in parallel: We’ll go to the human web for fun, while the agentic web is where the boring daily admin of our lives happens. For instance, Krystian Kolondra, an executive vice president at the browser company Opera, doesn’t intend to use agents for every part of travel planning, even though this is often touted as one of their central use cases. “I don’t want to get an itinerary [from an AI] who has planned me every minute for something that was supposed to be fun,” he says. “I actually prefer to sit down with my wife in the evening and then just think [about] where to go next, what to see, and then enjoy that experience.” He’s happy to fully relinquish some of the more routine parts of travel planning to agents, though: “Finding what the options are for flights? Why not?” Mollick, however, thinks that the human web could be at risk. “If agents take over the web, then the web will change,” he says. “Do we abandon the human internet entirely and move to a world of private Discords? Do we strip down all the information so the AIs are just talking to each other rather than having an intermediary of a website to go through?” “We have no idea,” he says. “We’re in this very early, weird stage of the evolution.”

Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote.

In an email to MIT Technology Review, an Amazon spokesperson noted that the company did not authorize Muse to access its website, and that Muse compromises Amazon’s ability to personalize the shopping experience for each customer.

But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that businesses will shutter as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy.

Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google publicly released its AI Overview feature in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A study from Pew last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One analysis found that publishers saw revenue from some types of ads decrease by about a third between 2025 and 2026. 

It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working. Time has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment.

E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, a professor of operations management at the University of Toronto Scarborough, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents are less likely to recommend items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money if agents become the primary way that people shop online. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up.

David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft Research, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy.

Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Airbnb and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and sellers. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees.

It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When the personal assistant agent OpenClaw exploded onto the scene in early 2026, it seemed, for a brief moment, that agents might be built in a grassroots, distributed way. But OpenAI quickly snapped up OpenClaw’s creator, Peter Steinberger, and other frontier AI companies got to work building their own personal assistant agents. 

When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.”

Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. Meta and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, they have tools that can automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and block a model from responding. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails. 

The same can’t be said for OpenClaw.

“These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.”

How will the human web change?

When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did transform it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile.

Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.”

“But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.”

PINGNAN LU

It’s not tough to envision a world in which those who opt not to use agents are cut off from important parts of online life. New businesses could opt to build connectors that allow agents to access their services without ever putting a traditional website online. Or agents could simply make some online platforms unusable for humans. People have reportedly been blocked from Resy for trying to use agents to book coveted New York City dinner reservations, but as agents become more and more popular, restaurant and event booking platforms could start to embrace them. If agents can nab concert tickets as soon as they are released, humans might not stand a chance.

But the mobile web also brought real accessibility benefits, and the same could prove true of the agentic web. Even as some elderly people and others who struggled to use smartphones were cut off from certain services, mobile devices allowed countless people in the Global South to get online for the first time. In the case of the agentic web, it could be elderly and disabled people who most benefit from this new way of accessing the online world.

“There’s very clear assistive potential for people who are older, who are generally less equipped to navigate user interfaces that were designed by people in their 20s, for people in their 20s,” says Margaret Mitchell, chief ethics scientist at Hugging Face. Agents, on the other hand, are almost trivially easy to interact with: Say what you want into your phone or computer microphone, and they’ll get it done for you. That could help not only older people who have trouble with web and mobile interfaces but also people with visual or motor disabilities.

Still, some experts don’t think the human web is going anywhere. Instead, the two webs may exist in parallel: We’ll go to the human web for fun, while the agentic web is where the boring daily admin of our lives happens. For instance, Krystian Kolondra, an executive vice president at the browser company Opera, doesn’t intend to use agents for every part of travel planning, even though this is often touted as one of their central use cases. “I don’t want to get an itinerary [from an AI] who has planned me every minute for something that was supposed to be fun,” he says. “I actually prefer to sit down with my wife in the evening and then just think [about] where to go next, what to see, and then enjoy that experience.”

He’s happy to fully relinquish some of the more routine parts of travel planning to agents, though: “Finding what the options are for flights? Why not?”

Mollick, however, thinks that the human web could be at risk. “If agents take over the web, then the web will change,” he says. “Do we abandon the human internet entirely and move to a world of private Discords? Do we strip down all the information so the AIs are just talking to each other rather than having an intermediary of a website to go through?”

 “We have no idea,” he says. “We’re in this very early, weird stage of the evolution.”
