items.title: Top Test Management Solutions for End-to-End Testing
items.summary: Managing testing throughout the software development cycle becomes challenging when test cases, execution, and reporting are handled separately. Fragmented workflows often lead to limited visibility, inconsistent tracking, and gaps in test coverage. End-to-end test management solutions address these challenges by bringing planning, execution, and reporting into a structured workflow. They help teams track progress, maintain traceability, and align testing activities with development cycles and release schedules. What are End-to-End Test Management Solutions? An end-to-end test management software helps teams plan, organise, execute, track, and report on testing throughout the software development lifecycle. These platforms support Agile and DevOps workflows by connecting testing activities with sprint cycles, CI/CD pipelines, and frequent releases. Instead of relying on spreadsheets or disconnected tools, teams can manage testing from a central workspace and maintain better visibility into software quality. Best Test Management Solutions for End-to-End Testing Here are some of the leading test management solutions and their capabilities. Test Manager by TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) Test Manager by TestMu AI is an AI test management solution that combines test creation, planning, execution tracking, and reporting in one workspace. It is part of TestMu AI’s broader Agentic Quality Engineering platform and integrates with Jira, Azure DevOps, GitHub, KaneAI for test automation, and HyperExecute for parallel execution across more than 50,000 real devices and 3,000 browsers. The platform supports AI-driven test case generation from multiple inputs, including text, Jira tickets, PDFs, images, audio, video, and spreadsheets. Teams can manage manual and automated tests in a central repository, organise workflows using custom fields and reusable preconditions, and conduct exploratory testing with automatic screenshot and video capture. Its bidirectional Jira and Azure DevOps integrations synchronise test cases, test runs, and defects across systems. Teams can also migrate historical testing data from Zephyr, TestRail, Xray, and qTest through API or CSV imports with automated field mapping. Test Manager provides real-time execution tracking and dashboards covering pass, fail, and skip rates, defect density, execution trends, and release readiness. It also links results from automation frameworks such as Selenium, Cypress, and Playwright to the relevant test cases. Integration with KaneAI allows teams to automate manual test cases using natural-language prompts and track the results within the same workspace. SpiraTest SpiraTest by Inflectra combines requirements management, test cases, defect tracking, and reporting in one platform. It is designed for teams that need traceability across testing activities, including those operating in regulated industries. Its capabilities include a central repository for manual and automated tests, parameterised testing, and a traceability matrix linking requirements, test cases, and incidents. The platform also supports exploratory testing, allowing teams to capture screenshots and logs during unscripted sessions and convert findings into formal test cases. OpenText DevOps Cloud OpenText Core Software Delivery Platform brings together functional, performance, and security testing with quality governance and DevOps workflows. It supports cloud, on-premises, and hybrid deployments, giving organisations flexibility in how they manage testing infrastructure. Its capabilities include AI-assisted test automation, object detection, self-healing tests, and CI/CD integration. Reporting and analytics help teams identify bottlenecks, monitor progress, and maintain visibility throughout the software delivery lifecycle. IBM Engineering Test Management IBM Engineering Test Management is a collaborative test management platform available through on-premises and SaaS deployments. It supports test planning, execution tracking, workflow management, and reporting for large organisations. The platform connects test cases with requirements through integrations such as IBM Engineering Requirements Management DOORS Next, helping teams maintain traceability when requirements change. It also supports reusable and version-controlled tests, customisable reporting, and collaboration features for distributed teams. PractiTest PractiTest is a SaaS-based test management platform that brings QA processes, teams, and tools into a shared workspace. It covers requirements mapping, test execution, defect tracking, and reporting, with integrations for tools such as Jira, GitHub, GitLab, Selenium, Jenkins, and JUnit. Customisable dashboards, dynamic filters, and traceability matrices help teams monitor coverage and testing progress. PractiTest also offers AI-powered features such as SmartFox for test case creation and a Test Value Score to help teams prioritise testing efforts. Why is Test Management Essential for End-to-End Testing? As applications become more complex and release cycles accelerate, structured test management helps teams maintain visibility across the development lifecycle. Centralising test data gives QA teams and stakeholders a shared view of requirements, test cases, execution results, and defects. Early involvement in planning also helps teams identify technical risks, dependencies, testing requirements, and realistic timelines before development progresses too far. Connected workflows improve collaboration between developers, QA engineers, and business stakeholders. Meanwhile, execution reports and defect trends help teams assess release readiness and prioritise issues based on their potential impact. Risk-based testing can further improve efficiency by directing resources towards areas where defects are more likely to occur or could have the greatest consequences. How to Choose the Right Test Management Tool The right platform depends on team size, project complexity, existing technology, and testing requirements. Team size and project complexity determine how much capacity a platform needs to support, particularly when multiple teams manage large test repositories and parallel releases. Compatibility with the existing technology stack is equally important. Integrations with tools such as Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, and Selenium can reduce disruption and make adoption easier. Teams should also consider their testing methodology, whether Agile, Scrum, Waterfall, or a combination, and whether the platform can support their planning and reporting workflows. Finally, a solution should accommodate both manual and automated testing. This gives teams the flexibility to adapt their approach as applications and quality requirements evolve. End-to-end test management helps teams connect planning, execution, tracking, and reporting throughout the software development lifecycle. As applications grow and testing requirements become more complex, managing these activities manually can limit visibility and increase the effort required to maintain quality. For teams looking to centralise test management while expanding automation and maintaining traceability across development workflows, it offers an option alongside established platforms such as SpiraTest, OpenText DevOps Cloud, IBM Engineering Test Management, and PractiTest.

items.title: Deep-Tech and Green Finance to Drive India’s Climate Investments in 2027
items.summary: India's climate-tech investment may shift in 2027, with deep-tech, energy storage, green-asset financing, and energy-efficient data-centre infrastructure set to drive the next phase of capital deployment, according to a new report by Ostara Advisors. India's first specialist investment bank for deep-tech and sustainability released its 2026-2027 India Climate Tech and Deep Tech Deal Report on Tuesday, describing a market that is becoming increasingly selective as capital follows energy security, domestic manufacturing, critical technologies and specific infrastructure bottlenecks. The report said the climate narrative has shifted strategically, with energy security, domestic manufacturing, critical minerals, and deep-tech capabilities becoming intertwined with the energy transition. It noted that public and private capital is now more targeted at addressing the bottlenecks that determine the pace and scale of technology deployment. The report identifies four areas expected to shape the next round of investment: deep tech, energy storage, green-asset financing and energy-efficient data-centre infrastructure. It also finds opportunities across storage, carbon markets, green hydrogen, nuclear power and the infrastructure supporting India's AI and data-centre build-out, including firm renewable power, grid equipment, cooling and water systems. A key finding is that Series A and Series B companies should find a deeper domestic investor pool over the next 12 to 18 months, as new India-domiciled growth funds and government-backed deep-tech capital come online. Regulatory milestones through FY 27-FY28, including carbon markets, solar manufacturing, green gas, and EV localisation, are expected to shape industry growth and investment decisions as India's energy transition enters a critical phase. Commenting on the outlook, Vasudha Madhavan, Founder of Ostara Advisors, said India's deep-tech and climate-tech sectors are approaching an inflection point. "The next phase of growth will depend not only on the availability of capital, but also on our ability to channel patient growth capital towards technologies that can be commercialised at scale ," Madhavan said. "The focus for investors will be to distinguish promising innovation from businesses that can build durable commercial models and deliver long-term value." The report reinforces the importance of a long-term investment approach, where technology development cycles can be extended, and commercial outcomes depend on patient capital, execution capability and supportive market infrastructure.

items.title: Open models are having a moment, but martech Jasper still relies on the frontier
items.summary: AI agents like Claude Code and Codex have transformed software engineering workflows. As of 2026, Google reports that 75% of new code is written by AI agents, while Anthropic’s CFO claims that over 90% of the lab’s code is produced by Claude. Jasper, one of the first marketing tech companies to commercialize generative AI, built early iterations of its content generation platform with GPT-3, but has since undergone a shift. Instead of maintaining a platform that produces AI-generated content, it now provides AI agents to execute marketing workflows end-to-end, and even produces most of its code with AI agents. Timothy Young, CEO of Jasper, told The Stack that when the company first started with generative AI there wasn’t any notion of a coding agent, the company worked with a more “traditional methodology” toward building SaaS software. “Today, it could not be more different right? Almost 100% of our code is written by agents,” Young said. “Our engineering team members and our product teams and design teams are really building the system that is writing the code,” he said, noting Jasper’s engineers are more focused on judgement architecture decisions, than writing any one piece of code. Call to action

NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology, an open library under the Apache 2.0 license. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong.

TL;DR
  • Library: Default LLM is nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b, with Nemotron embedding and reranking models.
  • Runs on: Docker Compose for a local stack, or Kubernetes via Helm. Inference uses hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints or self-hosted NIMs.
  • Performance: Strong engineering, thin public evidence.
  • Best: Ontology creation time cut by 90% in NVIDIA testing (self-reported).
  • Worst: 0 published text-to-SQL accuracy scores. The eval repo ships a harness, not results.
  • Bottom line: An open, MCP-ready context layer that any agent harness can query. But you must run the benchmarks yourself to trust it.
What is NVIDIA Auto Ontology?

It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from.

Here are the five jobs:

  • Discover: generate ontologies from metadata and connect existing semantic models.
  • Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships.
  • Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage.
  • Expose: serve context through MCP, CLI and API.
  • Learn: fold certified corrections back into the ontology.

NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it.

How does Auto Ontology work?

The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors.

Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works.

&&

What does the MCP server expose?

The MCP server docs describe 9 read-only tools. ask_question returns the answer, the SQL and the rows as separate fields. Results cap at 100 rows. check_readiness confirms a compiled semantic layer and a live database connection exist.

There is no tool for browsing raw schemas. NVIDIA chose that on purpose, so agents reach data through the semantic layer. The underlying OpenAPI spec publishes 87 operations. Sign-in runs through OAuth, and every call carries the signed-in user’s permissions.

How is it benchmarked?

NVIDIA ships a separate harness, auto-ontology-eval. It runs 2 arms in NeMo Gym: a schema-only LLM control and the ontology-grounded agent. Scoring is deterministic execution match, with no LLM judge.

Bundled datasets include BIRD Dev (1,534 questions, 11 databases) and Mini-Dev (500 questions). FDABench-Lite adds 169 questions, and BEAVER defaults to a 100-question sample.

The harness repo adds 2 limitations. Optional few-shot exemplars and value anchors go to the ontology arm only. A delta measured with them covers those inputs, not grounding alone. Its tested configuration also routes both arms through a Claude model on NVIDIA’s inference gateway.

How does it compare with other semantic layers? FeatureNVIDIA Auto OntologyWren AICube Coredbt MetricFlowLicenseApache 2.0Apache 2.0 core (open core)Apache 2.0 backend, MIT clientApache 2.0 (v0.209.0+)How the layer is builtGenerated from metadata, then certifiedAgent-assisted context files in GitDefined in codeDefined in code in a dbt projectAgent interfaceMCP, CLI, REST APIMCP, CLI, SDKsSQL, REST, GraphQL APIsPython library and CLIData sourcesDatabricks, Postgres, Snowflake, DuckDB22+All SQL data sourcesVia dbt adaptersDefault modelsNemotron via NVIDIA NIMNot disclosedNot applicableNot applicable Deployment and availability

Local setup is docker compose up -d --build after filling in .env. Kubernetes users get a Helm chart and a DEPLOYMENT.md guide. NVIDIA team also publishes the backend as an NGC container. An NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com covers the default models.

Key Takeaways
  • Auto Ontology generates a starting semantic layer from enterprise metadata.
  • Agents query it through 9 read-only MCP tools, plus CLI and API.
  • NVIDIA reports 90% faster ontology creation in its own testing.
  • No text-to-SQL accuracy scores are published yet.
  • Defaults to Nemotron on NIM, but accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

items.title: Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B With 45 Compiled GPU Layers That Run CUDA
items.summary: qwenGPU is an experimental model that compiles a SIMT GPU directly into the weights of Qwen3.5-2B . Developer Vixhal ( @TheVixhal ) released it on GitHub under the MIT license. The model runs real CUDA, compiled to NVIDIA PTX, inside its own forward passes. For developers, it tests one idea: exact computation inside a pretrained LLM, not beside it. TL;DR Size: Qwen3.5-2B (24 layers) along with 45 compiled GPU layers, 69 in total. Context: 262,144 tokens (base model). Runs on: Apple silicon, an NVIDIA GPU or a CPU, with about 16 GB of free memory. No quantized build. Performance: Every launch in the developer’s runs was exact; text drift is a KL of about 7e-4. Best: The reference interpreter matched a real NVIDIA Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels. Worst: About 10 to 15 tokens per second on Apple MPS; Qwen-written CUDA passed 4 of 5. What is qwenGPU? qwenGPU is Qwen3.5-2B with 45 compiled transformer layers placed in front of Qwen’s own 24. None of those layers are trained. A compiler computes every weight. How does a GPU fit inside model weights? The GPU is a 4-lane SIMT machine. It has 15 registers per lane, a 4-stage pipeline, a 32-block ROM and 126 memory words. It uses only Qwen3.5’s own layer types: Gated DeltaNet linear attention and SwiGLU MLPs. The trick is the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state. In the circuit’s heads, the gate is held open and the write strength is 1. Every key is one-hot. Each update overwrites exactly 1 row, and a one-hot query reads it back. So each row works as a memory cell. That state holds the program ROM, registers and global memory. The README lists 16 register rows per lane, with 1 that always reads zero. That matches the 15 usable registers in the X post. The GPU supports integer arithmetic, predicates, divergent branches and loops. It also supports shared memory, atomicAdd , __syncthreads() and warp shuffles. && What happens during a CUDA launch? The host plays the role of NVRTC and the CUDA driver. It compiles CUDA to PTX with clang, then lowers PTX to machine blocks. It feeds the program and input arrays to the model as tokens. From there, the model writes the launch itself. Each EXEC(b, w) token runs block b for warp w in 1 forward pass. The VAL tokens after it carry register results. Memory writes return as MEM records. The host reads results from the recurrent state and computes none of them. In the demo video , a dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] returns 32. The model wrote that launch in 47 tokens. Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B with a SIMT GPU inside its weights, 45 compiled layers in front of Qwen’s own, using its Gated DeltaNet layers as registers and memory. It runs real CUDA in its forward passes. The host compiles the kernel to PTX and loads it, then the model writes every… pic.twitter.com/iM5IETEbIv — vixhaℓ (@TheVixhal) November 1, 2026 Does the GPU break Qwen’s text ability? Not by the developer’s measure. The circuit is muted on text tokens, and Qwen’s own weights are unchanged. The merged model’s next-token distribution stays within a KL of about 7e-4 of the original. How accurate is qwenGPU? All numbers are self-reported, measured on Apple silicon with MPS in bf16: Every launch was exact under --check replay. The reference interpreter matched an NVIDIA Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 test kernels. Normal mode answered 20 of 24 sampled chat questions with GPU-computed numbers. Advanced mode wrote a correct kernel first try on 4 of 5 questions. In normal mode, Qwen writes an expression like [1, 2, 3] @ [4, 5, 6] for ready-made kernels. In advanced mode, Qwen writes the CUDA kernel itself. The README warns that a 2B model’s CUDA is still unreliable. How does qwenGPU compare with Qwenputer and Percepta? qwenGPU uses the transformer compiler from Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal. Qwenputer compiles a 32-bit RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. Percepta built a WebAssembly interpreter into a transformer with 2D attention heads in March 2026. Feature qwenGPU Qwenputer (RISC-V) Percepta Base model Qwen3.5-2B, 24 layers Qwen3.5-4B Custom transformer with 2D attention heads Machine compiled in 4-lane SIMT GPU 32-bit RISC-V (RV32IM + Zba + bignum) WebAssembly interpreter Programs it runs CUDA, lowered from PTX C and MicroPython C, compiled to WebAssembly Compiled layers 45 11 Not disclosed Where state lives Gated DeltaNet state Gated DeltaNet state Execution trace in context Host role Compiles CUDA to PTX, loads tokens, reads results Loads firmware; runs no computation Not disclosed Correctness check Interpreter matched Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels 0 mismatches in about 230,000 replayed positions Claims millions of reliable steps Reported speed 10 to 15 tokens/s (Apple MPS) About 3,200 trace tokens/s (L4, Triton) 30,000+ tokens/s (CPU) Text drift vs base KL about 7e-4 KL 6e-4 Not applicable License MIT code; Apache-2.0 checkpoint MIT code; Apache-2.0 weights Not disclosed The speed figures use different hardware and token types, so they are not directly comparable. What do you need to run it? The quickstart needs Python 3.11+, uv, just and about 16 GB of free memory. Advanced mode also needs clang with the NVPTX backend. just build downloads Qwen3.5-2B and compiles the GPU into it. No prebuilt checkpoint is published. A built checkpoint falls under Qwen’s Apache-2.0 license. Key Takeaways qwenGPU compiles a 4-lane SIMT GPU into Qwen3.5-2B as 45 untrained layers. Gated DeltaNet state serves as registers, program ROM and global memory. The model writes every CUDA launch step; the host only compiles and loads. The interpreter matched a Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels. At 10 to 15 tokens per second, it is a research demo, not a runtime. qwenGPU is an experimental model that compiles a SIMT GPU directly into the weights of Qwen3.5-2B. Developer Vixhal (@TheVixhal) released it on GitHub under the MIT license. The model runs real CUDA, compiled to NVIDIA PTX, inside its own forward passes. For developers, it tests one idea: exact computation inside a pretrained LLM, not beside it.

TL;DR
  • Size: Qwen3.5-2B (24 layers) along with 45 compiled GPU layers, 69 in total. Context: 262,144 tokens (base model).
  • Runs on: Apple silicon, an NVIDIA GPU or a CPU, with about 16 GB of free memory. No quantized build.
  • Performance: Every launch in the developer’s runs was exact; text drift is a KL of about 7e-4.
  • Best: The reference interpreter matched a real NVIDIA Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels.
  • Worst: About 10 to 15 tokens per second on Apple MPS; Qwen-written CUDA passed 4 of 5.
What is qwenGPU?

qwenGPU is Qwen3.5-2B with 45 compiled transformer layers placed in front of Qwen’s own 24. None of those layers are trained. A compiler computes every weight.

How does a GPU fit inside model weights?

The GPU is a 4-lane SIMT machine. It has 15 registers per lane, a 4-stage pipeline, a 32-block ROM and 126 memory words. It uses only Qwen3.5’s own layer types: Gated DeltaNet linear attention and SwiGLU MLPs.

The trick is the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state. In the circuit’s heads, the gate is held open and the write strength is 1. Every key is one-hot. Each update overwrites exactly 1 row, and a one-hot query reads it back. So each row works as a memory cell.

That state holds the program ROM, registers and global memory. The README lists 16 register rows per lane, with 1 that always reads zero. That matches the 15 usable registers in the X post.

The GPU supports integer arithmetic, predicates, divergent branches and loops. It also supports shared memory, atomicAdd, __syncthreads() and warp shuffles.

&&

What happens during a CUDA launch?

The host plays the role of NVRTC and the CUDA driver. It compiles CUDA to PTX with clang, then lowers PTX to machine blocks. It feeds the program and input arrays to the model as tokens.

From there, the model writes the launch itself. Each EXEC(b, w) token runs block b for warp w in 1 forward pass. The VAL tokens after it carry register results. Memory writes return as MEM records. The host reads results from the recurrent state and computes none of them.

In the demo video, a dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] returns 32. The model wrote that launch in 47 tokens.

Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B with a SIMT GPU inside its weights, 45 compiled layers in front of Qwen’s own, using its Gated DeltaNet layers as registers and memory.

It runs real CUDA in its forward passes. The host compiles the kernel to PTX and loads it, then the model writes every… pic.twitter.com/iM5IETEbIv

— vixhaℓ (@TheVixhal) November 1, 2026
Does the GPU break Qwen’s text ability?

Not by the developer’s measure. The circuit is muted on text tokens, and Qwen’s own weights are unchanged. The merged model’s next-token distribution stays within a KL of about 7e-4 of the original.

How accurate is qwenGPU?

All numbers are self-reported, measured on Apple silicon with MPS in bf16:

  • Every launch was exact under --check replay.
  • The reference interpreter matched an NVIDIA Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 test kernels.
  • Normal mode answered 20 of 24 sampled chat questions with GPU-computed numbers.
  • Advanced mode wrote a correct kernel first try on 4 of 5 questions.

In normal mode, Qwen writes an expression like [1, 2, 3] @ [4, 5, 6] for ready-made kernels. In advanced mode, Qwen writes the CUDA kernel itself. The README warns that a 2B model’s CUDA is still unreliable.

How does qwenGPU compare with Qwenputer and Percepta?

qwenGPU uses the transformer compiler from Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal. Qwenputer compiles a 32-bit RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. Percepta built a WebAssembly interpreter into a transformer with 2D attention heads in March 2026.

The speed figures use different hardware and token types, so they are not directly comparable.

What do you need to run it?

The quickstart needs Python 3.11+, uv, just and about 16 GB of free memory. Advanced mode also needs clang with the NVPTX backend. just build downloads Qwen3.5-2B and compiles the GPU into it. No prebuilt checkpoint is published. A built checkpoint falls under Qwen’s Apache-2.0 license.

Key Takeaways
  • qwenGPU compiles a 4-lane SIMT GPU into Qwen3.5-2B as 45 untrained layers.
  • Gated DeltaNet state serves as registers, program ROM and global memory.
  • The model writes every CUDA launch step; the host only compiles and loads.
  • The interpreter matched a Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels.
  • At 10 to 15 tokens per second, it is a research demo, not a runtime.

items.title: India’s Frontier AI Race Gets a 240M Model That Beats Liquid AI
items.summary: India’s frontier AI ambitions may have found an unlikely contender in a 240-million-parameter language model that challenges conventional approaches to building AI. NeuroDX, an Indian startup backed by the IndiaAI Mission that grew out of brain research, says its new model, Sphota, has outperformed a comparable model from Liquid AI across an average of about 11 benchmarks, while requiring significantly less training data. Sphota scored 52.4% against Liquid AI, which recorded 52.1%, according to the company’s reported benchmark results. Notably, NeuroDX CEO Siddharth Panwar claims Sphota achieves comparable performance with 50 times less training data and offers 4.5 times better memory efficiency. The results are preliminary and have not yet been established through independent public evaluations. However, they point to a potentially different approach to building language models, one that attempts to capture meaning directly rather than relying primarily on predicting the next word. “We didn’t go out to build an efficient small model. We just had an architecture, and we started with small sizes because that’s the size we can play at,” Panwar said in an exclusive interview with AIM’s Front Page. A New Architecture Built Around Meaning Sphota’s origins lie in an effort to understand the human brain. NeuroDX initially focused on healthcare, developing AI models that interpret electroencephalogram (EEG) signals recorded from the scalp. These signals contain information about brain activity but are difficult to interpret directly, unlike medical images such as MRI scans. While developing a foundation model for the brain with support from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the IndiaAI Mission, Panwar and his team encountered a problem with conventional AI architectures. Most language models divide text into tokens and learn patterns by predicting what comes next. However, EEG signals do not have the same natural divisions as written language. Splitting them into tokens requires arbitrary decisions, which can limit how effectively a model interprets the underlying information. The team began exploring whether it could move beyond tokens and model the meaning embedded in information instead. The resulting architectural innovations proved applicable beyond brain signals, leading the company to experiment with language models. Sphota takes its name from the linguistic concept associated with Bhartrihari, an Indian philosopher and linguist who argued that meaning is apprehended as a whole rather than assembled merely by processing individual words. Panwar believes conventional language models can eventually arrive at an understanding of meaning, but often require enormous amounts of training data and computing power to do so. Consider two sentences describing the same event: someone gives another person a book, and the recipient receives a book from the giver. Although the wording differs, the underlying event remains unchanged. A conventional model learns to recognise such relationships through extensive training. Sphota, by contrast, makes identifying these underlying similarities a design principle from the outset. “What you’re looking to build is that main layer not only about the tokens but consciously as an engineering architecture level you are trying to see how can you build this later,” Panwar said. The company argues that this approach could help smaller models develop certain capabilities with less training data. Whether those gains persist across a wider range of tasks and larger models remains to be established. 50x Less Training Data, 4.5x Better Memory Efficiency The most consequential claims surrounding Sphota concern the cost of training and running AI models. According to Panwar, the 50x figure compares the amount of training data used by Sphota and Liquid AI’s model to achieve similar benchmark performance. The 4.5x memory-efficiency claim relates to how much conversational context a model can retain under comparable conditions. Longer conversations and larger context windows require models to manage increasing amounts of information, placing additional demands on memory resources. Panwar said Sphota’s architecture could allow it to retain substantially more context than a comparable model while using less memory. However, these figures represent the company’s reported comparisons, not independently verified results across all models and workloads. The eventual gains will depend on how the architecture performs as it scales and how it compares with other systems under equivalent testing conditions. Panwar also cautioned that the efficiency gains observed so far may not translate directly into the same numbers when the model becomes widely available. The company has been working on Sphota for only a few months with a small team. It is now developing a larger model with between 1 billion and 2 billion parameters, with Panwar targeting a release around December. He said users could potentially access it through a chatbot on the company’s website. The next model will be an important test of whether Sphota’s early results hold up at larger scales. NeuroDX Becomes MANNAS AI Alongside its model ambitions, NeuroDX is preparing to change its identity. Panwar revealed the company is rebranding itself as Manaas AI, reflecting its transition from a healthcare-focused business towards a foundation model company. The startup remains involved in neurological healthcare, but its broader ambition is to develop general-purpose intelligence and build a global technology company from India. Panwar said the company’s brain foundation models are publicly available, while models developed with support from MeitY and the IndiaAI Mission are intended to be open source. However, the company plans to keep the underlying Sphota architecture proprietary for now, allowing it to build a competitive advantage and attract the resources needed to develop the technology further. “We are just making sure that this architecture stays proprietary,” Panwar said. Why India Cannot Afford to Abandon Frontier AI Sphota’s emergence also raises a larger question: Can Indian companies compete in frontier AI without access to the computing resources and capital available to global technology giants? NeuroDX is among the companies selected to develop sovereign AI models under the IndiaAI Mission. Panwar said the company was allocated 368 H200 GPUs for 18 months and ₹12.5 crore to develop a 20-billion-parameter multimodal EEG model. The allocation underscores the constraints facing Indian AI developers attempting to build ambitious models with limited resources. Panwar acknowledged the frustration of having engineers ready to experiment but insufficient GPUs to pursue every research direction. However, he argued that the shortage should not force India to abandon the frontier AI race. “Giving up on the frontier just because we don’t have enough risk capital is suicidal,” he said. For Panwar, the case for building frontier models extends beyond commercial returns. Developing these systems domestically would allow Indian researchers to understand how advanced AI works, investigate unexpected model behaviour and develop appropriate safeguards rather than relying entirely on technology built elsewhere. Established AI laboratories have invested heavily in transformer-based systems, giving startups an opportunity to investigate approaches that do not depend on the same underlying assumptions. “You can’t leaprog by chasing them. You can leaprog them by building something completely orthogonal in kind of the technological directions they were taking and then find yourself up ahead of them,” he said. Panwar said the company is looking to raise more than $10 million, although the interview did not establish a completed funding round. From Brain Signals to Village-Level Healthcare Despite its new focus on foundation models, Mannas AI’s healthcare ambitions remain central to its work. The company is developing EEG-based screening systems designed to identify people who may be at risk of neurological conditions, including dementia, epilepsy and depression. The system records brain signals using a small, relatively inexpensive device that can be operated without highly specialised personnel. Its AI models then generate a risk profile to help an MBBS doctor decide whether to refer a patient to a specialist. The aim is to extend screening to primary healthcare centres and villages where access to neurological specialists is limited. Panwar said the models were undergoing evaluation and could be ready for deployment by the end of 2026 or early 2027. Wider deployment would depend on working with the government and other healthcare stakeholders. The company has collected carefully labelled EEG data over an extended period, with the required ethical approvals and consent, to develop and fine-tune these models. Sphota's immediate test is whether its reported benchmark and efficiency gains survive independent scrutiny and scale beyond 240 million parameters. Its longer-term test is whether a small Indian team can turn an architectural breakthrough into a competitive foundation model. For Panwar, the ambition goes beyond building another AI startup. He wants Indian engineers to believe they can create frontier technology rather than merely work for companies that already have. “The whole purpose of Mannas is to show that there is absolutely nothing that we can't do,” he said.
items.summary_html:
India’s frontier AI ambitions may have found an unlikely contender in a 240-million-parameter language model that challenges conventional approaches to building AI. 

NeuroDX, an Indian startup backed by the IndiaAI Mission that grew out of brain research, says its new model, Sphota, has outperformed a comparable model from Liquid AI across an average of about 11 benchmarks, while requiring significantly less training data.

Sphota scored 52.4% against Liquid AI, which recorded 52.1%, according to the company’s reported benchmark results. Notably, NeuroDX CEO Siddharth Panwar claims Sphota achieves comparable performance with 50 times less training data and offers 4.5 times better memory efficiency.

The results are preliminary and have not yet been established through independent public evaluations. However, they point to a potentially different approach to building language models, one that attempts to capture meaning directly rather than relying primarily on predicting the next word.

“We didn’t go out to build an efficient small model. We just had an architecture, and we started with small sizes because that’s the size we can play at,” Panwar said in an exclusive interview with AIM’s Front Page.

A New Architecture Built Around Meaning

Sphota’s origins lie in an effort to understand the human brain.

NeuroDX initially focused on healthcare, developing AI models that interpret electroencephalogram (EEG) signals recorded from the scalp. These signals contain information about brain activity but are difficult to interpret directly, unlike medical images such as MRI scans.

While developing a foundation model for the brain with support from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the IndiaAI Mission, Panwar and his team encountered a problem with conventional AI architectures.

Most language models divide text into tokens and learn patterns by predicting what comes next. However, EEG signals do not have the same natural divisions as written language. Splitting them into tokens requires arbitrary decisions, which can limit how effectively a model interprets the underlying information.

The team began exploring whether it could move beyond tokens and model the meaning embedded in information instead.

The resulting architectural innovations proved applicable beyond brain signals, leading the company to experiment with language models.

Sphota takes its name from the linguistic concept associated with Bhartrihari, an Indian philosopher and linguist who argued that meaning is apprehended as a whole rather than assembled merely by processing individual words.

Panwar believes conventional language models can eventually arrive at an understanding of meaning, but often require enormous amounts of training data and computing power to do so.

Consider two sentences describing the same event: someone gives another person a book, and the recipient receives a book from the giver. Although the wording differs, the underlying event remains unchanged.

A conventional model learns to recognise such relationships through extensive training. Sphota, by contrast, makes identifying these underlying similarities a design principle from the outset.

“What you’re looking to build is that main layer not only about the tokens but consciously as an engineering architecture level you are trying to see how can you build this later,” Panwar said.

The company argues that this approach could help smaller models develop certain capabilities with less training data. Whether those gains persist across a wider range of tasks and larger models remains to be established.

50x Less Training Data, 4.5x Better Memory Efficiency

The most consequential claims surrounding Sphota concern the cost of training and running AI models.

According to Panwar, the 50x figure compares the amount of training data used by Sphota and Liquid AI’s model to achieve similar benchmark performance. The 4.5x memory-efficiency claim relates to how much conversational context a model can retain under comparable conditions.

Longer conversations and larger context windows require models to manage increasing amounts of information, placing additional demands on memory resources.

Panwar said Sphota’s architecture could allow it to retain substantially more context than a comparable model while using less memory.

However, these figures represent the company’s reported comparisons, not independently verified results across all models and workloads. The eventual gains will depend on how the architecture performs as it scales and how it compares with other systems under equivalent testing conditions.

Panwar also cautioned that the efficiency gains observed so far may not translate directly into the same numbers when the model becomes widely available.

The company has been working on Sphota for only a few months with a small team. It is now developing a larger model with between 1 billion and 2 billion parameters, with Panwar targeting a release around December. He said users could potentially access it through a chatbot on the company’s website.

The next model will be an important test of whether Sphota’s early results hold up at larger scales.

NeuroDX Becomes MANNAS AI

Alongside its model ambitions, NeuroDX is preparing to change its identity.

Panwar revealed the company is rebranding itself as Manaas AI, reflecting its transition from a healthcare-focused business towards a foundation model company.

The startup remains involved in neurological healthcare, but its broader ambition is to develop general-purpose intelligence and build a global technology company from India.

Panwar said the company’s brain foundation models are publicly available, while models developed with support from MeitY and the IndiaAI Mission are intended to be open source.

However, the company plans to keep the underlying Sphota architecture proprietary for now, allowing it to build a competitive advantage and attract the resources needed to develop the technology further.

“We are just making sure that this architecture stays proprietary,” Panwar said.

Why India Cannot Afford to Abandon Frontier AI

Sphota’s emergence also raises a larger question: Can Indian companies compete in frontier AI without access to the computing resources and capital available to global technology giants?

NeuroDX is among the companies selected to develop sovereign AI models under the IndiaAI Mission. Panwar said the company was allocated 368 H200 GPUs for 18 months and ₹12.5 crore to develop a 20-billion-parameter multimodal EEG model.

The allocation underscores the constraints facing Indian AI developers attempting to build ambitious models with limited resources.

Panwar acknowledged the frustration of having engineers ready to experiment but insufficient GPUs to pursue every research direction. However, he argued that the shortage should not force India to abandon the frontier AI race.

“Giving up on the frontier just because we don’t have enough risk capital is suicidal,” he said.

For Panwar, the case for building frontier models extends beyond commercial returns. Developing these systems domestically would allow Indian researchers to understand how advanced AI works, investigate unexpected model behaviour and develop appropriate safeguards rather than relying entirely on technology built elsewhere.

Established AI laboratories have invested heavily in transformer-based systems, giving startups an opportunity to investigate approaches that do not depend on the same underlying assumptions.

“You can’t leaprog by chasing them. You can leaprog them by building something completely orthogonal in kind of the technological directions they were taking and then find yourself up ahead of them,” he said.

Panwar said the company is looking to raise more than $10 million, although the interview did not establish a completed funding round.

From Brain Signals to Village-Level Healthcare

Despite its new focus on foundation models, Mannas AI’s healthcare ambitions remain central to its work.

The company is developing EEG-based screening systems designed to identify people who may be at risk of neurological conditions, including dementia, epilepsy and depression.

The system records brain signals using a small, relatively inexpensive device that can be operated without highly specialised personnel. Its AI models then generate a risk profile to help an MBBS doctor decide whether to refer a patient to a specialist.

The aim is to extend screening to primary healthcare centres and villages where access to neurological specialists is limited.

Panwar said the models were undergoing evaluation and could be ready for deployment by the end of 2026 or early 2027. Wider deployment would depend on working with the government and other healthcare stakeholders.

The company has collected carefully labelled EEG data over an extended period, with the required ethical approvals and consent, to develop and fine-tune these models.

Sphota's immediate test is whether its reported benchmark and efficiency gains survive independent scrutiny and scale beyond 240 million parameters. Its longer-term test is whether a small Indian team can turn an architectural breakthrough into a competitive foundation model.

For Panwar, the ambition goes beyond building another AI startup. He wants Indian engineers to believe they can create frontier technology rather than merely work for companies that already have.

“The whole purpose of Mannas is to show that there is absolutely nothing that we can't do,” he said.

items.title: "HMRC™ by Salesforce" - Tax office defends ~£4.4 billion CRM plan
items.summary: The UK’s tax authority, HMRC, says its controversial decision to spend up to £4.4 billion ($5.8 billion) on a new CRM system from Salesforce is justified, because building its own software platform would be too expensive, complex and slow. HMRC on Friday October 30 quietly published a summary business case for the decision to go all-in with Salesforce SaaS – saying it considered six options, including “do nothing” and a “best-of-breed” integration of various off-the-shelf systems. It rejected the latter idea due to “high integration complexity and coordination risk.” And it dismissed the idea of developing a "bespoke HMRC customer management solution" due to "delivery complexity, cost and timescale risk." That’s despite the argument that frontier model capabilities are “fundamentally shifting the economics of modernization” due to their growing ability to extract the business logic and flows of legacy technologies – something that is going to have to be mapped anyway in the migration from 70+ legacy systems to Salesforce. HMRC published details of its sprawling contract with Salesforce on 15 October. It described it as spanning procurement of Salesforce’s Agentforce, Data Cloud, Informatica, and Experience Cloud and put the figure at up to £2.4 billion. (That’s over quadruple the £500 million allocated to the UK’s Sovereign AI Fund.) Its newly published business case does not name Salesforce. But it cites “CRM Software as a Service platform, implementation and transformation costs, with estimated whole lifecycle costs (15 years) in the range of c.£1.7bn to £4.4bn (incl. optimism bias and VAT), reflecting the scale, complexity, and delivery over 15 years.” HMRC added: “Spend will be committed incrementally, including built-in review mechanisms at key points across the lifecycle to ensure cost is controlled…” HMRC says the new CRM system will serve 34 million citizens, five million businesses, and create a “generational shift in the way HMRC supports its customers” by replacing 70+ legacy customer management systems into a single CRM platform. Salesforce last month said that it will "unify legacy systems onto a single secure platform, delivering a 360-degree view of taxpayer interactions to enable faster, first-contact query resolution. The platform will equip HMRC teams with real-time taxpayer insights, automated workflows, and AI-assisted tools that significantly reduce manual workloads." See also: AWS wins controversial £473m hyperscaler-only HMRC contract HMRC expects to drive efficienciesof £815 million over a decade by joining up customer data. HMRC also said it expects to deliver cost savings of £924 million to £1.25 billion over its total over the 15-year contract length (albeit with a massive 40% “optimism bias”) by moving to a “unified customer engagement domain.” The decision to build the entire nation’s tax collection systems on a US software providers’ SaaS comes weeks after the government told the Science and Technology Committee (in response to its June 2026 “Rewiring The State” report) that it expects “public sector organisations to make proportionate, risk-based decisions that reduce overdependencies, strengthen resilience and deliver secure, value-for-money outcomes while maintaining access to the best technologies” available globally. Writing to the select committee on September 7, the government said that “the First Secretary of State and the Chancellor have written to their Ministerial colleagues, expressing the need to use procurement to support UK start-ups and scale-ups” and said work was underway to improve the digital capabilities of the civil service. The government meanwhile continues to contract large outsourcers to deliver failing projects like the civil service pension scheme, which is being run by Capita. In November 2025, a senior British government minister was told by the CEO of outsourcer Capita that with the company’s help “the UK Government would be presiding over the largest AI-enabled pension in the UK… a flagship use case.” The company is persistently missing agreed service levels and after having won the tender, Capita’s CEO Adolfo Hernandez then admitted to MPs in July that that the pension scheme is “very complex; more complex than we thought, realistically.” The UK’s Paymaster General, Nick Thomas-Symonds told MPs over the summer that his team was exploring “the long-term feasibility of a full in-house delivery model” for that service – but claimed it would “need a quite enormous state architecture.” See also: Crapita’s “AI-enabled” pension scheme is a sh*t sandwich

items.title: Google’s Project Suncatcher Satellite Generates First AI Response in Orbit
items.summary: Google said on October 30 that its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite had generated its first artificial intelligence response using a data centre-class tensor processing unit (TPU) in orbit. The milestone marks an early test of the company’s research into running AI workloads in space, according to a blog post by Travis Beals, Senior Director of Paradigms of Intelligence. Launched on October 1 , the satellite is part of Google’s research project exploring whether space could host scalable machine learning infrastructure. Built in partnership with Planet, the prototype was launched aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Google said it had completed the satellite’s commissioning checklist, including powering up the host and TPU trays and running initial machine learning tests. During a ground-station pass, Google uplinked a prompt to its onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space. As the satellite passed Svalbard, Norway, the response was transmitted back to Earth. The haiku generated by the model read: “Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨” Google said it subsequently tested the model with space-themed limericks and prompts requesting telemetry information about the payload systems. The company described the milestone as the first AI response from a data centre-class TPU in orbit. The next phase of Project Suncatcher will evaluate how the TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit. Google said these tests would help determine whether its hardware can reliably execute AI workloads in space. The company plans to use the findings to advance its next milestone, involving two interconnected satellites in 2027. The proposed system is intended to explore how multiple satellites could work together to support AI computing in orbit. Project Suncatcher explores the feasibility of solar-powered satellite networks equipped with Google’s TPUs. The company said the initiative aims to investigate the long-term potential of scaling machine learning infrastructure beyond Earth.

items.title: Genpact Certified as a Best Firm for Data Scientists
items.summary: Genpact, the Agentic Operations company, has been certified as a Best Firm for Data Scientists by Analytics India Magazine (AIM) through its workplace recognition programme. The certification is based on structured feedback from data science professionals within the organisation and evaluates how companies enable technical teams to contribute to enterprise decision-making and business transformation. The certification survey assesses workplace culture, access to leadership, collaboration,learning opportunities, and the nature of analytical work delivered. AIM conducts an independent analysis of survey responses to understand how effectively organisations support data science teams in their day-to-day work. Companies participate in the programme to gather employee-led insights and review internal practices that support long-term technical capability development. At Genpact , the certification recognises how data science teams work across the company and global client programmes, applying advanced analytics, machine learning, and AI to complex business problems for clients across industries including financial services, life sciences, manufacturing, and consumer goods. Data Science at Enterprise Scale Genpact’s data science practice is embedded within large-scale transformation programmes, giving data scientists exposure to some of the most complex analytical challenges in global enterprise. Teams work across the full spectrum of data science engagements, from exploratory analysis and model development through to production deployment and ongoing optimisation, ensuring that technical work translates directly into measurable client outcomes. The company’s scale and multi-industry footprint mean that data scientists encounter varied business problems and datasets, supporting both technical depth and the development of domain expertise across different sectors. Deeksha Gopalan, Lead Data Scientist at Genpact’s AI Practice and Innovation Labs,spoke about the culture that underpins this work and what the recognition reflects. “Genpact provided the ideal ecosystem to adapt and move into building advanced AI solutions,” Deeksha Gopalan, Lead Data Scientist, AI Practice and Innovation Labs, Genpact, says. “By combining deep domain expertise, advanced analytics, and engineering rigour, we work backwards from our clients' ambitions to turn complex enterprise challenges into measurable impact.” Collaboration Between Data Science and Business Teams Data scientists at Genpact work closely with business analysts, domain experts, and client stakeholders throughout the lifecycle of each engagement. This cross-functional model ensures that analytical work remains grounded in business context and that insights are designed for practical application rather than theoretical value alone. Employees describe an environment where data science teams are involved not only in technical delivery but also in problem framing and solution design, giving practitioners a clearer view of how their work influences client decisions and business performance. Learning, Growth, and Technical Development Genpact invests in structured learning pathways and technical communities that support data scientists across different career stages. Platforms including Genome and AI Guru allow employees to develop new skills in the flow of work, while access to emerging technologies such as generative AI and agentic AI is embedded within live client programmes rather than kept separate from day-to-day delivery. Arjun Seth, Lead Data Scientist at Genpact's AI Practice and Innovation Labs, described his own trajectory at the company and what has shaped his growth there. “At Genpact, data science is about more than models. It is about solving real business problems with the right AI,” Arjun Seth, Lead Data Scientist, AI Practice and Innovation Labs, Genpact, says. “Today, I build generative and agentic AI solutions that help enterprises solve complex challenges and create measurable impact.” Certification and the Data Science Talent Landscape Across industries, demand for experienced data science professionals continues to grow as organisations seek to unlock the value of their data assets and scale AI-driven decision-making. Beyond compensation, professionals increasingly seek roles that offer learning through practice, ownership of analytical work, and clear links between data science and business outcomes. The Best Firm for Data Scientists certification by AIM is a benchmark for organisations building credible, high-performance data science teams. For Genpact, the recognition reflects the environment it has built for its data science community, one where technical rigour, client proximity, and structured career development come together. .

items.title: DeepSeek Proposes Super-Agent Architecture to Automate AI Coding Workflows
items.summary: Chinese AI company DeepSeek on October 31 published a technical proposal for a ‘super-agent’ architecture designed to coordinate multiple artificial intelligence agents with limited human intervention. The proposal, titled ‘Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System’, was published by the DeepSeek Harness team on its official WeChat account. The article outlines an approach to reduce the time developers spend managing individual AI coding sessions. DeepSeek estimated that a person could typically oversee three to five active agent sessions simultaneously, making human attention a constraint on deploying multiple AI assistants. The proposed architecture separates coordination from execution. A central agent, called a Router, receives messages and distributes work to independent agents, or Workers, which execute tasks in parallel and report their results. The Router handles user interactions while the Workers perform assigned tasks. The system is also designed to respond to events such as messages and code updates without requiring explicit instructions for every task. DeepSeek described an example in which an agent detects a software bug reported in a group chat, attempts to reproduce and fix it, and submits a proposed code change for human review. In simulated experiments, DeepSeek’s super-agent architecture recorded a 95th-percentile task completion time of 15.7 minutes, compared with 29.5 minutes for a single-session approach using a neutral prompt and a subagent tool. The experiment involved about 300 messages per run, including around 20 work requests, with each configuration tested five times. DeepSeek said the workload was synthetic and coding tasks were simulated using a tool that consumed time. The tests measured scheduling and coordination capabilities, not the system’s ability to write or fix code. The proposal comes as AI developers expand coding assistants. Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex are among the tools designed to handle increasingly complex software development tasks. DeepSeek has also published an open-source research prototype, dsh-superagent-prototype, on GitHub under the MIT License. The prototype supports a single GitHub repository and can optionally listen to messages on Feishu, a workplace collaboration platform. The company said the public prototype is not an official product and differs from its internal implementation. Some architectural ideas in the technical article remain future development directions and are not implemented in the released code. DeepSeek also acknowledged security and privacy risks associated with autonomous agents connected to external services, including prompt injection and potential credential exposure. The company described the public code as a research prototype rather than production-ready software.

items.title: Designing a Reliable Influencer Research Workflow: From Campaign Brief to Creator Shortlist
items.summary: Influencer marketing research often starts with a simple question: How do we find the right creators for a campaign? But the actual process is rarely simple. Marketing teams often switch between social media platforms, spreadsheets, creator profiles, analytics tools, and email inboxes. They collect information in different formats, compare creators manually, and frequently repeat the same research for different campaigns. The real challenge isn't just finding influencers. It's building a repeatable workflow that connects campaign requirements with creator discovery, evaluation, and personalized outreach. Here is a practical framework for organizing that process. 1. Start With a Structured Campaign Brief Before searching for creators, define what a successful partnership should look like. A vague brief such as "We need tech influencers" doesn't provide enough information to guide research. What the proposed partnership involves. What the next step would be. Consider tracking the following stages: Stage Metric Discovery Creators discovered Evaluation Profiles reviewed Shortlisting Qualified candidates Outreach Messages prepared and sent Response Creator replies Qualification Relevant partnership opportunities These metrics help identify bottlenecks. If many suitable creators are shortlisted but few respond, the outreach approach may need attention. The goal is to improve the entire workflow, not simply increase the size of the database. A structured campaign brief, multiple discovery methods, evidence-based evaluation, organized shortlists, and personalized outreach can make the process more consistent and manageable. AI can help reduce repetitive work, but the quality of the final decisions still depends on clear requirements and thoughtful human review. The most useful workflow is one that connects every stage: Understand the brief → Discover → Evaluate → Organize → Outreach. items.summary_html:
Influencer marketing research often starts with a simple question:

How do we find the right creators for a campaign?

But the actual process is rarely simple.

Marketing teams often switch between social media platforms, spreadsheets, creator profiles, analytics tools, and email inboxes. They collect information in different formats, compare creators manually, and frequently repeat the same research for different campaigns.

The real challenge isn't just finding influencers. It's building a repeatable workflow that connects campaign requirements with creator discovery, evaluation, and personalized outreach.

Here is a practical framework for organizing that process.

1. Start With a Structured Campaign Brief

Before searching for creators, define what a successful partnership should look like.

A vague brief such as "We need tech influencers" doesn't provide enough information to guide research.

Instead, break the campaign into structured requirements:

  • Campaign objective
  • Target audience
  • Relevant content topics
  • Preferred social platforms
  • Target countries and languages
  • Creator profile and content style
  • Budget range
  • Campaign timeline
  • Excluded topics or creator characteristics

For software teams building creator research tools, these requirements can be represented as structured data.

For example:

{
  "campaign_objective": "Product awareness",
  "target_audience": {
    "regions": ["United States"],
    "interests": ["AI", "Productivity", "Technology"]
  },
  "platforms": [
    "YouTube",
    "Instagram",
    "TikTok"
  ],
  "content_topics": [
    "AI tools",
    "Software reviews",
    "Productivity workflows"
  ],
  "creator_preferences": {
    "content_style": "Educational and practical",
    "language": "English"
  },
  "constraints": {
    "budget": null,
    "timeline": null
  }
}

The values above are illustrative, not universal campaign requirements.

The important idea is to turn natural-language requirements into criteria that can be searched, reviewed, and updated.

2. Use Multiple Discovery Methods

Relying on one search method can limit the range of creators you discover.

A better approach combines several methods.

Keyword-based discovery

Start with topics, niches, and phrases that describe the campaign.

For example:

  • AI productivity tools
  • AI software reviews
  • No-code automation
  • Developer tools
  • Technology tutorials

Try variations of the same topic rather than relying on a single keyword.

Similar creator discovery

If you already know one creator who matches your target audience, use that creator as a starting point.

Look for other creators who cover similar subjects, attract comparable audiences, or publish content in a related style.

Content-based discovery

Don't evaluate a creator based only on their profile description.

Review their recent videos, posts, recurring topics, and the way they communicate with their audience.

A creator's actual content often provides more useful context than a short biography.

3. Evaluate Creator Fit Beyond Follower Count

One of the most common mistakes in influencer research is treating follower count as the main indicator of campaign suitability.

A large audience doesn't automatically mean a good partnership.

Consider these five dimensions:

1. Content relevance

Does the creator regularly publish content related to your product or industry?

2. Audience alignment

Does the available audience information match your target market?

3. Engagement context

Look beyond a single engagement percentage. Review views, comments, and interactions across multiple recent posts.

4. Content consistency

Does the creator publish regularly? Is their content quality relatively consistent?

5. Collaboration readiness

Is there publicly available business contact information? Does the creator appear to work with brands?

A useful evaluation table might look like this:

Criterion What to review Content fit Recent topics and videos Audience fit Available audience signals Engagement Views and interactions Consistency Publishing patterns Contact Public business information

These criteria should support human judgment, not replace it with a single automated score.

4. Build an Evidence-Based Shortlist

After reviewing creators, organize them into a shortlist.

Instead of saving dozens of profiles without context, record why each creator was selected.

A useful shortlist should include:

  • Creator name and profile URL
  • Main content niche
  • Relevant content examples
  • Available performance indicators
  • Audience observations
  • Public business contact information, if available
  • Reason for selection
  • Potential collaboration angle
  • Research status

You can also organize creators into three groups:

High priority: Strong content relevance and audience alignment.

Worth reviewing: Potential fit, but additional research is needed.

Low priority: Important campaign requirements are not currently met.

This makes it easier for marketing teams to discuss candidates and explain their decisions.

5. Personalize Outreach Instead of Sending Generic Messages

Finding a suitable creator is only half the process.

The next challenge is starting a meaningful conversation.

Generic outreach often looks like this:

"Hi, we love your content. Would you like to collaborate with us?"

It provides very little context.

A better message should explain:

  1. Why you selected this creator.
  2. Which specific content caught your attention.
  3. Why the collaboration could be relevant to their audience.
  4. What the proposed partnership involves.
  5. What the next step would be.

For example:

"Hi [Creator Name],

I recently came across your content about [specific topic] and particularly enjoyed your approach to [specific detail].

We're exploring a potential collaboration around [campaign topic], and I thought it might be relevant to the audience you've built.

Would you be open to discussing a possible partnership?

Best,
[Your Name]"

The key is relevance.

A personalized message demonstrates that the brand has actually researched the creator rather than simply collecting their email address.

6. Use AI to Reduce Repetitive Research

AI can make creator research more efficient, especially when teams need to process large amounts of information.

Some useful applications include:

  • Extracting campaign requirements from natural-language briefs.
  • Expanding keyword ideas for creator discovery.
  • Summarizing publicly available creator profiles and content.
  • Organizing research notes into structured fields.
  • Drafting personalized outreach based on verified context.

However, AI-generated insights should be treated as research assistance rather than unquestionable facts.

Always verify important information, especially audience data, business contacts, and campaign suitability.

Different social platforms also expose different data, so a consistent evaluation process should account for those differences.

Human review remains important before contacting creators or making campaign decisions.

7. Measure the Research Workflow

A creator research process should be evaluated by more than the number of profiles collected.

Consider tracking the following stages:

Stage Metric Discovery Creators discovered Evaluation Profiles reviewed Shortlisting Qualified candidates Outreach Messages prepared and sent Response Creator replies Qualification Relevant partnership opportunities

These metrics help identify bottlenecks.

For example, if a team discovers many creators but only a small number meet campaign requirements, the search criteria may need improvement.

If many suitable creators are shortlisted but few respond, the outreach approach may need attention.

The goal is to improve the entire workflow, not simply increase the size of the database.

Final Thoughts

Effective influencer research is a process, not a one-time search.

A structured campaign brief, multiple discovery methods, evidence-based evaluation, organized shortlists, and personalized outreach can make the process more consistent and manageable.

AI can help reduce repetitive work, but the quality of the final decisions still depends on clear requirements and thoughtful human review.

Understand the brief → Discover → Evaluate → Organize → Outreach.

items.title: Sharing an AI agent: what to keep, what to strip, and what never to trust
items.summary: You built an agent that works. Someone asks for it. What do you actually send them? An AI agent is more than a prompt. In AWFlow (a browser automation tool I build) an agent has a model, instructions, memory, skills, rules and routines, and agents can form teams with a handoff map (the coordination runtime behind teams has its own post). We recently added a marketplace where people can share agents and whole teams as templates . That raises a design question every "share your agent" feature has to answer: what's the reusable part, and what's personal? Get it wrong one way and templates are useless. Get it wrong the other way and people leak their memory, their sites and their credentials. Here's how we drew the line, and the rules we follow on install. Never the person: what it knows about its author, or what it is connected to. What travels and what stays An agent template should carry how the agent works , never what it knows about its author or what it's connected to on the author's machine . Drag the line to compare what travels. Here's the full split: Kept (the setup) Stripped (personal or device-specific) Name, handle, role, avatar, greeting, starter prompts Memory and chat history Instructions Knowledge-base contents (the collection references are emptied) Skills it uses (browser, web search, on-device AI…) Credentials and the author's MCP servers Rule preset and generic per-action rules Per-site rules and the author's allow/block site lists Portable routines (schedule, page triggers…) Routines tied to a local workflow or a recording Team: members, roles, way of working, handoff map IDs of the author's own workflows On-device model choice Cloud model choice (it names the author's provider) A few of these deserve a word. Models: on-device travels, cloud doesn't If the author picked an in-browser model, the template keeps it: anyone can download the same model. If they picked a cloud model, the template says "inherit" and the installer's own default applies. A cloud pick names the author's provider and account setup, which the installer may not have. On install, your own default applies. Rules: keep the intent, drop the specifics The agent's rule preset and its generic per-action rules ("ask before submitting forms") are the safety intent, so they travel. Rules tied to specific sites, and the author's allow/block site lists, are personal browsing context, so they're dropped. Peel them apart: the intent travels, the specifics stay home. Dependencies become "needs", not secrets If an agent uses one of the author's workflows as a skill, or an MCP server, the template can't include those. Instead it records what's needed : the workflow's name , the MCP server's host . You get a plain note. After installing, the user sees “Add these to finish setting it up: …”. The agent depends on the author's things A workflow that lives on the author's device, an MCP server they connected. Neither can travel. Export records the need The template keeps the workflow's name and the server's host, so the installer knows what is missing. Install creates the agent The new agent starts without those tools, rather than pretending to have them. You get a plain note After installing, the user sees "Add these to finish setting it up: …" . That's much better than an agent that silently has fewer tools than its description promises. Routines: only the portable ones A routine triggered by a schedule or a page event travels. A routine that depends on a local workflow or a recorded sequence can't work on someone else's machine, so it's left out rather than shipped broken. On install: never trust the file A template is just data, and data from strangers is untrusted. The rule: treat the file as untrusted input. Install follows a few rules: Same guardrails: "ask" asks, locked categories always ask. The re-mapping is worth seeing, because it's where a careless importer leaks or overwrites things. The built-in assistant is reused, not duplicated. The marketplace on top The marketplace adds the social layer. Listings are reviewed by a moderator before they go live, and anyone can browse agent and team templates in Marketplace › Agents & teams without signing in. Installing is one click, plus a single confirmation when the template's agents can act in your browser or run on their own. The install is counted on the server (once per signed-in person), but the agents themselves are created locally on your device. One honest limit: stripping protects your state and your connections, not your words. Instructions are shared as written. The marketplace checks a template again when it is submitted and refuses anything that looks like a key or personal data, but read your instructions before you share. The templates page in the docs lists everything that is and isn't shared. If you're building "share your agent" in your own product, this is the short list: Untrusted on install: fresh IDs, remapped references, same guardrails. AWFlow is free and runs in your browser. Interactive version with animations: https://awflow.io/blog/sharing-an-ai-agent-what-to-strip Try it Agentic Workflow (AWFlow) runs in your browser, on the model you choose, free and with no account needed to start. Install it from the Chrome Web Store here .
