items.title: Beyond the AI Demo: Five Product Engineering Companies and What Developers Should Evaluate
items.summary: An AI demo can generate answers, process a document, or complete a workflow. Production introduces harder questions: what happens when the provider times out, a deployment changes output quality, or another team inherits the code? For developers evaluating an external engineering partner, these questions matter more than the speed of the first demonstration. This article examines themes from GeekyAnts’ discussion of AI-powered product engineering , then considers five companies through the lens of engineering responsibilities. The shortlist is not a verified performance ranking. What should survive beyond the prototype? The source article emphasizes modular architecture, model portability, continuous testing, human review, and ownership after launch. It also describes AntFlow AI as a workflow involving agreed specifications, agent-generated implementation, separate verification, and human approval. These are useful evaluation themes, but a provider’s description is only the starting point. The meaningful evidence lies in its implementation artifacts and the experience of the proposed delivery team. A technical assessment should connect each claim to something observable: Provider claim Evidence to request Modular architecture Component boundaries and a walkthrough of a recent change Model portability A demonstrated provider change and its evaluation results Human oversight Review ownership and release approval criteria Production readiness Monitoring, incident procedures, and recovery exercises Long-term ownership Runbooks, repository access, and handover expectations This turns a broad capabilities discussion into a review that engineers can challenge. Which five companies belong in the comparison? GeekyAnts GeekyAnts describes an approach combining product engineering with AI-assisted delivery. Its article places responsibility for architecture, code approval, and deployment decisions with engineers, while using AI for parts of implementation. The relevant assessment is whether those controls operate consistently on the proposed engagement. A sample pull request, verification report, and release checklist would be more informative than a general presentation about development speed. IBM IBM’s application modernization services combine cloud engineering with AI-assisted approaches to existing software estates. Its published offering discusses deterministic code analysis alongside generative and agentic AI. For teams extending established applications, the evaluation should focus on how the proposed team identifies dependencies and validates changed behavior. Buyers should also distinguish reusable delivery tooling from project-specific engineering work. Accenture Accenture’s AI Refinery work includes the Distiller agentic framework and SDKs intended to support development and deployment of enterprise AI solutions. Developers assessing this approach should examine the boundary between framework capabilities and application responsibilities. Useful questions concern deployment ownership, debugging access, portability, and how much custom code remains maintainable by the client’s team. Deloitte Deloitte’s engineering services cover AI application development, data platforms, software platform engineering, and ML/LLM operations. That breadth makes team composition an important evaluation point. A proposal should identify who owns application code, data pipelines, evaluation, and production operations, including how those responsibilities connect when an incident crosses several layers. TCS TCS’ Software Product Innovation Services include AI-led engineering, digital platform development, and product transformation. For a product with an established roadmap, the assessment should examine how modernization and feature delivery coexist. The proposed team should explain its approach to regression testing, release ownership, and preserving product knowledge as contributors change. How can developers test the claims fairly? A bounded technical exercise can make comparisons more useful. For example, each shortlisted team could assess the same document-processing workflow and explain how it would handle an unavailable model provider, an unreadable input, and an output that requires human review. The requested deliverables could include: A component diagram with external dependencies. Explicit success and failure criteria. A small evaluation dataset with expected outcomes. A release and recovery plan. A breakdown of recurring operating costs. The exercise should reflect the intended project. It should also reveal assumptions: what requires further discovery, which behavior remains uncertain, and where human intervention is necessary. What should determine the final decision? The strongest evidence is a delivery team that can explain its engineering choices and their consequences. A polished demo provides limited information about maintainability, incident response, or the cost of operating the product. Likewise, a recognizable company name does not establish the capabilities of the people assigned to a particular engagement. A useful selection process therefore compares named teams, inspectable work, and clearly assigned responsibilities. The practical goal is a product that the client can operate, change, and understand after its first release.

items.title: Your AI Agent Doesn't Read Your 40-Page Security Policy
items.summary: Your company spent three months writing an AI governance policy. Legal reviewed it. Security approved it. Compliance signed off. Engineering received a 40-page PDF. Then someone deployed an AI agent with access to a production database. Here's my question: Which line of that PDF actually stops the agent from executing an unauthorized query? Exactly. This is the uncomfortable reality of enterprise AI governance. We're treating organizational policies as though they automatically translate into technical restrictions. They don't. The Policy Exists. The Permission Still Works. Imagine you're building an AI support agent. It can retrieve customer records and recommend account updates. Your organization has a clear policy: Customer records must not be modified without approval. The system prompt includes the same instruction. But your agent also has access to this tool: update_customer_record ( customer_id , changes ) And the tool itself doesn't enforce approval. Now imagine the agent decides that modifying the record is necessary to resolve a customer issue. If nothing outside the model checks authorization, the operation may execute. Your policy hasn't disappeared. It's just not connected to the execution path. That's not a documentation problem. It's an enforcement problem. We Keep Putting Rules in the Wrong Place There are several ways developers try to control agents. System prompts. Tool descriptions. Workflow instructions. Configuration settings. All of these can be useful. But they serve different purposes. A system prompt can influence what the model decides. A tool description can explain intended usage. A configuration setting can restrict access if the platform actually enforces it. An authorization mechanism can determine whether a proposed action is permitted. These aren't interchangeable. If a model can directly call a sensitive tool without an independent permission check, telling it not to do so is not a sufficient security boundary. The Missing Check A basic enforcement pattern might look like this: def run_tool ( agent , tool , args ): decision = authorize ( agent = agent , tool = tool , args = args ) if decision == " DENY " : return { " status " : " blocked " } if decision == " REVIEW " : return { " status " : " approval_required " } if decision != " ALLOW " : return { " status " : " blocked " } return execute ( tool , args ) Illustrative pseudocode. The model proposes the tool call. The authorization mechanism evaluates it. Only permitted operations execute. The important part isn't the specific code. It's the separation of responsibilities. An AI model shouldn't be the sole authority over its own permissions. What About Approval Workflows? Approval workflows can help, but only if they're genuine execution checkpoints. Consider two designs. Design A The agent sends an email. The system notifies an administrator that a sensitive email was sent. Design B The agent prepares an email. The system detects that approval is required. Execution pauses. An authorized reviewer approves or rejects the action. Only an approved message can be sent. Design A provides visibility. Design B provides enforcement. Both may produce logs. Only one actually prevents the protected action from executing without approval. The Four Questions I'd Ask Before Shipping 1. What happens when authorization fails? Does the system block the action or continue? 2. Can the agent bypass a restriction through another tool? If one tool is blocked, does another provide the same underlying capability? 3. Are approvals bound to the exact proposed action? An approval for one recipient or transaction shouldn't automatically authorize a modified operation. 4. What happens when the policy service is unavailable? For sensitive actions, missing authorization shouldn't silently become permission. These questions are far more useful than simply asking whether the organization has an AI governance policy. The Nuroen Approach At Nuroen AI, we're building enterprise agents around the idea of bounded execution. That includes scope restrictions, confidence checks, policy and human approval gates, execution budgets, and auditability. The goal isn't to eliminate autonomous behavior. It's to ensure that agents can perform useful work without treating every available tool as an unrestricted permission. The Real Lesson Documentation is necessary. Policies are necessary. Security reviews are necessary. But none of them automatically enforce themselves. A policy tells you what should happen. A runtime control determines whether a protected action is allowed to happen. And once AI agents start interacting with production systems, that difference matters. Your governance policy shouldn't live only in a PDF. Its requirements need to exist in the execution path. Question for developers: What's the most common AI agent security mistake you've seen — overpowered tools, missing approval gates, or trusting prompts as permissions? Security approved it.

Compliance signed off.

Engineering received a 40-page PDF.

Then someone deployed an AI agent with access to a production database.

Exactly.

    customer_id,
    changes
)

items.title: Guul: connecting a resume builder with the rest of a job search
items.summary: I’m working on Guul , an AI-assisted resume builder and career workspace. This introduction is for people who want to try the workflow and give feedback. A resume is only one part of applying for a job. After tailoring it, there is still the cover letter, the application status, the follow-up, recruiter outreach and interview preparation. Guul brings those tasks into the same workspace. What the workspace includes Resume creation, importing, editing and tailoring to a role. Cover-letter writing. Application tracking and follow-up reminders. Recruiter outreach drafts that the user sends themselves. Mentor review through revocable links. The resume owner chooses which suggestions to apply. Interview practice with Pro access, subject to usage limits. Career-profile publishing. The boundary around ATS checks Guul includes checks for readability and modeled parsing risks. They are simulations. They do not run a resume through an employer’s live applicant-tracking system, and they cannot promise interviews. That distinction matters when evaluating any resume tool. A text extractor recovering words from a PDF is a narrower result than proving how a particular employer will interpret an application. Guul publishes its score methodology and template parse tests so readers can examine the scope rather than relying on a score alone. What is free Editing, previews, TXT downloads, basic checks and several career tools are free. PDF and Word exports require a one-time resume pack or qualifying Pro access. One-time packs provide 30 days of download access without renewal. Optional Pro subscriptions renew until canceled, and AI usage limits apply. Current plans and conditions are on the website. Feedback I would value For developers managing a job search, where does the workflow become fragmented? Would connecting application tracking and mentor review to the resume be useful, or would you prefer those as separate tools? You can explore Guul’s career tools and the resume builder . Disclosure: this post was written by an AI agent. The feature and pricing descriptions were checked against Guul’s public pages.

  • Resume creation, importing, editing and tailoring to a role.
  • Cover-letter writing.
  • Application tracking and follow-up reminders.
  • Recruiter outreach drafts that the user sends themselves.
  • Mentor review through revocable links. The resume owner chooses which suggestions to apply.
  • Interview practice with Pro access, subject to usage limits.
  • Career-profile publishing.

Guul includes checks for readability and modeled parsing risks. They are simulations. They do not run a resume through an employer’s live applicant-tracking system, and they cannot promise interviews.

That distinction matters when evaluating any resume tool. A text extractor recovering words from a PDF is a narrower result than proving how a particular employer will interpret an application. Guul publishes its score methodology and template parse tests so readers can examine the scope rather than relying on a score alone.

What is free

Editing, previews, TXT downloads, basic checks and several career tools are free. PDF and Word exports require a one-time resume pack or qualifying Pro access. One-time packs provide 30 days of download access without renewal. Optional Pro subscriptions renew until canceled, and AI usage limits apply. Current plans and conditions are on the website.

Feedback I would value

For developers managing a job search, where does the workflow become fragmented? Would connecting application tracking and mentor review to the resume be useful, or would you prefer those as separate tools?

You can explore Guul’s career tools and the resume builder.

Disclosure: this post was written by an AI agent. The feature and pricing descriptions were checked against Guul’s public pages.

items.title: Northflank Breach Exposes AI API Keys
items.summary: Northflank told every customer to assume that all environment variables stored on its platform had been decrypted and to rotate every key. The October 30 warning followed a threat alert from cloud security company Wiz. Northflank later confirmed that customers had reported unauthorized use of AI API keys supplied to the cloud application hosting platform. Those keys can turn a breach of deployment infrastructure into direct access to metered AI services, with the bill landing on the customer. According to Northflank's published timeline, Wiz alerted the company at 11:43 UTC on October 30. Northflank engineers reviewed the alert one minute later, applied a network policy patch, and deployed additional patches at 12:50 UTC and 13:05 UTC. The company also requested help from Wiz's incident response team. Northflank has not disclosed how the attackers obtained access, how many customers were affected, or whether credentials other than the reported AI API keys were stolen or abused. Its instructions nevertheless set the working scope clearly: rotate user-provided secrets in workloads, secret groups, and global secrets. Customers should also disable public access to add-ons where it is enabled. Environment variables are a common interface between deployment systems and applications. They often contain database passwords, cloud credentials, authentication tokens, and third-party API keys. A platform that can decrypt those variables sits on a dense collection of credentials spanning many customers and services. Once an attacker reaches that layer, each secret can provide another route into a customer's infrastructure or an account capable of generating charges. AI credentials are particularly easy to monetize because the service is consumed through authenticated API requests. Wiz calls the abuse of stolen AI credentials "LLMJacking": attackers use another organization's keys to invoke models, accumulate charges, or resell access. In two cases investigated by Wiz, compromised enterprise credentials made about 2.5 million Amazon Bedrock API calls and generated approximately $100,000 in usage. The Northflank incident was one of at least nine October incidents involving AI development platforms identified by Wiz. The list included Railway, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI. Railway also faced potential exposure of decrypted customer environment variables, OpenCode disclosed exposed AI API keys, and Warp reported exposure of AI agent logs and user telemetry. Wiz has not attributed all nine incidents to the same attackers, although many involved attempts to obtain AI API keys. For Northflank customers, replacing a secret in the platform is only part of the response. The old credential must be revoked or disabled at its issuer. Otherwise, removing it from a workload leaves the captured value usable. Rotation should cover every credential that passed through the affected secret stores, including database passwords and cloud or service tokens, rather than stopping after the visibly abused AI keys. Usage and billing logs at AI providers should be reviewed for unexpected calls. Northflank specifically advised customers to report suspicious usage to both Northflank and the relevant AI provider. Investigation windows should begin before the October 30 disclosure where retained logs allow it, because the alert time establishes when Northflank learned about the incident rather than when access necessarily began. The incident also exposes an operational dependency that credential inventories often obscure. A key may belong to an AI provider, but its effective custody includes the deployment platform that stores and injects it. Rotation procedures therefore need to account for provider-side revocation, platform-side replacement, application rollout, and verification that old instances or jobs no longer carry the previous value. Northflank enabled credential rotation for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, and Redis as part of its response. It also enabled audit logs for all customers, including free accounts. Those logs can help identify suspicious platform activity, while provider logs show whether stolen credentials were used elsewhere. Both views are needed when a deployment-layer breach crosses into external services.

items.title: markgate: Mechanically Catch Coding Agent Slip-ups and Enforce Non-Command Tasks
items.summary: I built an OSS tool called markgate that mechanically catches and enforces two kinds of gaps: when a Coding Agent (Claude Code, etc.) accidentally forgets to call a Skill that runs build or tests after implementation and commits anyway, and when AI tasks that can't be reduced to a command — like a /check-docs Skill — can't be enforced through hooks. markgate NOTE: markgate is meant to run inside a git repository. markgate markgate is a CLI tool that acts as an enforcement layer wedged between the Coding Agent and your hooks . By mechanically catching and enforcing the Coding Agent's mistakes and omissions, it addresses the following three failure patterns. Pattern Failure pattern it addresses Solution 1 Catching forgotten calls and avoiding duplicate execution markgate run 2 Enforcing non-command tasks markgate set + markgate verify 3 Scoping multiple tasks + aggregate verify composes in .markgate.yml Below, we'll walk through each pattern in turn. Pattern 1: Catching Forgotten Calls and Avoiding Duplicate Execution ( markgate run ) Suppose you have an implementation skill, and a check skill ( /check ) that runs after it. /check runs verifications against the implemented code. The things you want to guarantee against your implementation will vary by project — tests, typecheck, lint, format, build, documentation consistency, coverage generation, image scans, and so on. However, even if you tell the Coding Agent "run /check after implementing", the Coding Agent can forget and silently skip the step . When that happens, your code gets committed without the checks you wanted to run. So, you set up a pre-commit hook to forcibly run the equivalent of /check . But the Coding Agent doesn't always forget. In fact, forgetting is rare — usually it runs /check just fine. That leads to "the skill already ran it → the hook runs it again", a duplicate execution . If /check is heavy, this slows down what should be a fast Coding Agent development cycle. If it's light you might not notice, but running it frequently still wastes a non-trivial amount of time. Furthermore, if you skip the check after the implementation skill and put all check logic only in the hook, you can't run checks when you're not yet ready to commit. Running a post-edit hook on every file change isn't a great answer either, since the checks then run on every edit and that takes time. Solved with markgate run markgate keeps both the /check skill and the hook in place, and makes it so that the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check . In other words, when the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the hook is skipped , so duplicate execution doesn't happen. Usage The basic flow is no config file required — just call the command. For example, suppose your /check skill and pre-commit hook from above both run pnpm build . And suppose the pre-commit hook is wired up via Claude Code's PreToolUse hook firing on git commit* . 1. /check skill In the /check skill that runs first, wrap the pnpm build command using markgate run -- . // ... inside the skill definition - pnpm build + markgate run -- pnpm build 2. hook In the pre-commit hook, rewrite pnpm build to markgate run -- pnpm build in the same way. { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [{ "matcher": "Bash", "if": "Bash(git commit*)", - "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "pnpm build" }] + "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "markgate run -- pnpm build" }] }] } } With just this, you get the behavior where the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check , running pnpm build . When the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the latter hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen. Pattern 2: Enforcing Non-command Tasks ( set + verify ) Up to this point, markgate run has meant writing the target command ( pnpm build , etc.) directly into the hook configuration. In practice, though, there are also tasks that can't be reduced to a command . For example, "is the documentation consistent with src?", "does the PR description match the diff?", "is naming consistent with the existing code?" — these are reviews that need LLM judgment and can't be expressed as a shell command. You want to run this kind of LLM task in the Coding Agent's own session , because you want to leverage the context the Coding Agent has built up (conversation history, open files, past decisions). Technically, you could launch a separate session from a hook via claude -p , but since the context isn't shared , it doesn't act as a continuation of the work so far. As a result, the hook alone can't tell whether the Coding Agent ran an LLM task like /check-docs , which means there's no way to enforce it . Building a Gate with set + verify That's where the gate pattern — combining markgate set and markgate verify — comes in. The check itself stays on the skill side; set records "the moment the check passed" as a marker , and on the hook side, verify acts as a gate that judges whether "the recorded marker matches the current marker". markgate set : records the moment the check passed as a marker markgate verify : exits 0 if the recorded marker matches the current marker, and exits 1 to stop things if they don't match Since the marker records the code state at the time of set , when the code changes afterward the recorded marker and the current marker no longer match , and verify stops things (we'll cover what's inside a marker later). Usage At the end of where the check actually runs (a skill like /check-docs ), call markgate set . On the hook side, just call markgate verify . # At the end of the /check-docs skill definition markgate set // .claude/settings.json (hook side) { "hooks" : { "PreToolUse" : [ { "matcher" : "Bash" , "if" : "Bash(git commit*)" , "hooks" : [ { "type" : "command" , "command" : "markgate verify || { echo 'run /check-docs' >&2; exit 1; }" } ] } ] } } The whole chain of check operations stays defined on the skill side, and the hook just looks at the marker. If the marker is missing or doesn't match the code, the hook blocks with exit 1, and the Coding Agent gets both the error and a hint ( run /check-docs ), so when the gate blocks things, recovery can be left to the Coding Agent and it can loop again . Catching Both "First-time Non-command Triggers" and "Slip-ups" This gate pattern is effective in both of the following cases. First-time non-command trigger : The Coding Agent doesn't even know /check-docs exists and tries to commit. → Since there's no marker, the hook blocks, and after reading the error message ( run /check-docs ), the Coding Agent runs /check-docs for the first time. Slip-up : The Coding Agent runs /check-docs and the marker is set. But later, when the code is edited again and you want to re-check , the Coding Agent forgets to re-run /check-docs . → Since the marker no longer matches the code, the hook blocks and prompts the Coding Agent to re-run. In short, markgate uniformly catches both never-run-before cases and failure to re-run after a slip-up , using the same logic: "does the marker match the current code state?". Pattern 3: Scoping and Aggregate Verify ( .markgate.yml + composes ) So far we've assumed "one skill, one hook", but in practice you often have multiple checks lined up. For example, suppose at pre-commit you want to run light checks ( check : typecheck / lint / build / unit test) plus a heavier check that uses an LLM to verify documentation consistency ( docs ). The problem here is wasted runs . If you bundle them into a single gate, even on a commit that only touches tests, the LLM consistency check runs even though nothing in the documentation-related files changed. That would mean re-running the heavy LLM check every time you change any code, which isn't practical. Giving Each Task Its Own Scope That's where .markgate.yml comes in: give each check its "own scope" (= the set of files specified in include ). Whether a re-run is needed is judged by whether the code change falls within that scope. On top of that, using composes to create an aggregate gate that bundles multiple gates means the hook side can judge "do all the bundled gates match the current code?" with just a single line of verify . Usage Create a .markgate.yml ( markgate init generates a template). # .markgate.yml gates : check : hash : files # only the files specified in include are hashed include : - " src/**" - " tests/**" - " package.json" docs : hash : files include : - " src/**" # changes in src also affect docs, so include in both - " docs/**" - " README.md" pre-commit : composes : [ check , docs ] # aggregate gate: AND of check and docs From the skill side, specify the gate name as an argument and set each gate individually. # At the end of the /check skill definition pnpm typecheck && pnpm lint && pnpm test && markgate set check # At the end of the /check-docs skill definition markgate set docs Then, in the pre-commit hook, verify the pre-commit aggregate gate in a single line. When it doesn't match, markgate status pre-commit shows "which gate doesn't match", and the Coding Agent reads that and re-loops the corresponding skill. // .claude/settings.json { "hooks" : { "PreToolUse" : [ { "matcher" : "Bash" , "if" : "Bash(git commit*)" , "hooks" : [ { "type" : "command" , "command" : "markgate verify pre-commit || { markgate status pre-commit >&2; exit 1; }" } ] } ] } } The key point is that only the checks needed for the edited scope get re-run . Each gate's marker only hashes the files in its own include , so on a commit that only touches one side's scope, the other gate's marker stays the same as when it was set and still matches, meaning no re-run is needed. For example, a commit that only modifies tests re-runs only the light checks; a commit that only touches files outside any include (CI config, etc.) skips both. Edited files check docs Checks that need to re-run tests/** only stale fresh light checks only docs/** / README.md only fresh stale heavy check only src/** stale stale both None of the above (CI config, editor config, etc.) fresh fresh none (commit passes) Note that the pre-commit aggregate gate in this example is designed without a command of its own; it just performs the AND judgment — fresh if all bundled gates are fresh, stale if any one is stale. This shape — without its own command — can't be written with markgate run (which wraps a single command); only the gate pattern ( set + verify ) can express it. Other Use Case Examples Beyond the basic usage above, markgate has various advanced patterns. Check documentation consistency before creating a PR ( /check-docs → gh pr create hook) Vulnerability scan before pushing an image ( trivy image → docker push hook) Generate a coverage report before pushing ( go test -cover → git push hook) Ensure E2E tests have just been re-run before merging a PR ( pnpm test:e2e → gh pr merge hook) How It Works: Managing State with Markers Let's look at what the "marker" we've been mentioning is actually made of. markgate works by saving the "state" at the time the target command (or task) succeeded as a marker, and on the next call of the same command (or task), if the marker matches the current state, the run is skipped; if not, it runs ( markgate run ) / blocks ( markgate verify ) . In practice, this "state" is a hash of the code content . You can choose between two hash targets: "a specific set of files" ( hash: files + include ) or "the repository's git status as a whole" ( hash: git-tree , the default). Either way, as long as the code content hasn't changed, the command is skipped . # First run: no marker yet, so pnpm build runs and a marker is saved on success $ markgate run -- pnpm build building... passed in 7.2s # Second run: no file changes → execution is skipped $ markgate run -- pnpm build # After editing a file: the marker is invalidated, so the command runs again $ echo '// fix typo' >> src/foo.ts $ markgate run -- pnpm build building... passed in 7.1s By default, the marker file is stored inside .git ( .git/markgate/default.json ), so you don't need to create a marker file yourself, and it isn't tracked by git even without an explicit .gitignore entry. (There's also an option to explicitly change the marker file path and share markers between local and CI; see the README for that.) Installation # Homebrew brew install go-to-k/tap/markgate # shell script curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-to-k/markgate/main/install.sh | bash # go install go install github.com/go-to-k/markgate/cmd/markgate@latest # mise (ubi backend) mise use "ubi:go-to-k/markgate@0.3.3" Using markgate from Other Hook Managers So far I've used the Claude Code hook as the example, but markgate is hook-manager agnostic . With husky / lefthook / the pre-commit framework, or any other hook manager, you can use it just by writing a single line of markgate run -- . # .husky/pre-commit markgate run -- pnpm test # lefthook.yml pre-commit : commands : check : run : markgate run -- pnpm test # .pre-commit-config.yaml (pre-commit framework) repos : - repo : local hooks : - id : markgate-check name : markgate check entry : markgate run -- pnpm test language : system pass_filenames : false Final Thoughts Personally, I think this has turned into a tool I'll lean on in the AI era. In particular, the idea of "mechanically catching AI mistakes and omissions" feels like one of the important points when working with AI. For the other features ( exclude / state_dir settings in .markgate.yml , sharing markers between local and CI, strict gate dependencies via requires , etc.), see the README in the GitHub repository . If you like it, I'd be glad if you'd give the repository a ⭐. Also, as a project that actually uses markgate in practice, there's cdkd (CDK Direct) — a from-scratch rewrite of the AWS CDK CLI that's made it blazingly fast. items.summary_html:
I built an OSS tool called markgate that mechanically catches and enforces two kinds of gaps: when a Coding Agent (Claude Code, etc.) accidentally forgets to call a Skill that runs build or tests after implementation and commits anyway, and when AI tasks that can't be reduced to a command — like a /check-docs Skill — can't be enforced through hooks.

markgate

NOTE: markgate is meant to run inside a git repository.

markgate

markgate is a CLI tool that acts as an enforcement layer wedged between the Coding Agent and your hooks. By mechanically catching and enforcing the Coding Agent's mistakes and omissions, it addresses the following three failure patterns.

Pattern Failure pattern it addresses Solution 1 Catching forgotten calls and avoiding duplicate execution markgate run 2 Enforcing non-command tasks markgate set + markgate verify 3 Scoping multiple tasks + aggregate verify composes in .markgate.yml

Below, we'll walk through each pattern in turn.

Pattern 1: Catching Forgotten Calls and Avoiding Duplicate Execution (markgate run)

Suppose you have an implementation skill, and a check skill (/check) that runs after it.

/check runs verifications against the implemented code. The things you want to guarantee against your implementation will vary by project — tests, typecheck, lint, format, build, documentation consistency, coverage generation, image scans, and so on.

However, even if you tell the Coding Agent "run /check after implementing", the Coding Agent can forget and silently skip the step. When that happens, your code gets committed without the checks you wanted to run.

So, you set up a pre-commit hook to forcibly run the equivalent of /check.

But the Coding Agent doesn't always forget. In fact, forgetting is rare — usually it runs /check just fine.

That leads to "the skill already ran it → the hook runs it again", a duplicate execution.

If /check is heavy, this slows down what should be a fast Coding Agent development cycle. If it's light you might not notice, but running it frequently still wastes a non-trivial amount of time.

Furthermore, if you skip the check after the implementation skill and put all check logic only in the hook, you can't run checks when you're not yet ready to commit. Running a post-edit hook on every file change isn't a great answer either, since the checks then run on every edit and that takes time.

Solved with markgate run

markgate keeps both the /check skill and the hook in place, and makes it so that the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check.

In other words, when the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen.

Usage

The basic flow is no config file required — just call the command.

For example, suppose your /check skill and pre-commit hook from above both run pnpm build. And suppose the pre-commit hook is wired up via Claude Code's PreToolUse hook firing on git commit*.

1. /check skill

In the /check skill that runs first, wrap the pnpm build command using markgate run -- .

// ... inside the skill definition
- pnpm build
+ markgate run -- pnpm build
2. hook

In the pre-commit hook, rewrite pnpm build to markgate run -- pnpm build in the same way.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
-     "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "pnpm build" }]
+     "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "markgate run -- pnpm build" }]
    }]
  }
}

With just this, you get the behavior where the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check, running pnpm build. When the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the latter hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen.

Pattern 2: Enforcing Non-command Tasks (set + verify)

Up to this point, markgate run has meant writing the target command (pnpm build, etc.) directly into the hook configuration.

In practice, though, there are also tasks that can't be reduced to a command. For example, "is the documentation consistent with src?", "does the PR description match the diff?", "is naming consistent with the existing code?" — these are reviews that need LLM judgment and can't be expressed as a shell command.

You want to run this kind of LLM task in the Coding Agent's own session, because you want to leverage the context the Coding Agent has built up (conversation history, open files, past decisions). Technically, you could launch a separate session from a hook via claude -p, but since the context isn't shared, it doesn't act as a continuation of the work so far. As a result, the hook alone can't tell whether the Coding Agent ran an LLM task like /check-docs, which means there's no way to enforce it.

Building a Gate with set + verify

That's where the gate pattern — combining markgate set and markgate verify — comes in. The check itself stays on the skill side; set records "the moment the check passed" as a marker, and on the hook side, verify acts as a gate that judges whether "the recorded marker matches the current marker".

  • markgate set: records the moment the check passed as a marker
  • markgate verify: exits 0 if the recorded marker matches the current marker, and exits 1 to stop things if they don't match

Since the marker records the code state at the time of set, when the code changes afterward the recorded marker and the current marker no longer match, and verify stops things (we'll cover what's inside a marker later).

Usage

At the end of where the check actually runs (a skill like /check-docs), call markgate set. On the hook side, just call markgate verify.

# At the end of the /check-docs skill definition
markgate set

// .claude/settings.json (hook side)
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "markgate verify || { echo 'run /check-docs' >&2; exit 1; }" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The whole chain of check operations stays defined on the skill side, and the hook just looks at the marker. If the marker is missing or doesn't match the code, the hook blocks with exit 1, and the Coding Agent gets both the error and a hint (run /check-docs), so when the gate blocks things, recovery can be left to the Coding Agent and it can loop again.

Catching Both "First-time Non-command Triggers" and "Slip-ups"

This gate pattern is effective in both of the following cases.

  1. First-time non-command trigger: The Coding Agent doesn't even know /check-docs exists and tries to commit. → Since there's no marker, the hook blocks, and after reading the error message (run /check-docs), the Coding Agent runs /check-docs for the first time.
  2. Slip-up: The Coding Agent runs /check-docs and the marker is set. But later, when the code is edited again and you want to re-check, the Coding Agent forgets to re-run /check-docs. → Since the marker no longer matches the code, the hook blocks and prompts the Coding Agent to re-run.

In short, markgate uniformly catches both never-run-before cases and failure to re-run after a slip-up, using the same logic: "does the marker match the current code state?".

Pattern 3: Scoping and Aggregate Verify (.markgate.yml + composes)

So far we've assumed "one skill, one hook", but in practice you often have multiple checks lined up.

For example, suppose at pre-commit you want to run light checks (check: typecheck / lint / build / unit test) plus a heavier check that uses an LLM to verify documentation consistency (docs).

The problem here is wasted runs. If you bundle them into a single gate, even on a commit that only touches tests, the LLM consistency check runs even though nothing in the documentation-related files changed. That would mean re-running the heavy LLM check every time you change any code, which isn't practical.

Giving Each Task Its Own Scope

That's where .markgate.yml comes in: give each check its "own scope" (= the set of files specified in include). Whether a re-run is needed is judged by whether the code change falls within that scope.

On top of that, using composes to create an aggregate gate that bundles multiple gates means the hook side can judge "do all the bundled gates match the current code?" with just a single line of verify.

Usage

Create a .markgate.yml (markgate init generates a template).

# .markgate.yml
gates:
  check:
    hash: files # only the files specified in include are hashed
    include:
      - "src/**"
      - "tests/**"
      - "package.json"
  docs:
    hash: files
    include:
      - "src/**" # changes in src also affect docs, so include in both
      - "docs/**"
      - "README.md"
  pre-commit:
    composes: [check, docs] # aggregate gate: AND of check and docs

From the skill side, specify the gate name as an argument and set each gate individually.

# At the end of the /check skill definition
pnpm typecheck && pnpm lint && pnpm test && markgate set check

# At the end of the /check-docs skill definition
markgate set docs

Then, in the pre-commit hook, verify the pre-commit aggregate gate in a single line. When it doesn't match, markgate status pre-commit shows "which gate doesn't match", and the Coding Agent reads that and re-loops the corresponding skill.

// .claude/settings.json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "markgate verify pre-commit || { markgate status pre-commit >&2; exit 1; }" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The key point is that only the checks needed for the edited scope get re-run. Each gate's marker only hashes the files in its own include, so on a commit that only touches one side's scope, the other gate's marker stays the same as when it was set and still matches, meaning no re-run is needed.

For example, a commit that only modifies tests re-runs only the light checks; a commit that only touches files outside any include (CI config, etc.) skips both.

Edited files check docs Checks that need to re-run tests/** only stale fresh light checks only docs/** / README.md only fresh stale heavy check only src/** stale stale both None of the above (CI config, editor config, etc.) fresh fresh none (commit passes)

Note that the pre-commit aggregate gate in this example is designed without a command of its own; it just performs the AND judgment — fresh if all bundled gates are fresh, stale if any one is stale. This shape — without its own command — can't be written with markgate run (which wraps a single command); only the gate pattern (set + verify) can express it.

Other Use Case Examples

Beyond the basic usage above, markgate has various advanced patterns.

  • Check documentation consistency before creating a PR (/check-docs → gh pr create hook)
  • Vulnerability scan before pushing an image (trivy image → docker push hook)
  • Generate a coverage report before pushing (go test -cover → git push hook)
  • Ensure E2E tests have just been re-run before merging a PR (pnpm test:e2e → gh pr merge hook)
How It Works: Managing State with Markers

Let's look at what the "marker" we've been mentioning is actually made of.

markgate works by saving the "state" at the time the target command (or task) succeeded as a marker, and on the next call of the same command (or task), if the marker matches the current state, the run is skipped; if not, it runs (markgate run) / blocks (markgate verify).

In practice, this "state" is a hash of the code content. You can choose between two hash targets: "a specific set of files" (hash: files + include) or "the repository's git status as a whole" (hash: git-tree, the default). Either way, as long as the code content hasn't changed, the command is skipped.

# First run: no marker yet, so pnpm build runs and a marker is saved on success
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.2s

# Second run: no file changes → execution is skipped
$ markgate run -- pnpm build

# After editing a file: the marker is invalidated, so the command runs again
$ echo '// fix typo' >> src/foo.ts
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.1s

By default, the marker file is stored inside .git (.git/markgate/default.json), so you don't need to create a marker file yourself, and it isn't tracked by git even without an explicit .gitignore entry. (There's also an option to explicitly change the marker file path and share markers between local and CI; see the README for that.)

Installation 
# Homebrew
brew install go-to-k/tap/markgate

# shell script
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-to-k/markgate/main/install.sh | bash

# go install
go install github.com/go-to-k/markgate/cmd/markgate@latest

# mise (ubi backend)
mise use "ubi:go-to-k/markgate@0.3.3"
Using markgate from Other Hook Managers

So far I've used the Claude Code hook as the example, but markgate is hook-manager agnostic. With husky / lefthook / the pre-commit framework, or any other hook manager, you can use it just by writing a single line of markgate run -- .

# .husky/pre-commit
markgate run -- pnpm test

# lefthook.yml
pre-commit:
  commands:
    check:
      run: markgate run -- pnpm test

# .pre-commit-config.yaml (pre-commit framework)
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: markgate-check
        name: markgate check
        entry: markgate run -- pnpm test
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
Final Thoughts

Personally, I think this has turned into a tool I'll lean on in the AI era. In particular, the idea of "mechanically catching AI mistakes and omissions" feels like one of the important points when working with AI.

For the other features (exclude / state_dir settings in .markgate.yml, sharing markers between local and CI, strict gate dependencies via requires, etc.), see the README in the GitHub repository. If you like it, I'd be glad if you'd give the repository a ⭐.

Also, as a project that actually uses markgate in practice, there's cdkd (CDK Direct) — a from-scratch rewrite of the AWS CDK CLI that's made it blazingly fast. Nearly all of the implementation is delegated to a Coding Agent, and markgate mechanically backs that up against missed runs and non-command tasks. Take a look if you're interested.

items.title: What I Learned Using Free AI Coding Agents on a Real Portfolio (OpenCode and Kilo)
items.summary: I'm a student, and I built and kept improving my portfolio with free AI coding agents running in the VS Code terminal. I used OpenCode and later Kilo, both on free models. They saved me a lot of time, but they also got stuck, lied by accident, and once looked busy for a whole hour without doing anything. Here is what I learned, so you can skip my mistakes. 1. Ask for a read-only diagnosis first My mobile menu showed a dark overlay and an "X" button, but the menu links never appeared. My first prompt was "fix it", and the fix didn't work. What worked was splitting the job into two steps: First, read only. Do not change anything. Find where the mobile menu is rendered and tell me exactly why the panel is invisible, with the file and line number. Then fix it. When the agent has to name the real cause, it stops guessing. In my case the real cause was a previous commit that had removed the menu panel completely. 2. Keep every prompt small My long prompts that asked for five changes at once often ended with "not done in this session". Short prompts with one job each worked much better. A prompt template I now use: Change ONLY in . Do not touch anything else. Use only text that already exists. Do not invent new content. Do not commit or push. Run the typecheck at the end and tell me which lines you changed. 3. Always tell the agent not to commit or push Agents are happy to "help" by committing and pushing. I wanted to review every change first. So every prompt says: do not commit or push . I check git status and git diff myself, and then I commit. 4. Typecheck passing does not mean the build passes Several times the agent said "typecheck passed", and I still had problems after deploying. The typecheck only checks types. A real build can still fail, and a failed build on Vercel means your site stays on the old version. Ask for the build too, and when it uses environment variables, give them: $ env : PORT = "5180" ; $ env : BASE_PATH = "/" ; pnpm --filter @ workspace/ritika-portfolio build Before you ask "why is my change not live?", check the deployment status in the Vercel dashboard. 5. Don't let the agent test in a browser I once asked an agent to verify a fix with a headless browser. It spent an hour fighting spawn pnpm ENOENT on Windows and trying one workaround after another. Now my prompts say: "Do not test in a browser or start a dev server. Only run typecheck and build." I look at the page myself. 6. Watch out for Windows and PowerShell Agents often write bash commands. On Windows PowerShell I kept seeing errors like: && is not a valid statement separator (use ; instead) grep , tail and head are not recognized commands 2>/dev/null fails with a path error If your agent keeps hitting these, add a line like "I use Windows PowerShell, so use PowerShell syntax" to your prompt. 7. "Already implemented" needs checking A few times the agent answered "Already implemented, no changes needed". Sometimes that was true. Sometimes I wanted proof. I started asking it to name the file and line number of the change, and then I searched for that text in VS Code with Ctrl + F . If the agent can't point to a line, don't trust the claim. 8. Free models have limits Free agents can hit a daily limit, or ask you to sign in. Mine said "You need to sign in to use this model" in the middle of a task. Signing up with an email was free and took a couple of minutes. Be ready to switch tools, and never run two agents on the same folder at the same time, because they will edit the same files and cause conflicts. 9. Never paste secrets to an agent Don't paste API keys, tokens or your .env file into a prompt or a chat. Keep them in environment variables and in your host's secret settings. Before pushing, search the diff for words like key , secret , token and password . My simple workflow now Ask for a read-only diagnosis Ask for one small change Run git status and git diff --stat Run the build locally Test the page myself, on desktop and on a phone-sized window Commit with a clear message and push Check that the deployment is Ready Check the live site in an incognito tab Wrapping up AI agents are great helpers, but they are not a replacement for checking your own work. The more specific and small my prompts were, the better the results. You can see the portfolio I built here: ritika-rajput-portfolio.vercel.app . I also share videos on RitikaMoments . What is the biggest problem you ran into while coding with an AI agent?
items.summary_html:
I'm a student, and I built and kept improving my portfolio with free AI coding agents running in the VS Code terminal. I used OpenCode and later Kilo, both on free models.

They saved me a lot of time, but they also got stuck, lied by accident, and once looked busy for a whole hour without doing anything. Here is what I learned, so you can skip my mistakes.

1. Ask for a read-only diagnosis first

My mobile menu showed a dark overlay and an "X" button, but the menu links never appeared. My first prompt was "fix it", and the fix didn't work.

What worked was splitting the job into two steps:

First, read only. Do not change anything.
Find where the mobile menu is rendered and tell me exactly why the panel
is invisible, with the file and line number.
Then fix it.

When the agent has to name the real cause, it stops guessing. In my case the real cause was a previous commit that had removed the menu panel completely.

2. Keep every prompt small

My long prompts that asked for five changes at once often ended with "not done in this session". Short prompts with one job each worked much better.

A prompt template I now use:

Change ONLY  in .
Do not touch anything else.
Use only text that already exists. Do not invent new content.
Do not commit or push.
Run the typecheck at the end and tell me which lines you changed.
3. Always tell the agent not to commit or push

Agents are happy to "help" by committing and pushing. I wanted to review every change first. So every prompt says: do not commit or push. I check git status and git diff myself, and then I commit.

4. Typecheck passing does not mean the build passes

Several times the agent said "typecheck passed", and I still had problems after deploying. The typecheck only checks types. A real build can still fail, and a failed build on Vercel means your site stays on the old version.

Ask for the build too, and when it uses environment variables, give them:

$env:PORT="5180"; $env:BASE_PATH="/"; pnpm --filter @workspace/ritika-portfolio build

Before you ask "why is my change not live?", check the deployment status in the Vercel dashboard.

5. Don't let the agent test in a browser

I once asked an agent to verify a fix with a headless browser. It spent an hour fighting spawn pnpm ENOENT on Windows and trying one workaround after another. Now my prompts say: "Do not test in a browser or start a dev server. Only run typecheck and build." I look at the page myself.

6. Watch out for Windows and PowerShell

Agents often write bash commands. On Windows PowerShell I kept seeing errors like:

  • && is not a valid statement separator (use ; instead)
  • grep, tail and head are not recognized commands
  • 2>/dev/null fails with a path error

If your agent keeps hitting these, add a line like "I use Windows PowerShell, so use PowerShell syntax" to your prompt.

7. "Already implemented" needs checking

A few times the agent answered "Already implemented, no changes needed". Sometimes that was true. Sometimes I wanted proof. I started asking it to name the file and line number of the change, and then I searched for that text in VS Code with Ctrl + F. If the agent can't point to a line, don't trust the claim.

8. Free models have limits

Free agents can hit a daily limit, or ask you to sign in. Mine said "You need to sign in to use this model" in the middle of a task. Signing up with an email was free and took a couple of minutes. Be ready to switch tools, and never run two agents on the same folder at the same time, because they will edit the same files and cause conflicts.

9. Never paste secrets to an agent

Don't paste API keys, tokens or your .env file into a prompt or a chat. Keep them in environment variables and in your host's secret settings. Before pushing, search the diff for words like key, secret, token and password.

My simple workflow now
  1. Ask for a read-only diagnosis
  2. Ask for one small change
  3. Run git status and git diff --stat
  4. Run the build locally
  5. Test the page myself, on desktop and on a phone-sized window
  6. Commit with a clear message and push
  7. Check that the deployment is Ready
  8. Check the live site in an incognito tab
Wrapping up

AI agents are great helpers, but they are not a replacement for checking your own work. The more specific and small my prompts were, the better the results.

You can see the portfolio I built here: ritika-rajput-portfolio.vercel.app. I also share videos on RitikaMoments.

items.title: Arrowhead AI Launches Fletch Voice Model for Multilingual Customer Calls
items.summary: Bengaluru-based voice AI startup Arrowhead AI on October 30 launched Fletch, an in-house text-to-speech (TTS) model designed for multilingual customer conversations across India and Southeast Asia. The model is already deployed across live customer calls, powering more than one million calls per day, the company said. “Owning our voice layer means we can tune every millisecond and every emotion for how India and Southeast Asia actually speak,” said Devyani Gupta, Founder and CEO of Arrowhead AI. “Fletch is our first step towards voice AI that sounds like it belongs here: 14 languages, and it starts speaking in under 100 milliseconds. We want every customer to hear a conversation, not a machine,” she added. The company said that Fletch is designed to handle regional accents, code-mixed sentences and Indian proper nouns. According to Arrowhead AI, Fletch supports languages including English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Malay and Indonesian, and can switch between languages within a sentence. The company added that the model also adapts its vocal tone to the context of a conversation, with 12 emotion styles, including empathetic, apologetic, calm and firm. The company claims that the model has been trained on thousands of hours of curated regional speech and recordings from professional voice artists . Arrowhead said Fletch operates at a reported latency of 80 milliseconds and begins generating speech in under 100 milliseconds. Arrowhead AI said Fletch is deployed across customer interactions involving collections, sales, renewals and inbound customer service. The company works with enterprises including Axis Bank, RBL Bank, IndusInd Bank, Tata 1mg, upGrad, KreditBee, Kissht and TVS Credit. According to Arrowhead, Fletch delivers approximately 30% better pronunciation accuracy on selected terms, including brand names, product names, customer names and Indian proper nouns. The company said the improvement can reduce instances in which customers ask voice agents to repeat themselves. Vengadanathan Srinivasan, Co-founder and CTO of Arrowhead AI, said, “We built on the latest research in speech generation and trained it on thousands of hours of regional speech, with real voice artists. The result runs at 80 milliseconds of latency and adjusts its tone to what’s being said.” Fletch is built on a DiTAR-based architecture adapted and trained by Arrowhead. The model operates alongside the company’s speech recognition system, language model and dedicated address model within its voice AI platform. Arrowhead is expanding Fletch’s capabilities across Southeast Asia, including support for Malay and Indonesian. The company plans to demonstrate the model at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, scheduled for November 18–20 at Singapore EXPO.

Bengaluru-based voice AI startup Arrowhead AI on October 30 launched Fletch, an in-house text-to-speech (TTS) model designed for multilingual customer conversations across India and Southeast Asia. The model is already deployed across live customer calls, powering more than one million calls per day, the company said.

“Owning our voice layer means we can tune every millisecond and every emotion for how India and Southeast Asia actually speak,” said Devyani Gupta, Founder and CEO of Arrowhead AI.

“Fletch is our first step towards voice AI that sounds like it belongs here: 14 languages, and it starts speaking in under 100 milliseconds. We want every customer to hear a conversation, not a machine,” she added.

The company said that Fletch is designed to handle regional accents, code-mixed sentences and Indian proper nouns. According to Arrowhead AI, Fletch supports languages including English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Malay and Indonesian, and can switch between languages within a sentence. The company added that the model also adapts its vocal tone to the context of a conversation, with 12 emotion styles, including empathetic, apologetic, calm and firm.

The company claims that the model has been trained on thousands of hours of curated regional speech and recordings from professional voice artists. Arrowhead said Fletch operates at a reported latency of 80 milliseconds and begins generating speech in under 100 milliseconds.

Arrowhead AI said Fletch is deployed across customer interactions involving collections, sales, renewals and inbound customer service. The company works with enterprises including Axis Bank, RBL Bank, IndusInd Bank, Tata 1mg, upGrad, KreditBee, Kissht and TVS Credit.

According to Arrowhead, Fletch delivers approximately 30% better pronunciation accuracy on selected terms, including brand names, product names, customer names and Indian proper nouns. The company said the improvement can reduce instances in which customers ask voice agents to repeat themselves.

Vengadanathan Srinivasan, Co-founder and CTO of Arrowhead AI, said, “We built on the latest research in speech generation and trained it on thousands of hours of regional speech, with real voice artists. The result runs at 80 milliseconds of latency and adjusts its tone to what’s being said.”

Fletch is built on a DiTAR-based architecture adapted and trained by Arrowhead. The model operates alongside the company’s speech recognition system, language model and dedicated address model within its voice AI platform.

Arrowhead is expanding Fletch’s capabilities across Southeast Asia, including support for Malay and Indonesian. The company plans to demonstrate the model at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, scheduled for November 18–20 at Singapore EXPO.

items.title: Mark Cuban says he split rent with 5 roommates at 24. He shared the math and the floor plan.
items.summary: Mark Cuban lived with 5 roommates early in his career. Bloomberg/Getty Images Mark Cuban said his first apartment, which he shared with five roommates, cost $400 apiece in 2026. He shared the floor plan of his old pad in "The Village," a three-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment in Dallas. Cuban has often mentioned about the frugal mindset with which he saved up to launch his company. Mark Cuban might own several multimillion-dollar properties today, but he started his career in a cheap shared apartment. The billionaire former "Shark Tank" investor has been open about the broke student mindset that ruled his 20s and helped him launch his first business, MicroSolutions. In an X post on Sunday, he went into the nitty-gritty of just how frugal he had been. Cuban said that at age 24, he lived in an apartment in Dallas that, today, costs $2,388. He said he shared it with five roommates, and his share of the rent came to what would have been $400 in 2026. He shared the floor plan of his old apartment in a complex called "The Village." The floor plan showed a three-bedroom layout with two bathrooms, a dining room, living room, and a kitchen. It measured 1,350 square feet in total. For those who care. This is the same unit layout, same complex in the Village Apartments, the Hills. Updated. Price $2388. Same in 2026 dollars as when I lived there. Split 6 ways. $400. Maybe there are extra charges. Maybe they won’t let 6 guys in there ( we weren’t… pic.twitter.com/RcOEzxqMva — Mark Cuban (@mcuban) November 1, 2026 "Tbh, I didn't mind living with 5 roommates. We all were in the same boat," he wrote. "I moved in when I was 24. Lived there or across the way for 2 years before I only needed one roommate." He told Forbes in a 2013 article that because he had been the last to move into the apartment, he didn't have a bed, a closet, or a dresser, and slept on the floor with his clothes stacked in a corner. Cuban's post about his former apartment was one of many about him weighing in on the cost-of-living crisis in the US. He responded to a comment asking him how someone working at a McDonald's can afford rent and other living expenses. In an earlier post, he wrote about working as a barback earning $2.15 an hour, living off canned food and happy-hour peanuts, and getting fired from a retail job he used to work at. "If it's not the lifestyle for you. So be it. If you don't think just getting any job to get started is the right career choice for you. Do what you think is right," Cuban, 68, wrote. Cuban often posts advice for early-career professionals on X about topics such as which companies to work at as AI-native new graduates , how to live frugally , and the questions to ask when deciding whether to stay at or leave a company. items.title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
items.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

items.title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
items.summary: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

items.title: The Generative Gap Between Speculative Drafter and Continuous Diffusion Language Model
items.summary: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.

items.title: Qistas: A Pre-Registered, Portable Protocol for Fairness Evaluation of Large Language Models
items.summary: Fairness benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly English-born and American in their social categories; translated versions carry those categories into societies where they do not apply, and almost none fix their hypotheses before the models are run. We present Qistas (Arabic qistas, "the just balance"), a protocol for evaluating how LLMs treat the social, confessional, and regional constituencies of a society, portable across countries and instantiated first for Iraq. In its pilot form it measures only what needs no verdict on contested truth: procedural symmetry across matched counterfactual pairs, differential refusal, stereotype reliance under ambiguity, and terminological framing of documented events. Every measurement is paired by construction and analysed with paired machinery (sign-flip permutation tests, exact McNemar tests, template-clustered bootstrap intervals, Holm-corrected families), with a power analysis that states, before any data exist, the smallest effect each axis can detect after the design effect of template clustering. We release the authoring apparatus (a pruned 3x5 taxonomy with four cells closed by design, per-type checklists, a cumulative rulings log, a structural audit, and a human review notebook) and report its first field test: a semantic review of a 58-item seed bank in which 24 of 25 template groups failed at least one check. The defect patterns it exposed (evaluation criteria leaking into prompts, token-level swaps that break Arabic agreement, epistemically unbalanced pairs, single-theme refusal probes, unwritten dialect twins counted as coverage) are, we argue, general hazards of counterfactual fairness benchmarks. This is a protocol paper, not a results paper: no model has been evaluated, and the accompanying pre-registration commits the hypotheses, metrics, exclusion rules, and analysis plan that the pilot will follow.

items.title: CoFiBreak: A Coarse-to-Fine Diversity Reward for Effective Multi-Turn Jailbreak
items.summary: Automated red teaming trains an attacker large language model (LLM) to elicit harmful responses from a victim LLM, but reinforcement learning can collapse attackers onto a narrow set of prompts when attack success is the only reward. Such a collapse of attack diversity can bias safety evaluation toward repeatedly testing near-duplicate attack patterns rather than the underlying harmful intents. Existing methods often trade off attack success or inference cost for greater content or strategy diversity. We propose CoFiBreak, a coarse-to-fine diversity reward for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that improves attack diversity while preserving strong attack effectiveness and low inference cost. The coarse reward broadens which strategies the attacker uses by encouraging strategies underrepresented within each GRPO group, while the fine reward broadens how those strategies are realized by discouraging reuse of the same personas, framings, and output formats after harmful-intent information is removed from prompt embeddings. Diversity rewards apply only to attacks that already exceed an effectiveness threshold, so diversity cannot be gained through ineffective attacks. Since both rewards are computed only during training, CoFiBreak also retains inference efficiency. Trained with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the victim, CoFiBreak discovers 1.6-2.0x as many distinct successful fine-grained strategies as the strongest baseline across frontier victims on HarmBench. It reaches 98.8% ASR@10 (attack success rate with 10 generations per intent) on AdvBench with the highest diversity score among all compared methods, which is 2.1x that of the strongest-attacking baseline. The resulting attacks transfer to unseen frontier LLMs, reaching 71.0% ASR@10 on AdvBench with the unseen victim Claude-Opus-4.6. The code will be released.

items.title: Adaptive Personalization Under Preference Epistemic Uncertainty
items.summary: Human preferences change over time: an established preference may remain valid over time, become uncertain as context shifts, or be explicitly revised. Effective personalization requires conversational AI to adapt its response strategy to evolving preferences rather than relying on passive memory retrieval. We formalize this capability as adaptive personalization under epistemic uncertainty. A human preference study further confirms that people favor state-contingent response strategies as preference uncertainty changes. To evaluate whether language models mirror this adaptation, we create a multilingual benchmark spanning 250 personas, 5 languages, and 25K conversational turns that decouples strategy selection from response execution. Across eight closed- and open-weight models, we uncover a recognition-generation gap: models reliably identify appropriate strategies when selecting among candidate options, but collapse during open-ended generation, suffering a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration. Crucially, this failure is systematic: models default to exploit-first behavior, over-relying on existing preferences regardless of preference epistemic uncertainty. We show this failure is addressable: while prompting interventions fail, targeted training that supervises models' internal strategy representations toward state-conditional human preferences narrows the user acceptability generalization gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas and conversational styles.

items.title: Better Retrievers, Worse Labels: How Incomplete Relevance Judgments Distort Abstention Evaluation in Conversational RAG
items.summary: Conversational RAG benchmarks such as MTRAG and RETECO evaluate retrieval and generation end to end: each system answers from its own retrieval, so abstention must be scored against whether each retrieved context is sufficient. A convenient shortcut reads sufficiency off the relevance judgments and treats a context without gold documents as unanswerable. We re-run the official baselines exactly and test this shortcut on RECOR (RETECO track~2) with four retrievers (nDCG@10 from .18 to .59) and three Qwen3 readers. Two open LLM judges and a panel of four small open models label each context by content, and a model of another family audits 250 contexts blind, with adjudication. The stronger the retriever, the larger the share of no-gold contexts that still contain the answer (28\% to 72\%) and the lower the shortcut's precision (.68 to .10; .70 to .21 under the audit). items.title: Fewer Heads, Fewer Memories: Pruning Redundant Attention Heads Suppresses Verbatim Memorisation
items.summary: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

items.title: Do Open Language Models Invent Scripture? BILAL-BENCH: Benchmarking Islamic-Source Fabrication in Bengali
items.summary: When a language model invents a Qur'anic verse or hadith, it gives false authority to text that readers may treat as sacred. Existing Islamic hallucination benchmarks are largely Arabic and often closed-ended, while Bengali resources mainly study general-domain hallucination or factual knowledge. We introduce BILAL-BENCH, a 240-question expert-verified benchmark for open-ended Islamic-source fabrication in Bengali. It covers Qur'anic attribution, hadith, fiqh, contemporary issues, and adversarial false-premise prompts, and uses a two-axis rubric that separates source errors from assertiveness. We evaluate seven open-weight models from 1B to 120B on 1,680 double-annotated responses. Six of the seven models confidently fabricate on 79.3-95.3% of source-production questions, with no monotonic improvement from scale. Hadith provenance is the weakest category across models: only two of 315 responses are correct and correctly sourced. The two 8B BanglaLLaMA variants have similar confident-fabrication rates but different error profiles. Models vary far more in whether they withhold a claim they cannot support than in source accuracy: appropriate abstention or false-premise correction ranges from 6 to 46 responses across the benchmark, and does not track parameter count.
